problems.name: Mama ji
problems.line: test[9], to you: 'Full fit! Amma ne dawai li? Didi kaisi hain? Pakka?' | 'फ़ुल फ़िट! अम्मा ने दवाई ली? दीदी कैसी हैं? पक्का?'
problems.problem: Rules 8 and 66. This line is said to the player. 'Didi, kaisi hain?' with a comma is how you ask an elder sister 'how are you'. Spoken aloud, or with a misplaced comma, it can read as Mama ji calling the player Didi, and the feminine कैसी then gives the player a gender. The file says the verb settles it, but this particular verb is the one that does the harm.
problems.fix: Name Mummy the way he would to the child of the house: 'Full fit! Amma ne dawai li? Tumhari Mummy kaisi hain? Pakka?' | 'फ़ुल फ़िट! अम्मा ने दवाई ली? तुम्हारी मम्मी कैसी हैं? पक्का?' | 'Fighting fit! Has Amma had her medicines? How's your Mummy? Sure?' (9 counted words). 'Didi ki dukaan' in test[8] is a possessive and can stay.

problems.name: Nani
problems.line: samples[16]: 'Koi party nahin. Jab sab phir aayein.' | 'कोई पार्टी नहीं। जब सब फिर आएँ।'
problems.problem: The Hindi is unfinished. 'जब सब फिर आएँ।' is a when-clause with nothing after it ('when everyone comes again...'), so it does not say the English 'not till everyone comes again'.
problems.fix: 'Koi party nahin. Sab phir aayein, tab.' | 'कोई पार्टी नहीं। सब फिर आएँ, तब।' | 'No party. Not till everyone comes again.' (7 words)

problems.name: Mama ji
problems.line: samples[15]: 'Kursiyaan kam padin toh log khade-khade, khaana jaldi niptega.' | 'कुर्सियाँ कम पड़ीं तो लोग खड़े-खड़े, खाना जल्दी निपटेगा।'
problems.problem: A verb is missing after 'log khade-khade' (people... standing), so the joke reads as broken Hindi, not as his run-on.
problems.fix: 'Kursiyaan kam padin toh log khade-khade khaayenge. Jaldi niptega!' | 'कुर्सियाँ कम पड़ीं तो लोग खड़े-खड़े खाएँगे। जल्दी निपटेगा!' (9 words)

problems.name: Cast (Tinku, Mausi, Papa, Mummy, Mausa ji, Mama ji)
problems.line: Pasts with ने where the player did the deed: Tinku samples[11] 'Tumne bahut kiya.' and samples[18] 'Kal raat ki dawai tumne sambhali.'; Mausi samples[5] 'Pichhle saal tumne kaha tha', samples[8] 'Kuch khaya bhi?', typing[1] 'khana khaya??'; Papa samples[8] 'Is saal chaar baar gaadi pakdi', samples[21] 'Achha kiya'; Mummy samples[12] 'Bahut achha kiya'; Mausa ji samples[9] 'Achha kiya'; Mama ji samples[6] 'Poora week inhone chalaya'
problems.problem: Rule 66 wording. None of these lines marks a gender, because the verb agrees with the thing done. But rule 66 allows तुम in only three shapes: commands, 'who should' asks, and lines where the player is not the doer. In every line here the player is the doer. The files clear them as 'a ने past', and the rule does not name that shape.
problems.fix: Ask the owner either to add 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' to rule 66 as a fourth shape, or to have the native reader clear each line and put it on the build's cleared list. No wording change is needed if the owner agrees.

problems.name: Mami
problems.line: samples[20], taking a report (rule 22): 'Mujhe yakeen hai. Bolo, kya likhoon?' | 'मुझे यक़ीन है। बोलो, क्या लिखूँ?'
problems.problem: Rule 22, consistency across files. Mami believes first, which is right. But the player's file fences writing and proof words ('likhit', 'in writing') away from any report beat, and Tinku's file bans 'Kitaab mein.' after a report. A pen raised straight after a report can read as wanting it on paper.
problems.fix: Keep the belief and turn the list habit into action: 'Mujhe yakeen hai. Bolo, ab kya karna hai?' | 'मुझे यक़ीन है। बोलो, अब क्या करना है?' | 'I believe you. Tell me, what do we do now?' (8 words; करना है marks no gender). Or have a reader confirm the current line reads as help.

problems.name: Mausa ji
problems.line: samples[10] and test[6]: 'Hmm. Isme kya.' | 'हम्म। इसमें क्या।'
problems.problem: The same brush-off appears in four voices: Mummy (her file's thanks-received line, and test[6] 'Arre Jija ji, isme kya.'), Nani samples[9], Mama ji test[6] and Mausa ji. In test moment 7 three of the eleven answers share the words, and Masterji's 'Isme kaunsi badi baat hai' makes a fourth. The player's file treats it as the elders' shared line, but moment 7 is now the weakest moment in the test set.
problems.fix: Give it to one owner, Mummy, whose file names it. Mausa ji: just 'Hmm.' | 'हम्म।' | 'Hmm.' as he stands and leaves. That fits his two-blunt-words shape, and the readers' complaint about 'Kaam tha' stays answered.

problems.name: Nani
problems.line: samples[9], to Mami: 'Arre, isme kya. Ghee poora daaliye.' | 'अरे, इसमें क्या। घी पूरा डालिए।'
problems.problem: This is Mummy's thanks-received line word for word (see the Mausa ji entry). Nani already has her own brush-off, the echo word in test[6].
problems.fix: 'Thank you-vank you rehne dijiye. Ghee poora daaliye.' | 'थैंक यू-वैंक यू रहने दीजिए। घी पूरा डालिए।' | 'None of your thank-yous. Don't skimp on the ghee.' (8 words; आप to Mami kept)

problems.name: Mama ji
problems.line: test[6]: 'Arre, isme kya! Credit Jija ji ka, Boss ka, sabka!' | 'अरे, इसमें क्या! सारा काम जीजा जी का, बॉस का, सबका!'
problems.problem: Mummy's brush-off again, in the same test moment as hers. The Hindi also drifts from the Hinglish ('Credit' becomes 'सारा काम').
problems.fix: Open on his own exclamation: 'Oho, no no! Credit Jija ji ka, Boss ka, sabka!' | 'ओहो, ना ना! क्रेडिट जीजा जी का, बॉस का, सबका!' | 'Oho, no no! Credit's Jija ji's, and Boss's, everyone's!' (8 words)

problems.name: You
problems.line: test[6], to Mami: 'Arre Mami, kis baat ka? Pehle Mausa ji ko boliye.' | 'अरे मामी, किस बात का? पहले मौसा जी को बोलिए।'
problems.problem: Same moment, same words and same move as Captain sahab test[6] ('Kis baat ka, Scorer?' with the credit sent elsewhere). Two voices sound alike in the test set. The 'Arre' also takes Captain sahab's word (matrix 2.15).
problems.fix: 'Mami, mujhe nahin. Pehle Mausa ji ko boliye.' | 'मामी, मुझे नहीं। पहले मौसा जी को बोलिए।' | 'Not me, Mami. Thank Mausa ji first.' (5 words; मुझे marks no gender; keeps the player's 'Pehle ___')

problems.name: Nani
problems.line: test[5], on the platform to Mama ji: 'Chhote. Khush raho. Pahunchkar phone zaroor karna.' | 'छोटे। ख़ुश रहो। पहुँचकर फ़ोन ज़रूर करना।'
problems.problem: 'Pahunchkar phone karna' is Mummy's love line ('the line every mother says on a platform'), and Mummy says it in the same test moment.
problems.fix: Put it in Nani's order gear, as a closed fragment: 'Chhote. Khush raho. Pahunchte hi phone.' | 'छोटे। ख़ुश रहो। पहुँचते ही फ़ोन।' | 'Stay happy. Phone the minute you arrive.' (5 words)

problems.name: Papa
problems.line: samples[21], thanking you: 'Achha kiya. / Wo list ab tumhari hai.' | 'अच्छा किया। / वो लिस्ट अब तुम्हारी है।'
problems.problem: Three people now thank the player with the same words: Papa 'Achha kiya.', Mausa ji 'Achha kiya.' and Mummy 'Bahut achha kiya.' (Mausi also says 'Bahut achha kiya' to Aji). Papa's own thanks shape in the matrix is the deed logged ('6:00, gate par. Noted.'), and that is gone.
problems.fix: 'Raat bhar, list ke saath. Darj hai. / Wo list ab tumhari hai.' | 'रात भर, लिस्ट के साथ। दर्ज है। / वो लिस्ट अब तुम्हारी है।' | 'All night, with the list. Noted. / That list is yours now.' (no verb about you). Optionally, Mausa ji samples[9] becomes 'Hmm. Baitho.' | 'हम्म। बैठो।' | 'Hmm. Sit.' as he clears the chair.

problems.name: Papa
problems.line: test[6]: 'Arre, roz ka kaam hai. / Ab wapsi ka ticket dekhta hoon.'
problems.problem: In moment 7 this opens on 'Arre', as Mummy's line does. The matrix gives 'arre' to Captain sahab.
problems.fix: Drop it: 'Roz ka kaam hai. / Ab wapsi ka ticket dekhta hoon.' | 'रोज़ का काम है। / अब वापसी का टिकट देखता हूँ।'

problems.name: Mausi
problems.line: test[8]: 'Gali mein nadi? Arre, copiyan upar! Chalo, chalo!' | 'गली में नदी? अरे, कॉपियाँ ऊपर! चलो, चलो!'
problems.problem: Here 'Arre' works as an exclamation, and matrix 2.15 takes 'arre' out of Mausi's mouth for Captain sahab. (As a filler, 'arre' opens lines for ten of the eleven people, which is real speech and fine.)
problems.fix: Use her own word: 'Gali mein nadi? Haay! Copiyan upar! Chalo, chalo!' | 'गली में नदी? हाय! कॉपियाँ ऊपर! चलो, चलो!' (8 words; the English can stay as it is)

problems.name: Mausa ji
problems.line: samples[0], 2.03, to Nani: 'Amma ji, poori gali aayi hai.' | 'अम्मा जी, पूरी गली आई है।'
problems.problem: In the same beat Nani says to you 'Meri poori gali aayi hai.' Two people say the same sentence back to back, and his is a full subject-verb sentence, which is not his shape.
problems.fix: 'Amma ji, bahar poori gali.' | 'अम्मा जी, बाहर पूरी गली।' | 'Amma ji, the whole lane's outside.' (his bare state of a thing)

problems.name: Papa
problems.line: samples[2]: 'Ab checker aayega.' | 'अब चेकर आएगा।' (also address[0] 'चेकर के लिए टिकट कौन रखे?')
problems.problem: A railwayman would say TT (or TTE), not 'checker'. 'Checker' is an outsider's word, and Papa's source is the railway.
problems.fix: 'Ab TT aayega.' | 'अब टीटी आएगा।' | 'The TT comes next.'; also 'टीटी के लिए टिकट कौन रखे?'

problems.name: Mummy
problems.line: test[4], to the family with elders present: 'Chalo, ye mere khaate mein daal do.' | 'चलो, ये मेरे खाते में डाल दो।'
problems.problem: Politeness. Her own file says that to elders it is 'mere khaate mein daaliye'. Here she says the तुम form to a group that includes Nani and other elders.
problems.fix: Drop the verb so no level is needed: 'Achha? Meri galti. / Chalo, ye mere khaate mein.' | 'अच्छा? मेरी ग़लती। / चलो, ये मेरे खाते में।'

problems.name: Mami
problems.line: test[5], at the coach door: 'Ticket, tiffin, done. Jaldi aana.' | 'टिकट, टिफ़िन, सब रख दिया। जल्दी आना।'
problems.problem: Tinku's answer to the same moment opens 'Jaldi aana, yaar.', so the two goodbyes share their words. This is minor.
problems.fix: End on her status shape: 'Ticket, tiffin, done. Agli visit: pending.' | 'टिकट, टिफ़िन, सब रख दिया। अगली बार कब?' | 'Ticket, tiffin, done. Next visit: pending.'

problems.name: Mausi and Masterji (typed)
problems.problem: Rule 62. If a message card is held to the 10-word bubble cap, these are over it. The rulebook does not yet say whether a message card counts as a spoken line or as sign words.
problems.fix: Ask the owner. If the cap applies, split each message at her '....' or his '..' into separate cards of 10 words or fewer. Mausi typing[0], for example: 'suno suno suno....kal raat wali train....' / 'tum bhi saath ho na??' / 'apni baatein seedha mujhe batana....tumhari mummy se nahi 😊'

problems.name: Papa
problems.line: voice.exclamation example: 'Kal ki gaadi ka ticket aaj raat book kiya? Kamaal hai.'
problems.problem: In the prose example the whole thing is one quoted bubble of 11 counted words. samples[5] rightly splits it in two.
problems.fix: Write it as two bubbles: 'Kal ki gaadi ka ticket aaj raat book kiya? / Kamaal hai.'

problems.name: Masterji
problems.line: samples[5]: 'Ab toh aap incharge hain.'
problems.problem: The spelling does not match the rest of the cast, where every other file writes 'in-charge'.
problems.fix: 'Ab toh aap in-charge hain.'

problems.name: Mausi and Masterji (address tables)
problems.line: Mausi voice.address[10]: 'Masterji: Behenji'; Masterji voice.address[5]: 'Mausi: Mausi ji'
problems.problem: The two files disagree on what Masterji calls Mausi.
problems.fix: Pick one and use it in both files. 'Behenji' is what a neighbour of 60 would say to a schoolteacher of 55; 'Mausi ji' borrows the household's word.

problems.name: Mausa ji and You (thanks note)
problems.line: Mausa ji changed[]: 'your thanks to him is now Thank you, Mausa ji. in Hinglish (शुक्रिया in Hindi mode)'; You samples[13] HI: 'थैंक यू, मौसा जी।'
problems.problem: The two files disagree. The player's file uses थैंक यू in Hindi mode and keeps शुक्रिया for strangers.
problems.fix: Change Mausa ji's note to थैंक यू, so both files follow the player's rule.

problems.name: Nani
problems.line: typing[0]: HI 'अस्सीवां। मई। सब आएं।' | EN 'My eightieth. May. Everyone's coming.'
problems.problem: The English does not match the Hindi. सब आएँ is an order (everyone must come), which is the more Nani reading. The spelling also mixes forms: the file's other lines use ँ, this one uses ं.
problems.fix: EN 'My eightieth. May. Everyone, come.'; HI 'अस्सीवाँ। मई। सब आएँ।', unless the voice-typed look is meant on purpose.

problems.name: Tinku
problems.line: samples[7] EN: 'Your one trial again, Captain sahab? Eleven times this season.'
problems.problem: 'Your one trial again' is odd English for 'Phir wahi trial'.
problems.fix: 'That one trial again, Captain sahab? Eleven times this season.'

clean: The checker is /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-priyanshu-Sex-Ed/f50ea7ee-0855-46a2-8572-0aa08df5b855/scratchpad/voice/check2/check.py; run it with python3 -I check.py. It writes /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-priyanshu-Sex-Ed/f50ea7ee-0855-46a2-8572-0aa08df5b855/scratchpad/voice/check2/report.txt and report.json. /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-priyanshu-Sex-Ed/f50ea7ee-0855-46a2-8572-0aa08df5b855/scratchpad/voice/check2/dump.py prints one person's lines with their flags for reading. It read 5,824 quoted lines and 4,082 bubbles across the 11 files.

Rule 66, by and to the player: the script flagged 334 lines that are by, to or about the player. I read every one and all clear: the word agrees with a noun (गली आई, याद आई, दवाई सँभाली), is the speaker's own gender (Nani's जा रही, Tinku's लिखूँगी, Mama ji's भेज रहा हूँ), is a 'who should' subjunctive (कौन जाए, किसे रखें) or is an infinitive or -ओ command (आना, करना, सो जाओ). No gendered future, participle or bare past for the player appears anywhere. The player's own 30 samples, 12 typed lines and 12 test lines are fully clean.

Rules 8 and 66, address words: nobody calls the player beta, bhaiya, didi or a pet name. The words used are 'yaar' (Tinku), the role 'In-charge' (Mama ji, Masterji), 'Front foot' (Captain sahab) or no word at all. Every 'Didi', 'Bhai sahab', 'Beti' and 'Bhaiya ji' hit refers to another person (Mummy, Papa, Mami's daughter, a vendor). The one risky case is in the problems (Mama ji test[9]). No English line gives the player he or she.

Rule 62: no spoken or test bubble is over 10 counted words. Many sit exactly at 10 (Papa test[2], [10]; Mausi samples[2], [5], [18], test[2], [3], [5]; Masterji samples[20], [27], test[0], [5], [11]; Mama ji test[2], [8]; Mami test[7]), so any edit to those must not add a word. All the suggested fixes are 10 words or fewer.

Rule 3: no religious word or exclamation appears in any spoken, typed or test line. Banned words such as 'Hai Ram', 'Shukar hai', 'Waheguru', 'ख़ुदा का ग़ज़ब' and 'Arre Ram' appear only in never lists and guard notes that name them as banned. The blessings 'Khush raho', 'Sukhi raho' and 'Jeeti raho' call on no one.

Rule 3: no caste or caste-trade word appears anywhere (Masterji is never called darzi). No brand appears in any line. 'WhatsApp uncle' appears once, in Captain sahab's typing note as a trap to avoid, never on screen. 'Ghadi' is the clock.

House style: no em dash, en dash, spaced hyphen or double hyphen in any of the 11 files. No American spelling in any English line or in the prose ('meter' is the electricity meter, which is British too).

Politeness: every younger-to-elder line uses आप and -इए or has no verb. The script's 7 politeness hits are false (सो जाइए, सब सुना, सबको). Spouses use तुम as the files intend. Nani's आप to her son-in-law and daughter-in-law, until the December switch to तुम, is deliberate and natural.

Rule 22: the belief lines (Nani 'Mujhe yakeen hai. Poori baat batao.', Mama ji 'Didi, main aa raha hoon. Abhi.', Mami) believe at once. Nani's weighing sayings, Captain sahab's proof line and Tinku's 'Kitaab mein.' are all fenced away from report beats.

Sayings and idioms are real ones a Hindi-first reader knows: डंडी मारना, दूध का दूध पानी का पानी, बूँद-बूँद से घड़ा भरता है, राई का पहाड़, तोल-मोल के बोलो, पानी सिर से ऊपर, बाल की खाल निकालना, बखिया उधेड़ना, मुँह फुलाना, बत्ती गुल, ऐन वक़्त, रास्ता देखना, खाते में डालना, आज नक़द कल उधार (clipped to 'Udhaar? Kal.'), अच्छे-अच्छे आउट होते हैं, and Mausi's traditional riddle 'एक थाल मोती से भरा, सबके सिर पर औंधा धरा'. Papa's Tamil count (naalu, anju, aaru) is correct.

Clean apart from the shared-phrase and cross-file notes above: Mummy, Tinku, Captain sahab and Masterji read as natural, distinct Hindi, with trade words in the right place (काज, थान, सदरी, अस्तर, तिरपाल, गोटी, चार्ट बन चुका, गाड़ी लगना).

notes.name: Nani
true_lines: 'Saare kaam. Dandi mat maarna.' A real grocer's idiom that every north Indian reader knows, used for the job it really means.
'Mujhse poochhiye. Beemar hoon, behri nahin.' Sharp, polite even when she is cross, and exactly how an 80-year-old talks to a doctor who talks over her head.
'Achha? Agle hafte? Pichhle hafte bhi yahi kaha tha.' and 'Rehne do ye thank you-vank you.' These are the real sly, everyday voice of a nani.
'Bori upar. Chappal upar. Bachche andar.' and 'Paani hi toh hai. Ghee nahin.' The counter's habits come out in a flood and in comfort, and they stay warm.
'Khush raho. Pahunchkar phone zaroor karna.' with her palm on his head. A real blessing with no religious word in it, and her warmth said out loud.
Her voice typing ('Bahut phone ho gaye. Ab aa jao.', 'Haan, subah ho gayi.') and the September voice note where she rambles. This is how a real 80-year-old uses a phone.
The sayings (raai ka pahaad, doodh ka doodh, boond-boond, tol-mol ke bolo) are all real, and each is fenced off from any report.
problems: She gives orders to 'koi' in the subjunctive: 'Koi torch laaye.', 'Koi kapda laaye.', 'Koi pakde.' In a real house it is the plural command: 'Koi torch lao.', 'Arre, koi kapda lao.' The command marks no gender either, so rule 66 still holds. As written, a Hindi-first reader hears a wish ('may someone bring') instead of a grandmother's order, and it reads like a device.

Her rule 22 line 'Mujhe yakeen hai. Poori baat batao.' opens with the same formula as Mami's 'Mujhe yakeen hai. Bolo, kya likhoon?'. Said aloud to a granddaughter or grandson, 'I believe you' sounds like a counsellor or POSH training, not a nani (see the cast-wide note). Belief should show by going straight to the person and the facts, with no doubt in it: 'Idhar aao. Poori baat batao.'

notes.name: Mummy
true_lines: 'Haan ji, boliye.' to her own children on the phone, then 'Achha, tum!'. Every small-town shop owner does this, and it is her best tell.
'Tinku ji, nau baj gaye. Aap kahaan hain?' and 'Chhote ji, aap hi chala lijiye. Chaabi ye rahi.' Her anger comes out as rising politeness, which is very real.
'Main hi hoon. Boliye, delivery kab?' to the wholesaler's man who asks for the owner. A woman who runs her own counter, with no speech about it.
'Bhindi itni mehngi? Kal se sabzi main laaungi.', 'Letter bhejo, counter pe lagaungi.' and 'Amma aapka raasta dekhte-dekhte so gayin.'
'Torch, charger, extension, sab bag mein hai. / Pahunchkar phone karna.' Love as a packed bag, with the line every mother says on a platform.
Her typing: lowercase, commas only, 'haan ji' as the whole reply, 'khud kab aa rahe'.
problems: 'Mere khaate mein daal do / daaliye' is offered as an idiom for taking the blame, but in real speech it is mostly the sulky 'go on, blame me then' ('haan haan, sab mere khaate mein daal do'). Coming straight after 'Achha? Meri galti.' in moment 5, 'Chalo, ye mere khaate mein daal do.' reads as sarcasm. 'Masterji, kal raat ki zid, mere khaate mein daaliye.' reads as a coined apology. Use plain words: 'Masterji, kal raat ki zid meri galti thi.' Keep 'khaata' for her real credit book.

Hinglish 'Le jaiye ji. Credit book mein likh diya, aaram se.' sounds translated. In Latin letters a small-town shop says 'khaate mein likh diya' too, so Hinglish should say khaata, as the Hindi already does.

Minor: 'Tinku, ye cup return karo.' is a writer's joke given to the one person who never jokes, and it is the line the blind sort will remember her by. 'MCB check karo' is natural in an electrician's house; the tea cup is a gimmick. 'Cheeni kam, dobara banao.' keeps her list shape without it.

notes.name: Papa
true_lines: 'Kripya dhyan dein. Dal platform number ek par aa chuki hai.' Every Indian player will hear the station loudspeaker, and it is funny at nobody's cost.
'Reached?' as his only love word by text, and the 6:35 good-morning flower. This is the real Indian father.
'Batti das baje bujhegi.', 'Nahin. Chart ban chuka hai.' and 'Gaadi lag gayi hai.' Real railway Hindi with Hindi verbs.
'Kis din pahunchna hai? Ticket main book kar deta hoon.' He shows love as a booking made ahead, exactly as fathers do.
'Suno,' to Mummy, the way couples who use no first names really talk.
'Pata nahin, Tinku. Dal andaaze se banti hai.' The man of minutes, once, about the one thing he never times.
problems: '9:40 mera time tha. / Galat nikla.' still sounds translated in Hinglish and Hindi. 'मेरा टाइम था' is heard as 'it was my turn' or 'my era'. Only the English was fixed. Say it the way people do: 'Maine 9:40 kaha tha. Galat nikla.' This is his own past with ne, so nothing marks the player.

'Mere father maal gaadi ke guard the.' is the default-mode line, said to his 80-year-old Hindi-first mother-in-law. A 56-year-old railway-colony man says 'mere pitaji' or 'babuji' to her, not 'father'. 'Pitaji' is plain everyday Hindi with no lean to any community. Holding it back as possibly leaning is the common-word ban the brief warns against. Use 'Mere pitaji' in Hinglish as well.

'Dhanyavaad.' as his spoken thanks to strangers and the ticket checker is announcement Hindi. In a person's mouth it reads Sanskritised, which is exactly what makes P2 Ravi quit. 'Thank you, ji.' says the same and stays his by his whole-sentence shape.

notes.name: Mama ji
true_lines: 'Aa gaye, bhai? Ghar mein sab theek? Achha. Tent. Abhi.' He asks after the family first, even when cross, then the chop. It is word-perfect.
'Kursiyaan kam padin toh log khade-khade, khaana jaldi niptega.' and 'Jija ji, ekdum mithai! Thodi aur dijiye. Boss ko mat bataiye.' Big, kind jokes at himself.
'Boss' for his wife, 'Didi!!', 'ok ok call me' and 'DISTRICT LEVEL!! 🎉🎉'. This is the real city uncle on WhatsApp.
'Naukri lagi? Ab promotion, phir aur upar, phir sabse upar!' and 'Gali mein sabko bataiye, mithai meri taraf se!'
'Didi, main aa raha hoon. Abhi. / Aap unke saath rahiye.' This is how belief really sounds: he acts at once, with no question back.
'Aaj poora ghar tumne sambhala. Maine dekha. Thank you.' and 'Main wahan nahi tha, Boss. Phir se.'
problems: 'Amma, aapko roz miss kiya.' is a little off. A city son says 'Amma, aapko bahut miss kiya.' The line bends only because 'bahut' was given to Mausi. 'Bahut' is the commonest word in the language. Let Mausi keep her phrase 'bahut yaad aayi' and give him back 'bahut'.

'Haan, Didi! Just checking in, kuch khaas nahi.' 'Just checking in' is American office English. An Indian city man ringing his sister says 'Bas aise hi phone kiya', which the Hindi mode already has. Use it in Hinglish too, or 'Bas yaad aa gayi.'

notes.name: Tinku
true_lines: 'Gazab! Batti gul, khel band.' It is quick, sounds like UP, and suits a commentator.
'Main? Papa aaj 4 baar tok chuke. Record.' She dodges a question about herself, and it is in character.
'Jaldi aana, yaar. Main din ginungi.' Her counting turns into tenderness through a real idiom, and 'yaar' marks no gender.
'Mausi, 4 chammach? Sabko sugar ho jaayegi, haan?' and 'Mummy, wo dukaan is saal 3 baar "band" ho chuki hai.'
'Papa, please, not now. Exam ki baat baad mein.' and 'Mama ji, seriously? Phir se "sabse chhoti"?' A real 21-year-old at home, cheeky but still using aap.
'80, not out, Nani.', a real birthday line, said once.
Her typing ('oye / mama ji called u again / 3 today / 3-0 to u lol', 'mausi ka voice note / 2x pe bhi khatam nahi 😂'), and switching to Devanagari for Nani.
problems: Minor: 'Mera wicket, Captain sahab.' as a sorry and 'Run aapka, Captain sahab.' as thanks are coined cricket codes. No one says 'my wicket' to mean sorry. They are fenced to Captain sahab at once a chapter, so the harm is small. If a Hindi-first reader stalls on them, 'Galti meri, Captain sahab.' is the fix.

notes.name: Mausi
true_lines: 'Haay! Bahut yaad aayi.' with her arms wide. Spelling it 'Haay' instead of the film's 'Haaye' keeps her out of the Punjabi screen aunty.
'Rishta main laayi thi. Berth bhi main laaun?' This is her best line, and it is true to every elder sister who arranged a marriage.
'Kaisi hoon? Batati hoon! Ghutna dukhta hai, dil nahin!'
'Chehre pe thakaan! Kuch khaya bhi? Nahin? Pehle khao!' She asks a question and answers it herself, which is a real shape, not a tic.
'Haan, awaaz oonchi hai! Meri class aise hi sunti hai.' She laughs first, so the joke is never on her.
The riddle 'ek thaal moti se bhara, sabke sir par aundha dhara' is a real children's paheli. The '....' typing with 😊 and 'khana khaya?? kya kya khaya??' are exactly right.
problems: The schoolroom has become her stamp. In the test set alone there are 'Late mark! Kaan pakdo!' (2), 'Aaj teacher fail' (5), 'meri class ka inaam' (8) and 'copiyan upar' (9), and the samples add 'first class', 'topper' and 'meri class'. One source in a third of her lines tips into the 'teacher aunty' gimmick. Move one or two, such as the flood line, to her other source, the kitchen and her exact memory of what people said. The flood could be 'Gali mein nadi? Achaar ke martbaan upar! Chalo, chalo!'.

Minor, for the readers: 'Aji' with aap to her husband is real, but it is the 1970s film wife. Many 55-year-old small-town teachers say 'Suniye' or nothing at all. If the Hindi-first readers hear the film in it, her shape still marks her without it.

notes.name: Mausa ji
true_lines: 'Lo. Aadha.' with half a sweet lime set down. 'So jao.', and 'Hmm. Ho jayega.' He is blunt in words and soft in deeds, the strongest device in the cast.
'Ji. Drip theek hai?' said standing to the night nurse, and 'Waqt lagega. Amma ji mazboot hain.'
'Haath dho lo. Garam karta hoon.' to the latecomer. He scolds no one, does the next job and warms the food himself.
'Cheeni zyada hai, Tinku. Chalega.' His kind word for a thing that is not quite right.
'Load zyada. Line trip ho gayi.' and 'Hain? Sach? Light jalaata hoon.' This is a lineman's talk and a lineman's joy.
The single missed call for 'reached', and 'Ok.' an hour late. This is the real phone of a man of 58.
problems: No line needs fixing. One leftover ban on a common word remains: his never list bars 'pakka' because 'पक्की' said of a woman can mean shrewd. 'Pakka' is one of the commonest words in Hindi. He speaks so little that it costs nothing to drop the ban, and keeping it goes against the brief.

notes.name: Masterji
true_lines: 'Bas abhi.', which means an hour, and he blames the trains. Every player has a tailor who says it.
'Bhai sahab, cheeni ungli bhar zyada. Kapda hota, kaat deta.' A measure by feel and a kind joke, in a single bubble.
'Apni sadri jaisa. Astar naya, kapda wahi purana.' His answer to 'how are you', said sideways, as the brief wanted.
'Geela kapda sookh jaata hai, Bhabhi ji. / Fikr phate ki hoti hai.' A picture any Hindi-first reader follows at once.
'Dekhiye, kaaj meri gharwali ke haath ke hain. / Main bas kaatta hoon. Baareek kaam unka.' He gives his wife the credit, with no speech about it.
'Kurta phone par nahin silta.', 'Sunkar achha laga. Ab toh nayi kameez banti hai.' and 'Rehne do, daro mat. Paani ka daag nahin padta.'

His real trade idioms (paani sir se upar, bakhiya udhedna, baal ki khaal), one to a run, and 'Sukhi raho' to the player, where सुखी never changes with gender. His typing ('trial kal shaam ji.. hawa me nami h') is exactly right.
problems: No remaining real problem. The whimsy is now rationed, the coined sayings are gone, and the town's Urdu-rooted words no longer mark him alone.

notes.name: Captain sahab
true_lines: 'Straight bat. Front foot.' as his hello to every child he coached, and 'Happy birthday front foot' typed.
'Arre waah. Clean catch.' said quietly, to nobody.
'Retired hurt. Sirf ghutna.' and 'Purana model hoon, Scorer. Parts nahin milte.' Bone-dry jokes about his own age, in depot words.
'Next ball, Bhabhi ji. Shutter kal bhi uthega.' His one coded comfort, and it lands.
'Ab aaye? Catch bhi aise hi chhoota tha.', 'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Achhe-achhe out hote hain.' and 'Badi meherbani, Lineman sahab.'

He calls people by their trade (Master, Lineman sahab, Madam ji), which is a real habit of a lane elder. His telegram typing ('Route clear', 'Scorer chair in shade bring book') is the real retired uncle.
problems: 'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin.' is still in his uses. It is a coined maxim, and it is a demand for proof, the one screenshot A2 is waiting for ('the family wants proof'). Fencing it to harmless rumours does not protect a one-line clip. Cut it. His moment 8 line 'Not out, Bhabhi ji. Subah bhatti jal rahi thi.' already does the same job without it.

He collides with You in the blind sort. In moment 7 both answer thanks with 'Kis baat ka?' ('Kis baat ka, Scorer?' and 'Arre Mami, kis baat ka?'), and both call Tinku 'Scorer' all through. 'Kis baat ka' is everyone's phrase, and Scorer fits his habit of naming people by trade, so the fix belongs on You's side (see You).

notes.name: Mami
true_lines: 'Bhaiya ji, beti ka paper kaisa gaya?' She asks every vendor about their children, and it is quietly about her own daughter.
'Ghar mein thank you nahin chalta.' This is the real brush-off in an Indian house.
'Aur mehmaan? Approved. Extra thaaliyan tum dhona.' and 'Saare cook booked the. Tumhara aa gaya. Maan gayi.' Sly and fond, aimed at her husband.
'Congratulations. Joining kab se? Somvaar? Bahut achha.' and 'Ticket, tiffin, done. Jaldi aana.' The desk finishes its line, then the home voice speaks.
'Arre, baitho. Fikr mat karo. Mummy ji ka BP normal hai. / Maine khud poochha.'
The ✅ ⏳ ❓ lists, the 'Beti ka bag' line she never ticks, and a single ✅ under Papa's flower every morning.
problems: Moment 11, said to a child who has spilt water: 'Papers, safe. Glass, safe. Tumhari aasteen geeli hai?'. The desk voice comes into a home moment, which her own file forbids, and the child is checked after the papers. The file means the order as a joke, but on the page it reads cold. Put the child first: 'Ish. Aasteen geeli hui? Papers main utha leti hoon.'

The joke about her husband appears three times in one frame: 'Tumhare Mama ji: still pending.', 'Tumhare Mama ji ka dinner: still in progress.' and 'Tumhare Mama ji ki ginti: still growing.'. By the third, she is a one-joke character. Keep one, the 'still pending' one, and let the other two moments stop at the plain line.

'Ish.' in Hindi mode: many Hindi-first players will hear the coy 'इश्श' of old films whatever the context, so even 'इश्श। बच्चे का बुख़ार उतरा?' may land wrong. This is already a reader check. Have the fallback 'Ajeeb.' ready for Hindi mode at least, and keep 'Ish' in Hinglish and English, where the Bengali sense survives.

notes.name: You
true_lines: 'Papa, zara dikhaiye.' at every hand-over. The 'zara' makes it a real polite ask from a young person to an elder.
'Torch main laaun?' and 'Ticket main book kar doon?' Offers in the subjunctive, which mark no gender and are exactly how you speak to elders.
'Mama ji. Pehle Nani se miliye.' Anger on someone else's behalf, with the name standing alone.
'Mummy, cheeni ka stock khatam?', 'Papa, pahunchkar "Reached" bhejiye.' and 'Nani, dard? Sach-sach bataiye.' Their own words handed back.
'Nani, sorry. Aap hi sahi thin.' and 'Arre, theek hai. Pehle haath dikhao.' The young person's plain sorry, and warmth to a child first.
'Scorer, aaj hi jalebi le aao. Kya pata.', 'Badhiya. Papa, jaldi aaiye, aapka phone.' and the album line 'Nani, main bhi.'
problems: You call Tinku 'Scorer' in nearly every line ('Scorer, zara dikhao.', 'Scorer, run tumhara.', 'Scorer, khud likho.', 'scorer, bottles tumhare paas?'). The real-India note took this label off Nani for being a label. Siblings use the name, and 'Tinku' is already a pet name. It also makes you sound like Captain sahab, whose habit is naming people by trade. Say 'Tinku' by default and 'scorer' at most once a chapter, at the moment the scorebook matters.

'Scorer, run tumhara.' hands back a phrase Tinku no longer says. Her pass cut 'Run tumhara' as a cricket code for a feeling and kept cricket only with Captain sahab. You now carry the very code that was removed, as a stale reference between files. Use plain praise: 'Tinku, ye tumne kiya.' This is a ne past that agrees with 'ye', so it is still free of gender.

In moment 7, 'Arre Mami, kis baat ka?' collides with Captain sahab's 'Kis baat ka, Scorer?' in the same moment. Change yours: 'Arre Mami, rehne dijiye. Pehle Mausa ji ko boliye.' keeps your someone-else-first shape.

india.verdict:
The pass worked. All eleven now sound like real, different people. In the default Hinglish and in Hindi mode a Hindi-first reader would believe most lines, and the cast is told apart mainly by the shape of each person's speech and where their words come from. It holds against the six players. P2 Ravi gets warm, capable men and none drawn against men, Hindi that is mostly as people talk it, and scoring that never preaches. P3 Sunita and P4 Meena get Hindi mode with only the English loans a Hindi-first home already uses. P5 Mr Natarajan and P1 Shruti get English mode that reads as Indian English, with Papa's Tamil count as a quiet nod to the south. Rule 3, rule 8, rule 66 and rule 22 held in every line I read: no religious word, caste word or brand; no beta, bhaiya or didi; no gendered form to or from the player; no doubt of a report. No file has an em or en dash or an American spelling. Mausa ji, Masterji, Captain sahab, Tinku and Papa are the strongest.

What is left is small and fixable. These are the cast-wide items, separate from the per-person notes:
(1) Two people say the same rule 22 formula, 'Mujhe yakeen hai' (Nani, Mami). Said aloud in a family it sounds like a training script, which is P1 Shruti's quit trigger and a clip for A2. Mama ji's 'Main aa raha hoon. Abhi.' is the real way: belief shown by acting, with no doubt in it. Rewrite those two lines that way.
(2) Common words are still banned in two places. The never lists still bar everyday exclamations for everyone but their owner ('uff', 'haay', 'oho', 'baap re', 'waah'), and Mausa ji's list still bars 'pakka'. No visible line breaks because of it, but it is the ban-the-common-word pattern the brief ruled out. Reword these as 'not as their habitual cry' rather than banning the word. The same habit bent two visible lines: Mama ji's 'roz miss kiya' and Papa's 'mere father'.
(3) For P6 Farida, the house treats Hindi-side words as neutral and Urdu-side words as leaning. 'Mubarak ho', 'Ammi' and Masterji's Urdu courtesy forms are fenced off as leaning, while 'Badhai ho', 'Amma' and 'Dhanyavaad' pass as neutral, and 'pitaji' is held back for no good reason. Rule 3 bans religious words, not community-coloured everyday speech. Have the Urdu-speaking reader check that both sides are treated the same.
(4) In the blind sort, moment 7 will blur. Mummy, Mama ji and Mausa ji all open on 'isme kya', and You and Captain sahab share 'Kis baat ka?'. Their endings differ, but change You's line and accept the rest as real.
(5) The few remaining coined or translated lines are Papa's '9:40 mera time tha', Mummy's khaata sorry and 'credit book', Captain sahab's 'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin' (cut it), Nani's 'koi ... laaye' orders, and Mami's three-fold 'still pending' joke.

Fix these and the cast is ready for the Hindi-first readers (rule 65) and the sorting test.

polished: Mausa ji (मौसा जी), about 58, chapter 2's voice
Masterji (मास्टरजी), about 60, the tailor next door; chapter 3's voice

voices.name: Nani (नानी), turning 80

voice.register: Low, slow and final. She talks in two gears, and the gear is the tell. Orders and jobs come in closed fragments, one to three words each, one to three to a bubble, each shut with a full stop the way she ruled off each line of a bill ('Bori upar. Chappal upar. Bachche andar.'). Comfort, news and asides come in short whole sentences that keep their हूँ and है ('Main yahin hoon. Kahin nahin jaa rahi.'), because an old woman soothing someone does not talk in telegrams. On the phone she runs on: a voice note is four to six short sentences of lane news, 'Haan,' first and 'Bas.' last. Never a comma list (that is Mummy's shape); a saying or an 'X, not Y' keeps its one comma ('Beemar hoon, behri nahin.'). At most one real saying a scene, from the counter, never a coined one. Never hurried and never raised, except one 'Bas!' a year. Her questions are 'who should' asks or sly questions handed back to the speaker. Help still turns into her own order ('Doctor ki salaah thi. Maine haan kar di.'), but warmth is now said out loud: she blesses ('Khush raho.'), owns a mistake in plain words ('Main galat.') and asks for the call home. Sly, with a straight face, and never the comic one in her own chapter. She tells time by the lane (after the milk, when the lamps come on, after Mummy's call), never by a clock, and says no figure at all, apart from the album count.
voice.mix: The most Hindi in the cast: the everyday spoken Hindi of a small Hindi-speaking town, full of the counter's idioms, with the town's ordinary Urdu-rooted words in it as in anyone's mouth (ज़रूर, यक़ीन, फ़िक्र). English comes only as the nouns the world handed her: doctor, BP, ward, X-ray, ticket, berth, cake, party, flat, list, phone, torch, timetable. Where her lane puts kar or ho after one of those nouns, so does she ('phone karna', 'BP high ho gaya'), but she takes up no English verb of her own ('check karo', 'adjust karo' and 'miss kiya' are other people's habit) and no English clause or tag. The young people's English things she waves off with the everyday echo word ('cake-vake', 'thank you-vank you'), at most once a scene. Her images come from the scale and the sacks, never the account book or a price: तौल, डंडी, तराज़ू, बोरी, छुट्टा, and the goods she weighed out (गुड़, नमक, आटा, घी, राई, जीरा, चीनी); dal and chillies stay Papa's and Mummy's images. In English mode her orders keep the fragments and the stops, her comfort is whole plain English sentences, each saying becomes the English saying people know ('A mountain out of a molehill.', 'Little drops make an ocean.', 'Weigh your words.'), and 'Baap re.' stays as it is, the way Mami's 'Ish.' does.
tics: TWO GEARS. Orders and jobs: closed fragments, one to three words each, one to three to a bubble ('Seedhi. Jaldi.', 'Meri gali. Tumhari list.'). Comfort, news and asides: short whole sentences that keep हूँ, है or था ('Paani hi toh hai.', 'Mujhe gussa aa gaya tha.'). A reader can tell which she is doing from the shape alone.

THE BARE LINE stays for orders and for her cross moments ('Badi. Chhote. Bas.'). Verbs come in orders ('Kaam pe lagao.'), 'who should' asks ('Nani ke saath ghar kaun jaaye?'), facts about herself ('Giri nahin. Baith gayi.') and every comfort line.
ORDERS start with the thing, then the verb or nothing: 'Bori upar.', 'Seedhi. Jaldi.'

JOBS go to 'कोई' with the plain plural command, the way a real house gives them, never to a name: 'Koi torch lao.', 'Arre, koi kapda lao.', 'Koi pakdo.' The command marks no gender (rule 66). The 'should' form stays only where Hindi itself uses it: her 'kaun' asks ('kaun jaaye?'), her want ('Sab aayein.', 'Sab phir aayein, tab.') and the typed 'Koi na aaye.'
POSSESSIVES carry her orders and her no: मेरी गली, मेरा बिस्तर, मेरा बटुआ; and 'तुम्हारी लिस्ट' when she hands something over.

ONE SAYING a scene at most, and only a real one a Hindi-first reader knows: 'डंडी मत मारना।', 'राई का पहाड़।', 'बूँद-बूँद से घड़ा भरता है।', 'जितना गुड़, उतना मीठा।', 'आटे में नमक।', 'ऊँट के मुँह में जीरा।', 'दूध का दूध, पानी का पानी।', 'तोल-मोल के बोलो।', 'काम खरा उतरा।'. She never coins one.
SLY TURNS: a question handed back to the speaker, often with no verb ('Chai mein cheeni? Ya cheeni mein chai?'), sometimes with one ('Suraj bhi aapke timetable se nikalta hai?').
THIRD PERSON: she calls herself 'Nani' only when she needs help, because she cannot ask for it in the first person ('Nani ke saath ghar kaun jaaye?').

'BAS.' is her closer and her answer to 'how are you', and the question always goes straight back ('Bas. Apni sunao.'). The open palm presses down once, then her eyes go to the lane door, where her counter faced (the window is Mausa ji's look when he is moved). One raised 'Bas!' a year.

COMMON WORDS are anyone's, hers too: arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, suno and theek hai come and go mid-line as in any house ('Arre, koi kapda lao.', 'Achha? Agle hafte?'). What is hers is the shape, not a word. Other people's set phrases stay theirs ('Arre waah', 'Had hai!', 'Suno, suno, suno!', Mausa ji's one-word 'Theek.', Mummy's thanks-received 'Arre, isme kya.' and her platform 'Pahunchkar phone karna').
ECHO WORDS: the young people's English things get the everyday echo word when she waves them off ('cake-vake', 'thank you-vank you'), at most once a scene, never about a person.
ON THE PHONE SHE RAMBLES: she asks your news ('Apni sunao.') and then tells hers, short sentences about the lane, the milk, the rain and Mummy's call, before 'Bas.' ends it.
COUNTS SILENTLY: her left forefinger taps the air once a person, lips moving, no sound. Only the household, never card people. Aloud once in the game, in the album.
TIME BY THE LANE: 'doodh ke baad' (after the milk), 'batti jale' (when the lamps come on), 'phone ke baad' (after Mummy's call). Never a clock time.

ADDRESS BY BIRTH ORDER to their faces: बड़ी (Mausi) and छोटे (Mama ji) in Hindi and Hinglish; 'दुकानवाली' as a tease for Mummy; Tinku by her name. To you she names them plainly ('तुम्हारी मौसी', 'तुम्हारी मम्मी'), so you know who is meant.

TOLD FROM MAUSA JI, the other very short Hindi speaker: she owns things (मेरी, तुम्हारी), says मैं, hands jobs to 'koi', quotes the counter, blesses out loud and runs on in voice notes. He leaves himself out, speaks one verdict on the work ('Mazboot.', 'Dheela.') and lets his hands do the rest.
catchphrases: 'डंडी मत मारना।' | 'Dandi mat maarna.' | 'No thumb on the scale.' The grocer's own idiom (डंडी मारना, to short-weigh), known across the north: do the job honestly and in full. Said before a job she hands over.
'बस।' | 'Bas.' | 'Enough.' when it stops someone; 'Enough about me.' when it answers 'how are you'. Her closer, with the palm pressed down once.
'सब आएँ।' | 'Sab aayein.' | 'Everyone, come.' Her want, put as an order, and the game's first message (the phone types it 'सब आएं।'). In the album it turns into 'सब आए।' | 'Everyone came.'

'ख़ुश रहो।' | 'Khush raho.' | 'Stay happy.' (by sense in English mode: 'Well done.' for good news). Her good wish, with no religious word in it: for good news, at a goodbye with her palm on the bent head, and as her thank-you. The owner and the Hindi-first readers confirm it passes rule 3.
voice.exclamation: 'Baap re.' | 'बाप रे।' | English mode keeps 'Baap re.', as Mami keeps 'Ish.', because 'Well I never.' turned her into an English grandmother. For real astonishment only: news that truly surprises her. Said low and closed with a full stop, never an exclamation mark, so it is the one exclamation in the cast that is not raised. No religious meaning: literally 'O father', an everyday cry of surprise across the Hindi belt. Never followed by a name, and always in this one form ('Baap re baap' is not used). A power cut or a late guest does not earn it.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: plain words in her own मैं, then the tea. When she is wrong: 'मैं ग़लत।' | 'Main galat.' | 'I was wrong.'; after she snaps: 'मुझे ग़ुस्सा आ गया था।' | 'Mujhe gussa aa gaya tha.' | 'I lost my temper.'; then 'चाय पियो।' | 'Chai piyo.' | 'Drink your tea.', the steel tumbler pushed across. The tea follows the words and never stands in for them, and tea means sorry and nothing else. THANKS: the good wish 'ख़ुश रहो।' | 'Khush raho.' | 'Stay happy.'; her old way, the next job ('अब ये भी।' | 'Ab ye bhi.' | 'Now this one too.', the stick pointing at it), comes after the good wish at most once a chapter. THANKED HERSELF: she brushes it off with the everyday echo word, 'रहने दो ये थैंक यू-वैंक यू।' | 'Rehne do ye thank you-vank you.' | 'None of your thank-yous.', and to the in-laws with आप, 'थैंक यू-वैंक यू रहने दीजिए।' | 'Thank you-vank you rehne dijiye.' ('Arre, isme kya.' is Mummy's, not hers). LOVE: said in comfort with its verb ('मैं यहीं हूँ। कहीं नहीं जा रही।' | 'I'm right here. Not going anywhere.'), in the goodbye wish with her palm on a bent head ('ख़ुश रहो। पहुँचते ही फ़ोन।', the call home put as an order), in a hand on Tinku's shoulder, and in words once, the album's 'और तुम।' | 'Aur tum.' | 'And you.' habits: DEVICE: the large-screen phone Mama ji gave her (no brand ever named or shown), lying on her lap on speaker. Tinku set up the microphone key and she taught herself the rest, so no one has to read or write for her (her contradiction, on a phone).

SCRIPT: Devanagari only, because she dictates in Hindi, written the way the phone actually produces it: anusvara forms (अस्सीवां, आएं), English nouns in Devanagari letters (डॉक्टर, बीपी), and echo words without their hyphen (केक वेक). A Hindi-first reader checks every typed sample against a real phone's voice typing.

SHAPE: the same two gears as her speech. Orders go as fragments of one to three words; news goes as short whole sentences. Each is closed with one firm tap on the full stop (।), the way she ruled off each line of a bill. Voice typing adds no danda by itself, so the stops are hers. No commas, because the stop is the only key she taps.

NUMBERS: none. The one figure she ever sends is the occasion in the opening message, which the phone writes as it hears it (अस्सीवां or 80वां, checked on a real phone). No time, no price, no BP reading (Mami logs those).
NEVER: a greeting or sign-off, anyone's name, emoji, the folded hands, stickers, forwards or good-morning pictures.

VOICE NOTES: anything longer than three short pieces becomes a voice note, and that is where she runs on: four to six short sentences of lane news (the milk, the rain, the sacks, Mummy's call), each bubble at most 10 words. It starts with 'हाँ,' as if you had rung her and ends with 'बस।'. Shown as live text on the painted blank phone; the caption is her speech, in standard spelling like her bubbles.
REPLIES: she never answers a text with a text. She phones back, usually within the hour.
WHEN: before seven in the morning and just after the nine o'clock call with Mummy; never after ten, except once, the ward night, which is how Tinku knows she is not sleeping.

THE FAMILY GROUP: Mama ji added her. She reads it on her lap and posts only to stop news she does not want (the fall). The owner ruled out a group chat on screen on 23 Oct, so it exists for the writers only.
HOW YOU TYPE TO HER: you don't. You call, or send a voice note.

To you, July, the first big rain (voice bank, voice-typed; a 'who should' ask). HI: 'बारिश आ गई। छत पर कौन जाए?' | HINGLISH: 'Baarish aa gayi. Chhat par kaun jaaye?' | EN: 'The rain's here. Who goes up to the roof?'
To Papa, a voice note answering his good-morning flower (sly). HI: 'हाँ, सुबह हो गई।' | HINGLISH: 'Haan, subah ho gayi.' | EN: 'Yes, it's morning.'

To you, a September evening, a voice note after Mummy's call (she asks your news, then tells hers; her ramble). HI: 'हाँ, अपनी सुनाओ। आज गली में पानी भर गया था। / दूध वाला देर से आया। बोरियाँ ऊपर रखवा दीं। / चाय ठंडी हो गई। फिर बनाई। बस।' | HINGLISH: 'Haan, apni sunao. Aaj gali mein paani bhar gaya tha. / Doodh wala der se aaya. Boriyaan upar rakhwa di. / Chai thandi ho gayi. Phir banayi. Bas.' | EN: 'Yes, tell me your news. The lane flooded today. / The milkman came late. I had the sacks put up. / My tea went cold. Made it again. That's that.'

test_lines.moment: 1. The lights go out in the middle of dinner (to the whole table, you among them, so no -ते रहो; the plain plural command to 'koi', which marks no gender; no exclamation, since a power cut does not surprise her)
test_lines.en: Someone fetch a torch. The rest of you, eat.
test_lines.hinglish: Koi torch lao. Baaki sab khao.
test_lines.hi: कोई टॉर्च लाओ। बाक़ी सब खाओ।

test_lines.moment: 2. Someone everyone was waiting for arrives two hours late (to Mama ji; her cross tell, palm pressed down, no figure)
test_lines.en: Enough. Your plate's gone cold. Sit.
test_lines.hinglish: Chhote. Bas. Thali thandi ho gayi. Baitho.
test_lines.hi: छोटे। बस। थाली ठंडी हो गई। बैठो।

test_lines.moment: 3. A cousin phones to say they have got their first job (to the cousin; a good wish with no religious word in it, and no verb about them, so no gender)
test_lines.en: Well done. The sweets are on you.
test_lines.hinglish: Khush raho. Mithai tumhari taraf se.
test_lines.hi: ख़ुश रहो। मिठाई तुम्हारी तरफ़ से।

test_lines.moment: 4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it (to Mausi, who made it; she pushes the glass back)
test_lines.en: Sugar in the tea? Or tea in the sugar?
test_lines.hinglish: Badi. Chai mein cheeni? Ya cheeni mein chai?
test_lines.hi: बड़ी। चाय में चीनी? या चीनी में चाय?

test_lines.moment: 5. In front of the family, someone shows that she had a fact wrong (to Tinku, whose scorebook proves it: the one time she calls Tinku 'Scorer'; plain words first, then the tea)
test_lines.en: The scorer's right. I was wrong. Drink your tea.
test_lines.hinglish: Scorer sahi. Main galat. Chai piyo.
test_lines.hi: स्कोरर सही। मैं ग़लत। चाय पियो।

test_lines.moment: 6. Someone she loves is leaving, goodbye on a railway platform (to Mama ji; he bends, she lays her palm on his head and blesses him; the call home goes in her order gear, a closed fragment, so it is not Mummy's platform line)
test_lines.en: Stay happy. Phone the minute you arrive.
test_lines.hinglish: Chhote. Khush raho. Pahunchte hi phone.
test_lines.hi: छोटे। ख़ुश रहो। पहुँचते ही फ़ोन।

test_lines.moment: 7. Someone thanks her for something she did (to you; the everyday brush-off with its echo word, then the stick points at the next job)
test_lines.en: None of your thank-yous. Now this one too.
test_lines.hinglish: Rehne do ye thank you-vank you. Ab ye bhi.
test_lines.hi: रहने दो ये थैंक यू-वैंक यू। अब ये भी।

test_lines.moment: 8. A neighbour passes on a rumour that the corner sweet shop is closing (to the younger neighbour who brings it; a habit, not a character, and a harmless rumour, never a report)
test_lines.en: A mountain out of a molehill. Weigh your words.
test_lines.hinglish: Raai ka pahaad. Tol-mol ke bolo.
test_lines.hi: राई का पहाड़। तोल-मोल के बोलो।

test_lines.moment: 9. Heavy rain floods the lane outside the house (to the household; the counter's old rule in rain, sacks off the floor)
test_lines.en: Sacks up. Shoes up. Children inside.
test_lines.hinglish: Bori upar. Chappal upar. Bachche andar.
test_lines.hi: बोरी ऊपर। चप्पल ऊपर। बच्चे अंदर।

test_lines.moment: 10. Someone asks her how she is (to you; 'Bas' instead of 'I'm fine', then the question goes straight back)
test_lines.en: Enough about me. Tell me your news.
test_lines.hinglish: Bas. Apni sunao.
test_lines.hi: बस। अपनी सुनाओ।

test_lines.moment: 11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table (to the child, gently; water is cheap, ghee was dear)
test_lines.en: It's only water. Not ghee. Someone fetch a cloth.
test_lines.hinglish: Paani hi toh hai. Ghee nahin. Arre, koi kapda lao.
test_lines.hi: पानी ही तो है। घी नहीं। अरे, कोई कपड़ा लाओ।

test_lines.moment: 12. A phone call brings good news (to the caller; the one moment that earns 'Baap re', said low)
test_lines.en: Baap re. Say it again. Slowly.
test_lines.hinglish: Baap re. Dobaara bolo. Dheere.
test_lines.hi: बाप रे। दोबारा बोलो। धीरे।

changed: TWO GEARS IN PLACE OF ONE TELEGRAM (real-India note on telegram comfort; cast note 9): orders and jobs keep her closed fragments; comfort, news and asides get their verb and their हूँ or है. 'Main yahin. Kahin nahin.' becomes 'Main yahin hoon. Kahin nahin jaa rahi.'; 'Paani. Ghee nahin.' becomes 'Paani hi toh hai. Ghee nahin.'; 'Meri poori gali.' becomes 'Meri poori gali aayi hai.'; 'Mehmaanon ke paas.' gets its 'hai'; 'Thali thandi.' becomes 'Thali thandi ho gayi.'; the sun tease gets 'nikalta hai'; the age joke gets 'Bahut bhaari hai.'

SHE RAMBLES WHERE A REAL 80-YEAR-OLD DOES, on the phone (real-India note): voice notes now run four to six short sentences of lane news, and a September voice note is added in which she asks your news and then tells hers. The carrom voice note gets its verbs and a second bubble ('Rani maine li thi. Mujhe yaad hai.').

HELP TURNED INTO HER ORDER, said the way people say it (Hindi note on 'मेरी हाँ'; real-India note): 'Raat bhar. Doctor ki salaah. Meri haan.' becomes 'Raat bhar. Doctor ki salaah thi. / Maine haan kar di.'

COINED SAYINGS GONE (real-India note): the praise 'Poora taul.' becomes the real idiom 'Kaam khara utra.' | 'Right up to the mark.'; 'Tumhara taraazu sachcha.' becomes the plain 'Scorer sahi. Main galat.'; 'Taul ke bolo' becomes the fixed phrase 'Tol-mol ke bolo.'. 'पूरा तौल' and 'सच्चा' leave her uses list.

WARMTH SAID OUT LOUD (real-India note; cast note 3): the good wish 'Khush raho.' has no religious word in it and goes to the cousin's first job (moment 3), to the platform goodbye with her palm on Mama ji's head (now 'Chhote. Khush raho. Pahunchte hi phone.' in place of 'Chhote. Jhuko. Ab jaao.'), and to her thanks. English mode uses 'Well done.' or 'Stay happy.' by sense, never 'Bless you'. The owner and the Hindi-first readers confirm it passes rule 3.

SORRY AND THANKS IN PLAIN WORDS (cast note 3): sorry is now said first, in her own मैं ('Main galat.', 'Mujhe gussa aa gaya tha.'), and the tea follows the words instead of replacing them. Thanks is 'Khush raho.'; the next job ('Ab ye bhi.') stays as her own touch, at most once a chapter. Thanked herself, she brushes it off the everyday way ('Rehne do ye thank you-vank you.', and to Mami 'Thank you-vank you rehne dijiye.') in place of the coded 'Rehne do. Ab ye bhi.' alone.

COMMON WORDS FREED (cast note 1): the list of other people's words is gone from her never list (अरे, अच्छा, चलो, देखो, सुनो, ठीक, अभी, पहले, 'aur haan' and the rest); she now says 'Arre' and 'Achha' mid-line like anyone ('Arre, koi kapda lao.', 'Achha? Agle hafte?'). She keeps 'Bas.' as her closer, and other people's set phrases and exclamations stay theirs. Her images still keep away from the account book (C11), as a choice of where her words come from, not a ban on a word.

ENGLISH WITH KAR OR HO (cast note 2): at 80 and Hindi-first she takes up no English verb of her own, but the nouns the world handed her take kar or ho the way her lane says them ('phone karna', 'BP high ho gaya'). Still no English clauses or tags.

'SCORER' NO LONGER A LABEL (real-India note): Tinku is 'Tinku' in plain lines (a carrom line by name is added), and 'Scorer' is said once, in moment 5, when the scorebook proves Nani wrong. This also leaves Hindi mode one fewer English word for low-English readers (cast note 11).

ENGLISH MODE SOUNDS LIKE ENGLISH (real-India note; cast note 10): 'A mountain out of a molehill.', 'Little drops make an ocean.', 'The plain truth. No water in it. Tell me.'; 'Baap re.' now stays 'Baap re.' in English mode, as Mami's 'Ish.' does, because 'Well I never.' made her an English grandmother. Other English lines made idiomatic: 'Everyone, come.', 'Enough about me. Tell me your news.', 'Does the sun rise by your timetable too?', 'Nobody needs to come.', 'Don't skimp on the ghee.', 'Phone the minute you arrive.'

HINDI AND RULES NOTES: moment 1's 'बाक़ी खाते रहो' (the -ते रहो gap in rule 66) becomes 'बाक़ी सब खाओ।'; to you, Mausi is now 'तुम्हारी मौसी', not 'बड़ी'; 'बीमार। बहरी नहीं।' becomes 'बीमार हूँ, बहरी नहीं।', the line the real-India readers liked, now said as one thought; 'मेरी हाँ' is gone. Every new line to you is in the rule 66 flag list for a native reader.

RULE 22 GUARD (cast note 5): her weighing sayings ('Tol-mol ke bolo', 'Raai ka pahaad', 'Doodh ka doodh') are never said to anyone who brings a report of harassment or a dowry demand; a belief line is added for the voice bank ('Idhar aao. Poori baat batao.' | 'Come here. Tell me all of it.').
TOWN WORDS, NOT ONE MAN'S (cast note 8): 'zaroor', 'yakeen' and 'fikr' are open to her as town words; no line leans on them as a formula.

ECHO WORDS: the everyday Hindi echo word is how she waves off the young people's English things, at most once a scene; the April message becomes 'Cake-vake nahin. Halwa. Bas.' and moment 7 throws back 'thank you-vank you'.
CONGRATULATING (cast note 4): moment 3 blesses rather than congratulates; 'Badhai ho' is the owner's question and goes to Mummy if it is allowed.
SHARED BITS (cast note 6): the sugar tease stays hers, since the readers marked it true; Papa's file changes his version.

KEPT, as the readers marked them true: 'Baap re' said low, 'Dandi mat maarna', 'Raai ka pahaad', the doctor line, 'Giri nahin. Baith gayi. Zor se.', the sugar tease, 'Bori upar. Chappal upar. Bachche andar.', 'Bas. Apni sunao.', 'Badi' and 'Chhote', her voice typing and 'Haan, subah ho gayi.' under Papa's flower. Also kept: essence, want, fear and contradiction (help turned into her own order, the third-person 'Nani' when she needs help); 'Sab aayein'; the silent finger count and the album's spoken count; दुकानवाली; आप to all three in-laws and the December first तुम; every rule 3 and rule 22 guard. One flag for readers stays: in the album's Hinglish 'Ek, do, teen', 'do' (two) can be read as the English verb, though the counting run makes it clear.

FINAL POLISH, HINDI: the ch 2 'no party' line was an unfinished when-clause ('जब सब फिर आएँ।'); it is now 'Koi party nahin. Sab phir aayein, tab.' | 'कोई पार्टी नहीं। सब फिर आएँ, तब।', which says 'not till everyone comes again'.

FINAL POLISH, MUMMY'S LINES RETURNED: 'Arre, isme kya.' (Mummy's thanks-received line) leaves Nani; thanked by Mami she now says 'Thank you-vank you rehne dijiye. Ghee poora daaliye.' (आप kept). The platform goodbye drops Mummy's 'Pahunchkar phone zaroor karna' for her own order gear: 'Chhote. Khush raho. Pahunchte hi phone.' | 'Stay happy. Phone the minute you arrive.' Both are now in her never list as Mummy's.

FINAL POLISH, ORDERS TO 'KOI' (real-India note): the subjunctive 'Koi torch laaye.', 'Koi kapda laaye.', 'Koi pakde.' read as wishes; a real house says the plural command, so they are 'Koi torch lao.', 'Arre, koi kapda lao.', 'Koi pakdo.' The command marks no gender, so rule 66 holds. The 'should' form stays only where Hindi itself uses it: her 'kaun' asks, her want 'Sab aayein.' and the typed 'Koi na aaye.'

FINAL POLISH, RULE 22 (real-India note): 'Mujhe yakeen hai.' sounded like a counsellor and opened like Mami's line; her belief now shows by going straight to the person and the facts: 'Idhar aao. Poori baat batao.' | 'Come here. Tell me all of it.' No doubt in it, and her weighing sayings stay fenced off from any report.

FINAL POLISH, THE FIRST MESSAGE: 'सब आएं' is an order, so the English is now 'My eightieth. May. Everyone, come.' (and the catchphrase reads 'Everyone, come.'). The anusvara spelling (अस्सीवां, आएं) is kept on purpose as the phone's voice typing, as her SCRIPT habit says; her spoken lines keep ँ.

voices.name: Mummy (मम्मी), 52

voice.register: Brisk, mid-fast and level: the pace of a shop counter on a Saturday, warm underneath, never cold, never loud. MEDIUM length, the middle of the cast. She has two shapes, and the job of the line picks the shape. ORDERS, PLANS, A NO AND A SCHEDULE come as one comma list of people and jobs (or goods), five to ten words, closed by one full stop and usually with no verb: 'Tum bill, Tinku stock, main shutter.'. CARE AND COMFORT get their verb back: short whole sentences with hai or hoon in them ('Shutter hai, counter hai, haath hain.', 'Main glass laati hoon.', 'Sab bag mein hai.'), so she is not one more clipped voice in a house that already has five. A second thought is a second bubble, never a longer one. Her list is people and jobs; it is not Nani's closed one-to-three-word fragments, not Captain sahab's call and then a reason, not Mami's item-and-status readback, and not Papa's run of whole sentences. HUMOUR: none on purpose. She is the straight face; the family laughs at her shop voice at home ('Haan ji, boliye.' to her own children, 'Aur kuch?' at a goodbye) and she never hears the joke. FEELING is changed into shop news with no figure ('Copper phir mehenga.'); love is mostly a deed, and when it is spoken it is a packed list that keeps its hai. CROSS: very still, the voice drops, and politeness rises. The one slow subject is her roof chillies: there the list stops and she says whole, unhurried sentences.
voice.mix: A Hindi frame, the everyday Hindi of a small Hindi-speaking junction town, with English nouns from today's counter dropped in whole: shutter, stock, bill, counter, delivery, godown, customer, fuse, wire, switch, fan, bulb, copper, MCB, mains, extension. The English verb + kar/ho ('check karo', 'delivery ho gayi') is the commonest Hinglish pattern in India and the whole house shares it; what marks her is where she aims it. The shop's words come home with her, as they do in any electrician's house: a power cut at dinner is 'MCB check karo', the water at the door is 'mains off karo'. No whole English clauses (Mama ji and Mami switch clause by clause). The common Hindi fillers are hers as much as anyone's (achha, haan, haan ji, chalo, suno, dekho, bas, theek hai, arre inside a line), and so are the everyday Urdu-rooted town words (zaroor, waqt, zaroorat). What her English carries: goods. Hindi mode keeps the trade nouns in Devanagari as Hindi speakers say them (शटर, स्टॉक, बिल, चेक करो). Her credit book is 'khaata' | खाता in both scripts, as every small-town shop says it, and the word means only that book. English mode is Indian English as it is spoken, not a word-for-word copy: 'Haan ji, boliye.' is 'Yes, tell me.', 'Aur kuch?' is 'Anything else?', 'Had hai!' is 'This is too much!', and the rising 'ji' stays on names when she is cross (Tinku ji, Chhote ji). Her two marked figures are said in words in speech ('nau baje', 'nau bajkar das'), which collide with no other word (unlike 'saath'); in typing a figure is a digit.
tics: Answers every phone call with the shop greeting, 'Haan ji, boliye.' | 'हाँ जी, बोलिए।' | 'Yes, tell me.', to Nani and to you exactly as to a customer. When she knows the voice she drops to तुम with 'Achha, tum.' and carries on, so the reader hears the switch and never takes it for a slip. This is her first tell.

Orders, plans and a no come as one comma list of people and jobs, five to ten words, ticked off on the fingers of her left hand: 'Tum bill, Tinku stock, main shutter.'. Comfort keeps the list's bones but gets its verb: 'Shutter hai, counter hai, haath hain.'.

Closes a talk the way she closes a sale: 'Aur kuch?' | 'और कुछ?' | 'Anything else?', after a compliment, at a goodbye, when asked how she is. At most one bubble in four, because Mami's 'Correct?' holds the cast's other closing question.
Changes a feeling into shop news with no figure: 'How are you, Mummy?' 'Copper phir mehenga.' The dodge is hers alone; Papa and Tinku drop theirs (C10).

The shop's English comes home: the English verb + kar/ho that the whole house uses, carrying the trade words of an electrician's house: 'MCB check karo.', 'Mains off karo.'. Never a joke on the kitchen: a too-sweet tea is plain 'Cheeni kam, dobara banao.'.
When cross, politeness rises instead of volume: 'ji' goes onto names that never carry it ('Tinku ji', 'Chhote ji'), तुम becomes आप, commands become -इए and -लीजिए, and her hands clasp at her waist.
Gives the hour in whole hours by her father's watch, which runs two minutes fast ('nau baje'). Minutes only in an emergency ('Nau bajkar das.'), which is how the family knows it is one.
On the roof, with the chillies, the list stops: slow whole sentences with their verbs ('Mirchi bach gayi.'). It is the only time she speaks slowly.
Counts heads with one raised left forefinger, exactly as Nani does, in silence: the count is never said aloud (a head-count in speech is Nani's one album line).
catchphrases: 'Haan ji, boliye.' | 'हाँ जी, बोलिए।' | 'Yes, tell me.' (every phone call, every customer, and you)
'Nau baje. Shutter up.' | 'नौ बजे। शटर ऊपर।' | 'Nine o'clock. Shutter up.' (her one catchphrase with a number: the shutter hour, which her target allows)
'Aur kuch?' | 'और कुछ?' | 'Anything else?' (the counter's closer, which the family quotes back at her; it takes the place of 'Iska bill nahin.', now a rare line)
voice.exclamation: 'Had hai!' | 'हद है!' | English mode 'This is too much!', which is how Indian English says it. For exasperation only: the water at the door, the lights failing in an electrician's own house, a delivery gone wrong. Secular: it means 'this is the limit', it calls on no one, and it is never followed by any name. No one else in the cast uses it as an exclamation. She has no exclamation for joy: good news comes out as orders ('Tinku, mithai lao.').
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY, plain first: 'Meri galti.' | 'मेरी ग़लती।' | 'My mistake.', with the name ('Meri galti, Tinku.'). When her mistake cost someone, she names what she did and owns it in plain words, to an elder as to anyone: 'Masterji, kal raat ki zid meri galti thi.' | 'मास्टरजी, कल रात की ज़िद मेरी ग़लती थी।' | 'Masterji, I was stubborn last night. My mistake.'. No idiom: 'mere khaate mein daal do' is the sulky 'go on, blame me then', and khaata is her credit book. THANKS, GIVEN: plain words first, then a deed. To elders, 'Didi, aapne bahut kiya.' | 'दीदी, आपने बहुत किया।' | 'Didi, you did so much.', with something off the shelf put into their hands. To the young, 'Bahut achha kiya.' | 'बहुत अच्छा किया।' | 'That was really good.', and then something done for them ('Aaj raat ka khana mera.' | 'Dinner tonight is on me.'). When family reaches for a wallet at her counter: 'Aapse paise? Rehne dijiye.' | 'आपसे पैसे? रहने दीजिए।' | 'Money, from you? Put it away.'. 'Iska bill nahin.' survives only as a rare line, once a chapter at most, when a gift goes over the counter. THANKS, RECEIVED: the brush-off every elder in the north uses, 'Arre, isme kya.' | 'अरे, इसमें क्या।' | 'Oh, it's nothing.', and she turns straight to an order for someone else ('Tinku, agle ka bill banao.'). LOVE: mostly a deed: the red 'paid' pen laid down for you in January and the spare shop key in the album, each turned towards you, her hand coming back to her side; a handful of roof chillies for Nani every Sunday. When love comes out in speech it is a packed list that keeps its verb ('Torch, charger, extension, sab bag mein hai.') and the line every mother says on a platform ('Pahunchkar phone karna.').

stock, maal | स्टॉक, माल | stock, goods
bill, bill book, galla | बिल, बिल बुक, गल्ला | bill, bill book, the cash drawer
counter, delivery, godown, customer | काउंटर, डिलीवरी, गोदाम, कस्टमर

khaata | खाता | the book (her regulars' plain blue credit book; Hinglish and Hindi both say khaata, as a small-town shop does; in the flood week it is the whole lane's; the word is only ever this book, never a sorry)
mirchi, tamatar, chhat, dabbe | मिर्ची, टमाटर, छत, डब्बे | chillies, tomatoes, the roof, the tins (her one interest with no number in it)
the shop's English verbs at home: check karo, count karo, lock karo, off karo | चेक करो, काउंट करो, लॉक करो, ऑफ़ करो
'ye wala' | 'ये वाला' | 'this one' (the thing in her hand or in the photo)
'Aur kuch?' | 'और कुछ?' | 'Anything else?' (the counter's closer)
'Main hi hoon. Boliye.' | 'मैं ही हूँ। बोलिए।' | 'That's me. Tell me.' (to anyone who asks for the owner, the malik, one beat at most)
'Ek paisa bhi kam nahin.' | 'एक पैसा भी कम नहीं।' | 'Not a paisa short.' (her highest praise, the everyday idiom; 'ek' is idiom, not a count)
Shanivaar, nau baje | शनिवार, नौ बजे | Saturday, nine o'clock (the shutter hour)

habits: Device: a plain black Android phone in a plain black case, the screen painted blank with every word laid on as live text (rule 30). It lives in the side pocket of her kameez and comes out wedged between her left ear and shoulder.

Script: Roman Hinglish (Hindi in Latin letters), all lowercase. Commas only: no full stops, no question marks, no exclamation marks, even when she asks ('khud kab aa rahe'). Her spelling drifts (chabi, chaabi); her trade nouns never do.

HER HABIT: she acknowledges with the shop's 'haan ji', typed alone as the whole reply, to her own children as to a customer. Never 'ok', never 'done', never a thumbs-up. Anyone in the house may type haan ji inside a message; a bare 'haan ji' as the whole answer, every time, is her.

Shape: the same comma list of people and jobs as her speech ('daal tum banao, shutter neeche, ghar aa rahi'), two to eight words, one message per thought, never a paragraph, never a greeting or a sign-off.
Thanks are typed in plain words with a deed or a care after them ('bahut achha kiya, ab ghar jao'), never in a code.

Figures: only when the fact itself is a figure and only in an emergency, so a digit from her is rare and means trouble (the flood night's '6 baje'). Prices stay on the photographed bills, painted blank.
When cross, her texts get polite too: 'ji' on the name and -इए on the verb ('tinku ji counter pe aaiye').
Photos: of bills and stock cartons, painted blank, each with the same caption, 'ye wala check karo' or 'ye wala'.
Voice notes when her hands are busy in the shop. They start with her shop greeting even though she is the one calling ('haan ji boliye, achha tum'), shown as live text.

Emoji: none, ever (the thumbs-up is Mausa ji's, and your own reply to her). No stickers, no good-morning pictures (those are Papa's). The one news she sends unasked is the power-cut times, retyped the moment she hears them, shown as a message card (no group chat appears in the game).

Speed: reads within a minute between nine in the morning and half past eight at night, and replies only when she has the answer. Nothing between the shutter coming down and the end of Nani's nine o'clock call, and never after nine, so a late message from her means trouble. The flood night is the one time all year.
She never texts Nani. Nani rings her at nine every night, and Mummy waits for it.
Types fast with her left thumb, phone in her left hand, because her right hand is holding the keys or the pen.
