changed: COMMON FILLERS FREED (cast-wide 1). Her never list no longer bans arre, achha, chalo, suno, dekho, bas, theek hai, pakka, galti, galat, fikr, waqt or zaroor, and 'haan ji' is no longer hers alone. What other people keep are phrases and exclamations ('Arre waah.', a one-word 'Theek.', 'Bas.' as a closer, 'Suno, suno, suno!'), and only those stay off her. New lines use the freed words: 'Suno, aaj der hogi.' to Papa, 'Chalo, ab yaad rahega.', 'Arre Jija ji, isme kya.', 'Koi baat nahin.'. Her tell is the whole phone greeting 'Haan ji, boliye.', and in typing a bare 'haan ji' as the whole reply.

VERB + kar/ho SHARED (cast-wide 2). The claim that the English verb + kar/ho is hers alone is gone from mix, tics and uses. She is marked by where she aims it: the shop's English at home, as in any electrician's house ('MCB check karo', 'mains off karo').

SORRY AND THANKS IN PLAIN WORDS (cast-wide 3, real-India 1). Sorry is 'Meri galti.' first; the coined 'Ye mere hisaab mein.' becomes plain words, 'Masterji, kal raat ki zid meri galti thi.' (the khaata idiom tried in between is gone: see the final polish). Thanks given: 'Didi, aapne bahut kiya.' and 'Bahut achha kiya.', with the gift or a deed after the words; 'Aapse paise? Rehne dijiye.' when family tries to pay. Thanks received: the brush-off 'Arre, isme kya.'. 'Iska bill nahin.' leaves her catchphrases and is a rare line, once a chapter at most; 'Aur kuch?' takes its place as her third catchphrase. Her thanks to the young is a deed for them, not the next job, so it stays clear of Nani's 'Ab ye bhi.'.

CONGRATULATION (cast-wide 4, real-India 3). Moment 3 now says 'Badhai ho!', in English 'Many congratulations!', so it does not copy Mami's flat 'Congratulations.'. Owner question: if 'Badhai ho' is not allowed under rule 3, the line drops it and reads 'Achha, tum! Naukri? / Letter bhejo, counter pe lagaungi.'. 'Mubarak ho' is on her never list, as the note asks.

THE REGISTER SWITCH ON THE CALL (Hindi-rules 2). Moment 3 adds the recognition beat 'Achha, tum!' between the shop greeting (बोलिए) and the तुम command (भेजो), so the drop from आप to तुम is heard, as in her voice note; the address table and her first tic now say so.

THE CREDIT BOOK IN HINDI (Hindi-rules 1). Hindi mode says खाता, not क्रेडिट बुक, and drops the comma inside 'ले जाइए जी'; Hinglish now says khaata too (final polish). Customers get 'ji' with no comma before it.

WARMTH IN COMFORT (real-India 2, cast-wide 9). The 2 am schedule gets a second bubble of plain care, 'Ab let jao. Baaki subah.'. A new morning-after comfort keeps her list but gives it its verb: 'Shutter hai, counter hai, haath hain. / Kaafi hai.'. The platform goodbye keeps its packed list, adds 'hai' and the line every mother says ('Pahunchkar phone karna.'), and moment 11 opens with 'Koi baat nahin.' before the jobs.

FEWER CLIPPED LINES (cast-wide 9). The register now gives her two shapes: comma lists with no verb for orders, plans and a no; short whole sentences with hai or hoon for comfort and love ('sab bag mein hai', 'Main glass laati hoon.'). Test lines 2, 3, 5, 6, 10 and 11 now carry their verbs.

TRADER STEREOTYPE (real-India 4). The calendar joke ('Calendar muft. Keel ka bill alag.') is cut; 1.02 is wordless or 'Dukaan se.'. 'Udhaar? Kal.' stays only in chapter 3, before the flood, the chapter that later opens her credit book to the whole lane, and is now named as the clipped shop sign आज नक़द, कल उधार.

ENGLISH MODE (real-India 5, cast-wide 10). 'That's the limit!' becomes 'This is too much!'; 'Yes, go ahead.' becomes 'Yes, tell me.', the way Indian English answers a phone; moment 11 becomes 'Tinku, cloth. I'll get a glass. You, a biscuit.'; 'Put that on my account' is gone with the khaata sorry (final polish); 'Okra, that dear?' becomes 'Bhindi, this expensive?'; 'You're looking at her' becomes 'That's me.'; 'Credit? Tomorrow.' becomes the sign's own 'Today cash, tomorrow credit.'.

REAL IDIOMS ONLY. 'Ek rupaya kam nahin.' becomes the everyday 'Ek paisa bhi kam nahin.'; the coined sorry becomes plain words ('meri galti thi'); 'Copper phir chadh gaya.' uses the trader's own verb for a price going up.

SHARED BITS (cast-wide 6). Moment 2 moves off food, where five people reached for the cold dinner, to Amma: 'Amma aapka raasta dekhte-dekhte so gayin.', still with her cross politeness ('Aaiye, Chhote ji.').

TOWN WORDS (cast-wide 8). ज़रूर and वक़्त are in her mouth as everyday words ('Zaroor ji, kal tak mangwa deti hoon.', 'Shutter apne waqt pe uthega, Masterji.'), and ज़रूरत is in her uses, so these words belong to the town and not to the tailor.
RULE 22 GUARD (cast-wide 5). A new never line: near any report beat, none of her paper words may sound like a demand for proof ('bill dikhao', 'likh ke do', 'receipt', 'saboot').

KEPT, AS THE READERS MARKED TRUE: 'Haan ji, boliye.' even to her own children; 'Had hai!'; 'Main hi hoon. Boliye, delivery kab?'; 'Bhindi itni mehngi? Kal se sabzi main laaungi.'; 'Tinku ji, nau baj gaye. Aap kahaan hain?'; 'Chhote ji, aap hi chala lijiye. Chaabi ye rahi.'; the credit book opened in the flood week; 'Band? Unka shutter aaj bhi utha.'. Also unchanged: her essence (she runs the family like the shop), want (the shutter at nine, owing no one), fear (the shutter staying down, owing anyone), contradiction (swore never to sit behind a counter like her mother, runs hers exactly like her), the cost of her pride on the first flood night, the shutter hour and emergency minutes as her only figures, the dodge, 'Aur kuch?', the shop's English at home, her rising politeness when cross, the roof chillies, the address table and her typing habits.

FOR THE READERS (rule 65). A Hindi-first reader checks that 'Pahunchkar phone karna' and 'Kaafi hai' read as free of gender, and clears every rule 66 flag noted on the lines (आया, महँगा, गया, ग़लती, रहेगा, थी, करना, किया, काफ़ी, तुम्हारे, गई, भरा था, भी, जी: each agrees with a thing, is an infinitive or a word that never changes form, or is a particle, and none agrees with the player). The owner answers whether 'Badhai ho' passes rule 3, and whether rule 66 gains a fourth shape for 'Bahut achha kiya.' (final polish, rule 66).

FINAL POLISH, MOMENT 5 (Hindi rules and real-India 1). 'Chalo, ye mere khaate mein daal do.' used the तुम command to a family with Nani and other elders in it, and the khaata blame idiom read as the sulky 'go on, blame me then' straight after 'Meri galti.'. The Hindi note's fix, 'Chalo, ye mere khaate mein.', drops the verb but keeps the idiom the real-India note retires, so the line keeps the Hindi note's principle (no command, so no politeness level) in plain words: 'Achha? Meri galti. / Chalo, ab yaad rahega.' | 'अच्छा? मेरी ग़लती। / चलो, अब याद रहेगा।' | 'Oh? My mistake. / Right, I'll remember that.'. If the owner prefers the Hindi note's exact wording, it drops in with no other change.

FINAL POLISH, THE SORRY TO MASTERJI (real-India 1). 'Masterji, kal raat ki zid, mere khaate mein daaliye.' read as a coined apology; it is now the plain 'Masterji, kal raat ki zid meri galti thi.' | 'मास्टरजी, कल रात की ज़िद मेरी ग़लती थी।' | 'Masterji, I was stubborn last night. My mistake.'. The khaata idiom leaves her sorry and goes on her never list; khaata is only her real credit book.

FINAL POLISH, KHAATA IN HINGLISH (real-India 2). 'Credit book mein likh diya' sounded translated; Hinglish now says 'Khaate mein likh diya', as the Hindi already did, and her mix and uses name the book khaata in both scripts.

FINAL POLISH, THE TEA CUP CUT (real-India 3). 'Tinku, ye cup return karo.' was a writer's joke for the one person who never jokes. Moment 4 is now 'Tinku, cheeni kam, dobara banao.' | 'टिंकू, चीनी कम, दोबारा बनाओ।' | 'Tinku, less sugar, make it again.', her list shape with no gimmick. The counter-English tic now rests on what is natural in an electrician's house ('MCB check karo', 'mains off karo'), and 'return karo' leaves her uses.

FINAL POLISH, RULE 66 OWNER QUESTION (cast). 'Bahut achha kiya.' to you is a past with ने where you are the doer; किया agrees with the thing done and marks no gender, but rule 66 names only commands, 'who should' asks and lines where you are not the doer. No wording change: the owner either adds 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' to rule 66 as a fourth shape, or has the native reader clear the line onto the build's cleared list. The sample and her address table now say so.

voices.name: Papa (पापा), 56

voice.register: Measured, even and quiet; never raised and never an exclamation mark (chapter 1's one shout is Mausi's). He talks like a platform announcement: an ordered run of whole sentences, each three to eight words with its verb and its full stop, one fact to a sentence, across one to three bubbles, and the last one often names what comes next ('Ab TT aayega.'). That is his long shape, and it is unlike the other long talkers: Mama ji runs on with commas and 'aur haan', Mausi triples and overlaps, Masterji gives a verdict and wanders into cloth and weather; Papa closes each sentence before he starts the next. The everyday fillers of spoken Hindi come into his lines the way they come into anyone's, softly at the head of a sentence ('Suno,' to Mummy, 'Achha?' at a piece of news) or in the middle ('aap bas time bataiye', 'aayenge zaroor'), never as a tag at the end, so the closed announcement stays his. Slow and exact, but not a machine: a time stands where others put a feeling, in the words railway people really say ('do ghante der se', 'baarah minute late'), never a robot count, and good news goes straight to Nani ('Mummy ji ko abhi batata hoon.'). His only verbless lines are the logged ones, the time correction ('9:40, aaspaas nahin.') and the deed logged in his thanks to the young ('Raat bhar, list ke saath.'), the repeated word when cross ('Koi nahin.'), 'Thank you, ji.' to strangers, and the fixed replies he types. With Nani, who lets him finish, the run is longest (three bubbles); with everyone else it is usually two sentences. Numbers: one of the two people in the cast who lean on them (with Tinku), and only clock times, durations and the count before a noun; never prices, scores or ordinals. Budget: at most one figure a bubble, and at least one bubble in three with none (in the test set below, 3 lines of 12 carry a clock figure and one more says 'do ghante'). Humour is deadpan, about himself and clocks, in the same flat announcement voice.
voice.mix: Careful standard Hindi of the railway colonies, belonging to no one town: full verbs, आप and -इए to elders, no regional colour, and the town's common Hindustani used the way anyone uses it ('fikr mat kijiye', 'zaroor'; cast-wide 8: these words belong to the town, not to Masterji). English comes as single words: the railway nouns every Indian traveller knows (coach, berth, platform, PNR, chart, waiting list, booking, ticket, running status, TT, board; railway people say TT, and 'checker' is an outsider's word) and the everyday nouns of a colony boy grown up (time, battery, alarm, gate, colony, joining, walk); clock times stay figures in all three modes ('9:40'). His verbs are mostly Hindi, many of them the railway's own (gaadi lagna, chhootna, chalna, chart banna, berth milna). The everyday English verb with kar or ho now comes too, where it suits him, and what he turns into one is the booking counter's own work: 'book kiya', 'book kar deta hoon', 'confirm ho gaya', 'cancel karna' (cast-wide 2; Mummy's mark is home things in counter English, 'ye cup return karo', so the two still sort apart). He switches by single words, as older speakers do in the Dehradun study the realism notes cite, never by whole English clauses (Mama ji and Mami do that). टिकट is masculine in his mouth ('का टिकट', the standard booking-counter form); if Mama ji's file keeps 'की टिकट' it is Mama ji's colloquial mark and both files say so, otherwise both say 'का'. His late father is 'mere pitaji' | 'मेरे पिताजी' in Hinglish and Hindi alike: plain everyday Hindi with no lean to any community, and what a railway-colony man of 56 says to his Hindi-first mother-in-law ('father' was an outsider's word to her). Hindi mode uses plain Hindi where a low-English reader would stall: 'गाड़ी कहाँ है' for 'running status', 'सैर' for 'walk'. Tamil only in the coach count under his breath, kept in Tamil in every mode (a Tamil reader signs off the words and the script). When cross the English goes altogether: 'late' becomes 'der', 'halt' goes, and only the time stays. 'Darj hai.' | 'Noted.' is his reply to a fact (a PNR, a platform, 'Reached') and, to the young, his thanks as the deed logged ('Raat bhar, list ke saath. Darj hai.'); never his thanks for a kindness done for him (Nani's tea gets praise of its timing). His typed messages are English (see typing).
tics: Announces in order: whole sentences, one fact each, each closed with a full stop, the last naming the next step with 'ab ... aayega' or 'ab ... jaayenge' | 'अब ... आएगा' | '... comes next' ('Ab TT aayega.' | 'The TT comes next.'). Only for things that do arrive or go on their own (a train, the TT, the bags going up); a thing he fetches he fetches himself ('Kapda main laata hoon.').
Corrects any vague time to the minute: '9:40, aaspaas nahin.' | '9:40, not "around".' He hears 'about', 'around' and 'lagbhag' as errors; quoting the word back is the only time he says it.
The count before the thing: 'Hum solah log hain.' | 'There are sixteen of us.' (Tinku and Mama ji drop number-first).
Names a train by its time: '9:40 wali', '8:15 wali' ('the 9:40'), as railway people do.

A time where others give a feeling, in the words railway people really use: 'do ghante der se', 'baarah minute late', the 9:40 wali; never a robot count ('120 minute') and never a minute stamp on a kindness. Good news is not logged; it goes to Nani at once ('Mummy ji ko abhi batata hoon.').

Opens a sentence with an everyday filler, softly, as anyone does: 'Suno,' to Mummy (the way Indian couples who use no first names talk), 'Achha?' at news, 'bas' and 'zaroor' in the middle of a request. Never a tag at the end of a line (Tinku's 'haan?', Mama ji's 'aur haan').

Deadpan jokes in the station loudspeaker's frame: 'Kripya dhyan dein.' | 'Attention, please.' then a home fact ('Dal platform number ek par aa chuki hai.', 'Ye chai nahin, sharbat hai.'). At most once a chapter, never while he asks (rule 37), all of it waiting on rulebook Q5.
Never describes a person's temperament; he says what they did.
Counts the coaches under his breath in Tamil as a train comes in: '...naalu, anju, aaru.' (a whisper bubble; proposal, a Tamil reader signs off).
Looks up for a clock before he speaks in any new place (a gesture in the panel, not a word).
When cross: the time left, then one word said twice ('Koi neeche na utre. Koi nahin.'), the guard's flat hand lowered palm down; quieter, never louder, and the English goes.

His judging notes on cards: one time stamp, then the act, in the Hindi transitive past so a note reads the same of a woman or a man; no ordinal and no second figure: '10:20. Asked the coach number again.' | '10:20। फिर से डिब्बे का नंबर पूछा।'; '11:55. Changed seats again.' | '11:55। फिर सीट बदली।'; '1:40. Woke everyone for tea.' | '1:40। चाय के लिए सबको जगाया।'; '12:10. Repacked the bag again.' | '12:10। फिर से बैग बाँधा।'; '9:50. Finished all the snacks.' | '9:50। सारा नाश्ता ख़त्म किया।'; '10:00 onwards. Hummed the same tune.' | '10:00 से। वही धुन गुनगुनाई।'. Never on a decision whose task the note bears on (rule 20), as often on women as on men, lengths kept even within a decision (story_take.length_faults).
catchphrases: '9:40, aaspaas nahin.' | '9:40, आसपास नहीं।' | '9:40, not "around".' (the correction; his one catchphrase with a number in it, said whenever anyone gives a time with 'around' or 'about' in it; it replaced '9:40, not 9:45.', which held two figures; the owner may keep the old line as a marked exception, since the players' judge picked it)
'Nahin. Chart ban chuka hai.' | 'नहीं। चार्ट बन चुका है।' | 'No. The chart has been prepared.' (his final no: once the railway chart is out, nothing changes)

'Aakhri dibbe tak main yahin hoon.' | 'आख़िरी डिब्बे तक मैं यहीं हूँ।' | 'I'm here till the last coach goes.' (the platform vigil, the colony-gate boy grown up; the readers marked it true, and Mausa ji's goodbye now leaves before the train moves, so the vigil is Papa's alone)

'Pata nahin, Tinku. / Dal andaaze se banti hai.' | 'पता नहीं, टिंकू। / दाल अंदाज़े से बनती है।' | 'No idea, Tinku. / Dal is done when it tastes right.' (when anyone asks how long the dal takes: the one question the man of minutes answers 'Pata nahin', with the plain words every home cook uses; it replaces the maxim 'Dal ghadi dekhkar nahin banti. Swaad se banti hai.', which read as a made-up saying)
voice.exclamation: 'Kamaal hai.' | 'कमाल है।' | English mode 'Remarkable.' Said flat, with a full stop and never an exclamation mark, a whole sentence that keeps its verb. Two uses: real surprise at good news, which he then carries straight to Nani ('Kamaal hai. Mummy ji ko abhi batata hoon.'), and dry irony, in two bubbles ('Kal ki gaadi ka ticket aaj raat book kiya? / Kamaal hai.'; the power cut that came on time). No religious meaning: 'kamaal' is an everyday word for a wonder or a feat. His alone as an exclamation (Mama ji's 'Kamaal!' went in the matrix, 2.15). The English rendering avoids every mild oath (Gosh, Goodness, Good grief).
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: plain, said as a fact against himself: what he said, that it was wrong, and where the right answer is: 'Maine 9:40 kaha tha. / Galat nikla. / Board par 9:25 hai.' | 'मैंने 9:40 कहा था। / ग़लत निकला। / बोर्ड पर 9:25 है।' | 'I said 9:40. / I was wrong. / The board says 9:25.' No stamp and no trade word: 'Maine ... kaha tha. Galat nikla.' is how anyone owns a wrong fact ('9:40 mera time tha' was heard as 'it was my turn'). His own past with ने, so nothing marks you. It sorts apart by shape from Mausa ji's subjectless 'Galti hui.', Tinku's 'Sorry, meri galti.' and Mausi's tripled 'sorry'. THANKS, plain and warm: to Nani and the elders, never a register word; he praises the timing of what they did, the highest praise he knows: 'Mummy ji, chai bilkul time par thi.' | 'मम्मी जी, चाय बिल्कुल टाइम पर थी।' | 'Mummy ji, the tea was right on time.'; to you and Tinku, his own shape, the deed logged with no verb about the one he thanks, then the hand-over: 'Raat bhar, list ke saath. Darj hai. / Wo list ab tumhari hai.' | 'रात भर, लिस्ट के साथ। दर्ज है। / वो लिस्ट अब तुम्हारी है।' | 'All night, with the list. Noted. / That list is yours now.' (the matrix's '6:00, gate par. Noted.'; 'Achha kiya' is Mummy's and Mausa ji's); to strangers and the TT, 'Thank you, ji.' | 'थैंक यू, जी।' | 'Thank you, ji.', the plain words people say, his by the whole sentences around it ('Ji, S4 mein solah hain.') and apart from Mami's 'Thank you, Bhaiya ji.' by the bare 'ji' ('Dhanyavaad' is announcement Hindi and reads Sanskritised in a person's mouth). WHEN HE IS THANKED: the everyday brush-off, then the next job: 'Roz ka kaam hai. / Ab wapsi ka ticket dekhta hoon.' | 'रोज़ का काम है। / अब वापसी का टिकट देखता हूँ।' | 'It's nothing, I do it every day. / Now for the return tickets.' (no 'Arre': Mummy's thanks reply opens on it, and the matrix gives 'arre' to Captain sahab). By text: 'No need.' and the next job. 'Darj hai.' is never his thanks for a kindness done for him (Nani's tea gets praise of its timing); it logs a fact, or a duty you or Tinku carried, and is 'Noted.' in his typing. LOVE: never said in words. A deed done ahead of time, said as a plain fact ('Didi, neeche ki berth aapki hai. / March mein hi ho gayi thi.'); 'Reached?' typed after any journey you make without him (his alone); standing on the platform till the last coach has gone ('Aakhri dibbe tak main yahin hoon.'), the colony-gate boy grown up; good news carried first to Nani. The nearest he comes to pride is the album's count: 'Four trains this year. / Nobody ever had to remind you.'
uses: Clock times in figures, to the minute (9:40, 6:35, 8:55); durations in the words people say (do ghante, das minute, baarah minute late)

Kamaal hai | कमाल है | Remarkable
Sab confirm hai | सब कन्फ़र्म है | All confirmed (his railway praise to the group, at most once a chapter)
Nahin. Chart ban chuka hai | नहीं। चार्ट बन चुका है | No. The chart has been prepared
Kripya dhyan dein | कृपया ध्यान दें | Attention, please (only to open a joke)

Thanks: 'chai bilkul time par thi' (to elders, praise of the timing); the deed logged, then the hand-over: 'Raat bhar, list ke saath. Darj hai.' | रात भर, लिस्ट के साथ। दर्ज है। | All night, with the list. Noted. (to the young); 'Thank you, ji' | थैंक यू, जी | Thank you, ji (to strangers and the TT)
Being thanked: 'Roz ka kaam hai.' | रोज़ का काम है। | It's nothing, I do it every day, then the next job
Darj hai | दर्ज है | Noted (his reply to a fact, and his thanks to the young as the deed logged; never for a kindness done for him)
Everyday fillers, at the head or in the middle of a sentence: suno (to Mummy), achha, haan, bas; the town's Hindustani: fikr mat kijiye, zaroor

Railway Hindi verbs: gaadi lag gayi (drawn up at the platform), gaadi chhooti, gaadi chal padi, chart ban gaya, berth mil gayi; and the counter's English verbs with kar or ho: book kiya, book kar deta hoon, confirm ho gaya
'9:40 wali' (a train named by its time)

Railway nouns: gaadi, maal gaadi (goods train), dibba and aakhri dibba (coach, the last coach), patri (track), coach, berth, platform, PNR, chart, waiting list, booking, ticket (masculine), TT, running status, board
His past: 'mere pitaji' | मेरे पिताजी, a goods-train guard; colony ka gate; maal gaadi
The dal: dal, andaaze se (by feel, the cook's everyday word), which is how the one untimed thing in his life gets made
Mummy ji, Didi, Bhai sahab, Captain sahab, Masterji (with आप); Tinku (तुम); 'Suno,' to Mummy
never: Vague time words: about, roughly, around, nearly | लगभग, क़रीब, आसपास | lagbhag, kareeb (except quoting the word back in his correction); a script can check his lines for these
'sharp' as a time word: his minute is exact already, and three askers wore the word out

A robot count where people say hours ('120 minute' for two hours), a minute stamp on a family member's kindness ('5:52 par chai...'), or 'Darj hai.' or 'Noted.' as thanks for a kindness done for him (Nani's tea): a register is for parcels, not for Nani. To the young it logs a duty they carried, with no minute stamp ('Raat bhar, list ke saath. Darj hai.')
An English verb with kar or ho built on a home thing ('cup return karo', 'MCB check karo': Mummy's mark); a whole English clause (Mama ji's and Mami's way)
'jaldi karo' or any 'hurry up': he says the time left instead
'I missed you', 'I'm proud of you', 'love', 'Bahut khushi hui' or any word about his own feelings

Other people's set phrases (the common fillers are free; these are not): Captain sahab's 'Arre waah.', Mausa ji's one-word 'Theek.' and 'Lo.', his 'Hmm. Isme kya.' and his 'Achha kiya.', Nani's 'Bas.' as a closer and 'Khush raho', Masterji's 'Jeete raho' and 'Dekhiye' as an opener, Mausi's 'Suno, suno, suno!' and 'Shabaash!', Mummy's 'Badhai ho!' and her 'Bahut achha kiya', Mami's 'Congratulations.', 'Correct?' and 'Tick.', Tinku's 'haan?' tag and 'Sorry, meri galti.', Mama ji's 'aur haan' run-on and 'Don't worry', your 'Pehle ___' and 'Badhiya'; any cricket call ('not out', 'Next ball'); and 'Mubarak ho', which stays unused so the congratulation leans to no one community
'checker' for the TT (an outsider's word), and announcement Hindi in his own mouth ('Dhanyavaad'): his railway words are the ones railway people say
Prices or money (Mummy's), scores or cricket words (Tinku's and Captain sahab's), ordinals or numbered items (nobody's in speech)
Two figures in one bubble (the only exception is the Tamil whisper count)
beta, or any word for you that fixes gender (rule 8; rulebook Q7)
A Hindi form that marks your gender: no -ोगे/-ोगी future, no 'pahunch gaye/gayi', no 'thak gaye', no 'kaun jaayega?' (rule 66); questions to you use the subjunctive ('कौन रखे?')
Whether you travel on his pass: the pass rules treat a grown son and a grown daughter differently (rule 8)
A temperament word about anyone: moody, shy, emotional, bossy, lazy

Anything that doubts a report of harassment, of being followed, or a dowry demand, or calls one a misunderstanding (rule 22). Above all his own habit turned on one: no 'Kitne baje?', 'Kab?' or 'time bataiye' asked of a report as if it needs a time to count, and no proof word (saboot, likhit, writing, proof) near a report beat
A rule for choosing in his ask; only the goal of the moment, never the number the two tie on (rule 37); a card person's name or a card note's words in any bubble (rule 36)
A joke while he asks (rule 37); a joke at anyone's cost
Any religious word or exclamation (rule 3): no Hai Ram, Bhagwan, Allah, Rab, Wahe Guru, Ishwar; in English mode no Gosh, Goodness, Good grief, Thank God
Slang: chill, bro, scene, whatever
A shout bubble, an exclamation mark, or a year on screen (rules 2 and 35)
address: YOU: तुम only in lines that show no gender (rule 66): commands ('सो लो', 'देखो'), 'who should' asks in the subjunctive ('टीटी के लिए टिकट कौन रखे?'), and lines where you are not the doer ('आज रात इंचार्ज तुम हो।', 'तुम्हें कभी याद नहीं दिलाना पड़ा।'). His thanks to you has no verb about you ('रात भर, लिस्ट के साथ। दर्ज है।'). One line falls outside the three shapes: the album's 'इस साल चार बार गाड़ी पकड़ी।', a past with ने where you are the doer and the verb agrees with गाड़ी. It marks no gender, but rule 66 does not name that shape, so the owner either adds 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' as a fourth shape or has the native reader clear the line onto the build's cleared list; no wording change if the owner agrees. Possessives agree with the thing, not you ('बर्थ 36 तुम्हारी है', 'वो लिस्ट अब तुम्हारी है'). No name, no beta, no family word; he often opens with the time instead of 'you'. You answer 'Ji Papa' and आप, exactly as you speak to Mummy.

NANI: 'Mummy ji', आप and -इए ('Mummy ji, aap fikr mat kijiye.'). She is the one he talks to most and longest, because she lets him finish, and the one he carries good news to first. Readers confirm the word carries no community lean.

MUMMY: no name and no title; he opens with 'Suno,' or with the time ('Suno, nau baj gaye.'), the way Indian couples who never use first names talk; both say तुम, so the game's own couple carries no honorific-to-husband pattern.
MAMA JI: to his face तुम and no name (the household has no first names); to you he is 'Mama ji'. Mama ji calls him 'Jija ji'.
TINKU: 'Tinku', तुम.
MAUSI: 'Didi', आप. MAUSA JI: 'Bhai sahab', आप. Both wait on the Hindi-first and South Indian readers (rule 65) and the one family address table.
MASTERJI and CAPTAIN SAHAB: by their titles, आप.
MAMI: no name, आप (his formality, even to a younger in-law).
A CHILD: commands only ('Gilaas seedha karo.'), so no gender.
STRANGERS AND CARD PEOPLE: आप and 'ji', always; to the TT the count comes first ('Ji, S4 mein solah hain.' | 'जी, S4 में सोलह हैं।') and the thanks is 'Thank you, ji.'
samples: GIVING AN ORDER (the lead-in to the 1.08 ask: the headcount, then the goal of the moment; rule 37, both halves of the twin in this same three-bubble shape): 'There are sixteen of us. / We have only twelve berths. / The train leaves at 9:40.' | 'Hum solah log hain. / Berth sirf baarah hain. / Gaadi chhootne ka time 9:40 hai.' | 'हम सोलह लोग हैं। / बर्थ सिर्फ़ बारह हैं। / गाड़ी छूटने का समय 9:40 है।' (Kept. One figure a bubble. Count before the noun. The third bubble is a station announcement's own shape. No filler and no joke: it is the ask's lead-in.)

ANNOUNCING WHAT COMES NEXT (the train pulls in at the junction): 'The train is in. / S4 is at the front. / Bags go up next.' | 'Gaadi lag gayi hai. / S4 aage hai. / Ab bag upar jaayenge.' | 'गाड़ी लग गई है। / S4 आगे है। / अब बैग ऊपर जाएँगे।' (Kept: the readers marked his whole-sentence announcing true. 'Gaadi lagna' is railway Hindi with a Hindi verb.)

GIVING AN ORDER (the bay at night): 'Bags go under the berths. / Lights go out at ten. / The TT comes next.' | 'Bag berth ke neeche jaayenge. / Batti das baje bujhegi. / Ab TT aayega.' | 'बैग बर्थ के नीचे जाएँगे। / बत्ती दस बजे बुझेगी। / अब टीटी आएगा।' (Kept, with 'TT' for 'checker': a railwayman says TT. 'Batti das baje bujhegi.' rings true. The futures agree with bags, lights and the TT.)

MOVED (1.10: he lays the list on the lower berth, turned to you, taps it twice and takes his hand away): 'My battery has died. / Tonight, you are in charge.' | 'Meri battery khatam hai. / Aaj raat in-charge tum ho.' | 'मेरी बैटरी ख़त्म है। / आज रात इंचार्ज तुम हो।' (Kept word for word. You are not the doer of 'इंचार्ज तुम हो'.)

WORRYING (to Mummy on the platform; the refreshing is what kills his battery by ten): 'Listen, the train is twelve minutes late. / Now it is fourteen. / I will check the running status again.' | 'Suno, gaadi baarah minute late hai. / Ab chaudah ho gaye. / Running status phir dekhta hoon.' | 'सुनो, गाड़ी बारह मिनट लेट है। / अब चौदह हो गए। / मैं फिर देखता हूँ, गाड़ी कहाँ है।' ('Suno,' is how he opens to his wife, now that the filler belongs to everyone. Minutes are right here: running status shows minutes. Hindi mode says 'गाड़ी कहाँ है' for a low-English reader. Said to Mummy, not you.)

TEASING (Mama ji on the phone, who has booked the night before again; 'Kamaal hai.' as dry irony): 'You booked tomorrow's train tonight? / Remarkable.' | 'Kal ki gaadi ka ticket aaj raat book kiya? / Kamaal hai.' | 'कल की गाड़ी का टिकट आज रात बुक किया? / कमाल है।' ('Book kiya' is back: the counter's English verb with kar suits a railway clerk (cast-wide 2). टिकट masculine, his standard form.)

TEASING (Captain sahab, at the lane ground on cup day): 'Captain sahab, you said nine o'clock. / I have been here since 8:55.' | 'Captain sahab, aapne nau baje kaha tha. / Main 8:55 se khada hoon.' | 'कप्तान साहब, आपने नौ बजे कहा था। / मैं 8:55 से खड़ा हूँ।' (Kept. One figure a bubble.)

PRAISING (the bay at dawn, nobody missing): 'Everyone is on the train. / Nobody was left behind. / All confirmed.' | 'Sab log gaadi mein hain. / Koi peeche nahin chhoota. / Sab confirm hai.' | 'सब लोग गाड़ी में हैं। / कोई पीछे नहीं छूटा। / सब कन्फ़र्म है।' (His railway praise to the group, at most once a chapter. छूटा agrees with 'koi'.)

PRAISING YOU (the album, in its own panel, never Nani's): 'Four trains this year. / Nobody ever had to remind you.' | 'Is saal chaar baar gaadi pakdi. / Tumhein kabhi yaad nahin dilana pada.' | 'इस साल चार बार गाड़ी पकड़ी। / तुम्हें कभी याद नहीं दिलाना पड़ा।' (The Hindi note's fix: nobody says 'four trains happened'. पकड़ी agrees with गाड़ी and पड़ा is impersonal, so nothing marks you. No wording change if the owner agrees.)

A JOKE AT HOME (calling everyone to dinner; deadpan, like the station loudspeaker; never while he asks, rule 37; rulebook Q5): 'Attention, please. / Dal has arrived on platform number one.' | 'Kripya dhyan dein. / Dal platform number ek par aa chuki hai.' | 'कृपया ध्यान दें। / दाल प्लेटफ़ॉर्म नंबर एक पर आ चुकी है।' (Kept word for word: the readers say every player will laugh. At most once a chapter.)

A JOKE ABOUT HIMSELF: 'I was born at 6:10. / Right on time, my mother said.' | 'Main 6:10 par paida hua. / Maa kehti thin, bilkul time par.' | 'मैं 6:10 पर पैदा हुआ। / माँ कहती थीं, बिल्कुल टाइम पर।' (About himself, at nobody's cost. 'Bilkul' added, as a mother would say it.)

THE DAL (Tinku asks how long it takes; the one thing he never times): 'No idea, Tinku. / Dal is done when it tastes right.' | 'Pata nahin, Tinku. / Dal andaaze se banti hai.' | 'पता नहीं, टिंकू। / दाल अंदाज़े से बनती है।' (The man of minutes says 'Pata nahin' once, and 'andaaze se' is the word every home cook uses. It replaces the coined maxim about the clock and taste. Said plainly, never praised by anyone.)

No figure.)

(His thanks praises the timing, the highest praise he has, with no minute stamp and no 'Darj hai'. The second bubble is the timekeeper finding that someone kept time for him; it asks, it never says what he feels.)

The one marked exception to one figure a bubble: a whisper with no listener, once in chapter 1.)

habits: DEVICE: a plain black smartphone in a plain black case, in his trouser pocket, charged every night at ten; normal text size, since his eyes are good. On the night train it dies by 10 pm because he has refreshed the running status since noon (the worry line's reason, shown plainly, never as an age joke).

SCRIPT: English in Latin letters for everything he types, in all three language modes, because that is how he types and because 'Reached?' marks no gender while 'पहुँच गए?' does (rule 66). Devanagari versions are given in case the owner applies rule 65 to typed messages too.

SHAPE: he types the way he speaks. Each line is one short whole English sentence with its verb, a capital and a full stop, one fact to a line, in order. Times in figures with a colon (9:40, never 9.40 or 'nine forty').

NUMBERS: the speech budget carried onto the screen: at most one figure a line, and at least one line in three with none ('Charge your phone tonight.'). No prices, no scores, no numbered lists (no '1.', no ticks: Mami's), no ordinals.

FOUR FIXED LINES, his only ones with no full sentence: 'Reached?' (after any journey you make without him; it means 'I missed you'; his alone in the cast), 'Noted.' (his reply to a fact you send, a PNR, a platform, 'Reached'; never to a thank-you), 'No need.' (his reply to a thank-you, followed by the next job), 'Good morning.' (under the 6:35 picture).

FULL STOPS: the family reads them as cross; they are not. The method notes cite NPR's report of a study where a one-word text ending in a full stop read as less sincere. The story can use the misreading once, with Tinku explaining it.
SPEED: one slow forefinger, the phone in his other palm; he rereads before sending; no typos; autocorrect off.

REPLIES: within a minute, always, distinct from Mausa ji's 'Ok.' an hour later. Distinct too from Captain sahab's telegram style with no punctuation, Mummy's and Tinku's lowercase, and Mama ji's and Mausi's doubled marks.
EMOJI AND STICKERS: none. VOICE NOTES: never sends one (he says they have no time in them); he listens to Mausi's in full and replies in text.

FORWARDS: none, except one good-morning picture to the family at 6:35, after the walk with Captain sahab (a sunflower, or a glass of tea on a sunny windowsill; never a lotus, which is a party symbol, never a marigold, which leans to ritual, never a god or a famous face, rule 3) with 'Good morning.' under it. Never politics, never false news, never a forward he has not read. The readers marked the 6:35 flower true.
CALLS: anything that matters is a call, made at the minute he said he would call. Nani gets calls, never texts, and good news reaches her by a call before anyone else.
TIMING: 'Reached?' goes out within ten minutes of your train's due time, by the running status, not the timetable.
ON SCREEN: single messages only, as live text on a painted blank phone or a message card (rules 30 and 40); no app look, no 'forwarded' label, no group chat (owner, 23 Oct).
samples: TO YOU, MARCH, BOOKING DAY: 'The booking is done. / We have 12 berths. / They are on my railway pass and 2 PNRs.' then, a month later, on its own: 'Mausi has added 4 names. / No berths are left.' | Devanagari if wanted: 'बुकिंग हो गई। / हमारे पास 12 बर्थ हैं। / मेरे रेलवे पास और 2 PNR पर हैं।' then 'मौसी ने 4 नाम और जोड़े। / अब कोई बर्थ नहीं बची।' (who is on the pass is never said, rule 8; 'railway pass' because 'मेरे पास' alone also means 'with me')

TO YOU, THE NIGHT BEFORE: 'We are in coach S4. / Berth 36 is yours, a lower berth. / The train comes on platform 3. / It leaves at 9:40. / Carry your own water bottle. / Charge your phone tonight.' | Devanagari if wanted: 'हम कोच S4 में हैं। / बर्थ 36 तुम्हारी है, नीचे की। / गाड़ी प्लेटफ़ॉर्म 3 पर आती है। / 9:40 पर छूटती है। / पानी की बोतल अपनी रखना। / आज रात बैटरी पूरी रखना।' (four lines with one figure, two with none; 36 is a real lower berth in the run 33 to 44, so Mausi keeps 33; the last line is the irony nobody remarks on: by ten that night his own phone is dead)
TO YOU, AFTER ANY JOURNEY WITHOUT HIM: 'Reached?' (one word, in English letters in every mode; the readers marked it true)
TO YOU, AFTER THE WARD NIGHT, 10:02 AM: 'Nani reached home at 10:00. / Sleep now.' | 'नानी 10:00 बजे घर पहुँच गईं। / अब सो लो।'
TO YOU, A WEEKDAY, WHEN YOU WILL BE HOME LATE (his one message with no number and nothing to arrange; the readers marked it true): 'The dal is on the stove.' | 'दाल गैस पर है।'
TO YOU, REPLYING TO A FACT YOU SENT (a PNR, a platform, 'Reached'): 'Noted.' | 'दर्ज है।' (the readers' 'perfect': the register word as a reply to a fact, never as thanks)
TO YOU, WHEN YOU THANK HIM BY TEXT: 'No need. / Your return ticket is booked.' | Devanagari if wanted: 'कोई ज़रूरत नहीं। / वापसी का टिकट बुक है।' (the brush-off, then the next job, as he speaks)

TO MAMI, DECEMBER: 'The guest train times are below. / The morning train is at 6:10. / The night train is at 9:40. / Both are confirmed. / I will be at the station for both.' | Devanagari if wanted: 'मेहमानों की गाड़ियों का समय नीचे है। / सुबह की गाड़ी 6:10 पर है। / रात की गाड़ी 9:40 पर है। / दोनों कन्फ़र्म हैं। / दोनों बार मैं स्टेशन पर रहूँगा।' (the Hindi note's fix for 'दोनों पर मैं रहूँगा'; रहूँगा is Papa's own future; she answers with her own list, and his name heads her item 1 'Papa: trains', in her shape, not his)

THE FAMILY, EVERY MORNING (mentioned, never shown as a group; if a message is ever shown it is one message card with no group name, app look or 'forwarded' label): a picture of a sunflower at 6:35, then 'Good morning.'

test_lines.moment: 1. The lights go out in the middle of dinner.
test_lines.en: Remarkable. Even the power cut is on time tonight.
test_lines.hinglish: Kamaal hai. Aaj bijli bhi time par gayi.
test_lines.hi: कमाल है। आज बिजली भी टाइम पर गई।

test_lines.moment: 2. Someone everyone was waiting for arrives two hours late. (to Mama ji, the latecomer; cross: the time in the words people say, then one word twice; the English goes, so 'late' becomes 'der')
test_lines.en: You are two hours late. Dinner is cold. Cold.
test_lines.hinglish: Tum do ghante der se aaye. Khana thanda hai. Thanda.
test_lines.hi: तुम दो घंटे देर से आए। खाना ठंडा है। ठंडा।

test_lines.moment: 3. A cousin phones to say they have got their first job. (to the cousin; no verb agrees with the cousin; the congratulation words are Mummy's 'Badhai ho!' and Mami's 'Congratulations.', so his is the plain 'good news' and the train booked ahead)
test_lines.en: That is very good news. / Which day do you report? I'll book the train.
test_lines.hinglish: Ye toh bahut achhi baat hai. / Kis din pahunchna hai? Ticket main book kar deta hoon.
test_lines.hi: ये तो बहुत अच्छी बात है। / किस दिन पहुँचना है? टिकट मैं बुक कर देता हूँ।

test_lines.moment: 4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it. (to Tinku, who made it; the loudspeaker joke, in place of the sugar joke Nani owns)
test_lines.en: Attention, please. This is not tea. It is sherbet.
test_lines.hinglish: Kripya dhyan dein. Ye chai nahin, sharbat hai.
test_lines.hi: कृपया ध्यान दें। ये चाय नहीं, शरबत है।

test_lines.moment: 5. In front of the family, someone shows that they had a fact wrong. (he is the one who was wrong)
test_lines.en: I said 9:40. I was wrong. The board is right.
test_lines.hinglish: Maine 9:40 kaha tha. Galat nikla. Board sahi hai.
test_lines.hi: मैंने 9:40 कहा था। ग़लत निकला। बोर्ड सही है।

test_lines.moment: 6. Someone they love is leaving, and they say goodbye on a railway platform. (to you, as the train starts)
test_lines.en: The 7:25 is moving. I'm here till the last coach goes.
test_lines.hinglish: 7:25 wali chal padi. Aakhri dibbe tak main yahin hoon.
test_lines.hi: 7:25 वाली चल पड़ी। आख़िरी डिब्बे तक मैं यहीं हूँ।

test_lines.moment: 7. Someone thanks them for something they did. (the everyday brush-off, then the next job)
test_lines.en: It's nothing, I do it every day. / Now for the return tickets.
test_lines.hinglish: Roz ka kaam hai. / Ab wapsi ka ticket dekhta hoon.
test_lines.hi: रोज़ का काम है। / अब वापसी का टिकट देखता हूँ।

test_lines.moment: 8. A neighbour passes on a rumour that the corner sweet shop is closing. (to Captain sahab, who brought it; he asks when, then makes a plan for their walk; no proof demanded)
test_lines.en: Really? When does it close, Captain sahab? / We'll go that way on tomorrow's walk.
test_lines.hinglish: Achha? Kab se band ho rahi hai, Captain sahab? / Kal subah walk mein udhar se chalenge.
test_lines.hi: अच्छा? कब से बंद हो रही है, कप्तान साहब? / कल सुबह की सैर में उधर से चलेंगे।

test_lines.moment: 9. Heavy rain floods the lane outside the house.
test_lines.en: The tracks will be under water too. I'll check the 8:15.
test_lines.hinglish: Patri par bhi paani hoga. 8:15 wali gaadi dekhta hoon.
test_lines.hi: पटरी पर भी पानी होगा। 8:15 वाली गाड़ी देखता हूँ।

test_lines.moment: 10. Someone asks them how they are.
test_lines.en: All trains are running on time. So am I.
test_lines.hinglish: Sab gaadiyan time par hain. Matlab main bhi.
test_lines.hi: सब गाड़ियाँ टाइम पर हैं। मतलब मैं भी।

test_lines.moment: 11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table. (to the child; commands only, so no gender)
test_lines.en: Never mind. Stand the glass up. I'll get a cloth.
test_lines.hinglish: Koi baat nahin. Gilaas seedha karo. Kapda main laata hoon.
test_lines.hi: कोई बात नहीं। गिलास सीधा करो। कपड़ा मैं लाता हूँ।

test_lines.moment: 12. A phone call brings good news. (the news goes to Nani first, not into a register)
test_lines.en: Remarkable. I'll tell Mummy ji right away.
test_lines.hinglish: Kamaal hai. Mummy ji ko abhi batata hoon.
test_lines.hi: कमाल है। मम्मी जी को अभी बताता हूँ।

changed: COMMON FILLERS (cast-wide 1): the bans on 'arre', 'suno', 'theek', 'pehle se' and 'Dekhiye' as plain words are gone; only other people's set phrases stay off his tongue (Captain sahab's 'Arre waah.', Mausa ji's one-word 'Theek.', Nani's closing 'Bas.', Mausi's 'Suno, suno, suno!', Masterji's 'Dekhiye' opener). He now says 'Suno,' to Mummy, 'Achha?' at news, and 'bas' and 'zaroor' mid-line, always at the head or in the middle of a sentence and never as a tag, so the closed announcement shape still tells him apart.

ENGLISH VERB WITH KAR OR HO (cast-wide 2): allowed where it suits him, and a railway clerk says the booking counter's verbs that way: 'book kiya' is back in the Mama ji tease, and 'Ticket main book kar deta hoon' in moment 3. His everyday verbs stay Hindi railway verbs, and he never turns a home thing into an English verb, which is Mummy's mark.

THANKS (cast-wide 3 and the 'Darj hai' note): 'Darj hai.' is no longer his thanks for a kindness done for him; it stays his reply to a fact ('Noted.' in his typing, which the readers called perfect) and logs a duty the young carried. Thanks to Nani is now the readers' line, praise of the timing: 'Mummy ji, chai bilkul time par thi.', with a second bubble 'Aapko kaise pata tha?'. To the young, his own matrix shape, the deed logged: 'Raat bhar, list ke saath. Darj hai.'; to strangers and the TT 'Thank you, ji.'. When thanked, the everyday brush-off 'Roz ka kaam hai.' then the next job (moment 7), and 'No need.' by text. 'Isme kya' is left to Mausa ji and 'Shabaash' to Mausi, as their notes give them.

SORRY (cast-wide 3): kept as plain owning of a wrong fact, 'Galat nikla.', with no stamp and no trade word; all three modes now say it the way people do, 'Maine 9:40 kaha tha. Galat nikla.' | 'मैंने 9:40 कहा था। ग़लत निकला।' | 'I said 9:40. I was wrong.', in place of the translated '9:40 mera time tha', which was heard as 'it was my turn'. 'Meri galti' was not added, so his sorry stays apart from Tinku's new 'Sorry, meri galti.'

MINUTES INSTEAD OF FEELINGS (real-India note): '120 minute der se' is now 'do ghante der se' (moment 2, the readers' exact fix); the thanks with a 5:52 stamp is gone; the good news is no longer 'Khabar 11:52 par aayi. Darj kar li.' but 'Kamaal hai. Mummy ji ko abhi batata hoon.' (moment 12), so the news goes to Nani, which is his want. The tic now says a time in the words railway people use, never a robot count.

CONGRATULATION (cast-wide 4): 'Badhai ho!' goes to Mummy and 'Congratulations.' to Mami if the owner allows them, and Mami's fix already holds 'Joining kab se? Bahut achha.', so Papa's moment 3 avoids all of those: 'Ye toh bahut achhi baat hai. / Kis din pahunchna hai? Ticket main book kar deta hoon.' The plain good-news line, then love as a deed done ahead. The old 'Sab confirm hai.' made no sense for a job.

RULE 22 (cast-wide 5): the rumour line 'Bina time ke khabar nahin banti.' (no time, no news) was his time habit turned into a demand for proof, one screenshot from 'the family wants proof'. Moment 8 is now 'Achha? Kab se band ho rahi hai, Captain sahab? / Kal subah walk mein udhar se chalenge.', a question and a plan for their walk. The never list now bars his 'Kitne baje?' or 'Kab?' asked of any report, and proof words near a report beat.

SHARED BITS (cast-wide 6): the sugar joke is now the readers' fix in his own loudspeaker frame, 'Kripya dhyan dein. Ye chai nahin, sharbat hai.', so Nani keeps hers. The last-coach vigil stays his (the readers marked it true; Mausa ji's note moves his goodbye to before the train moves) and is now a catchphrase. Moment 11 says nothing about 'only water'.

ODD ANNOUNCEMENT (real-India note): 'Ab kapda aayega.' is now 'Kapda main laata hoon.' (moment 11, the readers' exact fix), and the 'comes next' tic now says it is only for things that arrive or go on their own.

URDU-ROOTED WORDS (cast-wide 8): 'fikr' and 'zaroor' now come to him as the town's ordinary words ('Mummy ji, aap fikr mat kijiye.', 'Mummy ji, aayenge zaroor.'), so they are no longer the tailor's badge.

'PITAJI' (real-India notes): Hinglish and Hindi now both say 'Mere pitaji maal gaadi ke guard the.' | 'मेरे पिताजी मालगाड़ी के गार्ड थे।'. 'Mere father', said to his Hindi-first mother-in-law, was an outsider's word, and 'pitaji' is plain everyday Hindi with no lean to any community, so the readers' hold and the 'मेरे पापा' fallback are gone.

HINDI NOTES: the album line is now 'Is saal chaar baar gaadi pakdi.' | 'इस साल चार बार गाड़ी पकड़ी।' (nobody says four trains 'happened'), with the second bubble kept; the typed line to Mami is now 'दोनों बार मैं स्टेशन पर रहूँगा।' | 'I will be at the station for both.'; टिकट is masculine in his mouth, and the mix says that Mama ji's 'की टिकट' is either Mama ji's colloquial mark, said in both files, or becomes 'का'.

COINED SAYING: the dal maxim 'Dal ghadi dekhkar nahin banti. Swaad se banti hai.' read as made up. It is now the plain answer every home cook gives, 'Pata nahin, Tinku. Dal andaaze se banti hai.': the man of minutes says 'Pata nahin' once, about the one thing he never times.

ENGLISH MODE (cast-wide 10): lines that read as word-for-word translation now say it the way an Indian English speaker would: 'I said 9:40. I was wrong.', 'The chart has been prepared.', 'All trains are running on time. So am I.', 'I'm here till the last coach goes.', 'Even the power cut is on time tonight.', 'Dal is done when it tastes right.', 'Right on time, my mother said.', 'Sleep for three of them.'. 'Don't worry' stays Mama ji's, so his comfort to Nani says 'there is nothing to worry about'.
HINDI MODE FOR LOW-ENGLISH READERS (cast-wide 11): 'रनिंग स्टेटस' becomes 'गाड़ी कहाँ है' and 'walk' becomes 'सैर' in Devanagari; Hinglish keeps the English nouns.

WARMTH (the readers' 'robot' complaint): new lines to Nani, his main listener: the friction over time ('Mummy ji, aayenge zaroor. / Aap bas time bataiye.'), the comfort the night before ('Mummy ji, aap fikr mat kijiye. / Subah 6:00 baje sab aapke gate par honge.'), and the tea thanks with 'Aapko kaise pata tha?'. A thank-you to you after 1.10, 'Raat bhar, list ke saath. Darj hai. / Wo list ab tumhari hai.' (proposed). None says a feeling word, so his contradiction holds.
NUMBERS: the test set now carries a clock figure in 3 of 12 lines (5, 6, 9) and 'do ghante' in one more, down from 5 figures; he still leans on times, as one of the two leaners.

KEPT AS THE READERS MARKED THEM TRUE: the whole-sentence announcing; 'Reached?'; the 6:35 good-morning flower; 'Kripya dhyan dein. Dal platform number ek par aa chuki hai.'; 'Batti das baje bujhegi.'; 'Aakhri dibbe tak main yahin hoon.'; 'The dal is on the stove.'; 'Sab gaadiyan time par hain. Matlab main bhi.'; the Tamil whisper count. Also kept: essence, want, fear and contradiction; 'Tonight, you are in charge.' at 1.10; the booking line at 1.04; the 6:10 birth joke; 'Nahin. Chart ban chuka hai.'; '9:40, aaspaas nahin.'; the cross tell; every address word and every rule-66 form to you.

RULE 66: the checker will flag पकड़ी, पड़ा, चल पड़ी, जाएँगे, बुझेगी, आएगा, छूटा and the like in lines to or about you; each agrees with a thing (गाड़ी, लिस्ट, the bags, the TT), with 'koi', or is impersonal or the transitive past, never with you, and a native reader clears them. One line sits outside rule 66's three shapes: the album's 'इस साल चार बार गाड़ी पकड़ी।' is a past with ने where you are the doer; the owner adds 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' as a fourth shape, or the native reader clears it onto the build's cleared list. No wording change if the owner agrees. No line to you uses a participle before रहो or रहना (the new fourth flag).

FINAL POLISH: his thanks to you is his own shape again, the deed logged: 'Raat bhar, list ke saath. Darj hai. / Wo list ab tumhari hai.', with no verb about you, since 'Achha kiya' was Mummy's and Mausa ji's too (optional, for Mausa ji's own file: his samples[9] could become 'Hmm. Baitho.' | 'हम्म। बैठो।' | 'Hmm. Sit.' as he clears the chair). Moment 7 drops 'Arre' ('Roz ka kaam hai.'), which Mummy opens on and the matrix gives to Captain sahab. 'Checker' is now 'TT' | 'टीटी', the word railway people say ('Ab TT aayega.', 'टीटी के लिए टिकट कौन रखे?'). The exclamation's irony example is two bubbles. The sorry says 'Maine 9:40 kaha tha.' in every mode. 'Mere pitaji' in Hinglish too. Strangers and the TT get 'Thank you, ji.' in place of the announcement Hindi 'Dhanyavaad.'. The album's ने past waits on the owner's rule 66 ruling.

voices.name: Mama ji (मामा जी), 47

voice.register: Fast, warm and run-on: a man walking between two building sites with his right arm up, talking to someone far away. His shape is the job that grows and the worry that stacks. Inside one bubble he chains clauses with commas, and the 'ek kaam' he started with becomes three ('Ek kaam karo, gate pe raho, sabko andar lo.'); his questions are worry checks about named people, stacked, and he waits only for the answer to the last one, 'Pakka?'. A long thought runs on into a second or third bubble, picked up with 'aur' or, once a scene at most, 'aur haan'. Every bubble still ends cleanly, on a full stop, a question mark or a '!', so on a phone nothing looks cut off. That is what tells his long runs from the other three: Papa's are whole sentences in order with the times in them, Masterji's a verdict and a wander, Mausi's a tripled word and a question she answers herself; his is a list that keeps growing and a stack he waits on, and he never answers his own question. The common fillers (arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, bas, theek hai) come into his talk the way they come into anyone's; what marks him is the shape and where his words come from: people, health and city logistics. Feeling is said out loud, warmly, to one person at a time, with a hug: he is one of the two elders who say it in plain words (Mausi says hers to the whole room, loud; he says his to one face). Fear he says only to Mami. Humour is big and kind and aimed at himself (he plans nothing, he talks too much, he cannot say no to sweets), never at anyone's age, town, shop or work. He talks most to people far away, Mummy first ('Didi!'); in chapter 5, with the phone in his pocket, to everyone at the gate. With Nani alone he slows to short whole sentences, the only person he slows for, and lets her finish before he speaks. When cross he does not go quiet or slow (that is Mami's tell in his chapter): he still asks after the other man's family first, then the run-on stops dead and breaks into single words, one downward chop of his free hand on each ('Aaj. Abhi. Yahin.'). Never at family, a woman, a worker's dignity or anyone on a card. When anyone brings a report of harassment or a dowry demand he believes it at once and moves ('Main aa raha hoon. Abhi.'), with no 'Pakka?' and no question back (rule 22). His voice is never raised except the chapter's one shout at 5.03 (rule 35). Warm, and never the comic one while he is the asker (rule 37).
voice.mix: The most English elder. Hinglish: a whole English clause first, at speed, then a Hindi landing ('Don't worry, Bade Jija ji ko bulao.'). His English carries the jobs and the comfort (don't worry, no problem, sorted, last minute, booking, advance, I'll miss you), and his Hindi lands on family, food and health (Amma, Didi, ghar, sab, khaana, dawai, man, roz). Like most city people under fifty he also builds everyday verbs from an English word with kar or ho, and his are people and logistics verbs: 'miss kiya', 'call karo', 'book kar dijiye', 'check hua', 'dispatch kar dijiye'. Mummy's English verbs are the shop counter turned on home things ('ye cup return karo', 'MCB check karo'), so the two stay apart by what they turn into verbs, not by who may use the pattern. Mami, the other whole-clause switcher, runs the other way: a Hindi clause, then an English status. 'Ek kaam karo' to you, Tinku and Mami; 'Ek kaam kijiye' to vendors and elders. Everyday Urdu-rooted words are his too, as they are the whole town's: 'zaroor aaiye', 'fikr mat kijiye', 'kasoor', 'ain waqt'. Figures in Hinglish bubbles are digits ('60? 70 kar do!'), because romanised 'saath' is also 'with'. He cheers good news by making it bigger, not with 'Badhai ho' or 'Congratulations', which go to Mummy and Mami if the owner allows them, so he does not echo them in a shared panel. HINDI MODE: everyday spoken city Hindi in Devanagari that keeps the English loan words a Hindi-first reader already knows (नो प्रॉब्लम, सेट, एक्स्ट्रा, प्रमोशन, बीपी, टेंट, लिस्ट, वेटिंग, डिपार्टमेंट, क्रेडिट), so he still sorts in Hindi; where his Hinglish has a whole English phrase, Hindi mode uses the Hindi a Devanagari speaker would say ('बहुत गर्व है', 'सबकी याद आती है'), never English spelled out in Devanagari; 'चिंता मत करो', 'चिंता नहीं' or 'फ़िक्र मत कीजिए' for 'don't worry'; with Nani, whole Hindi sentences and आप. ENGLISH MODE: plain British English with his rhythm; 'oh, and' for 'aur haan'; 'Do one thing' at most once a chapter (his one Indian-English turn), otherwise 'One small job'; 'Oho!' stays; kin words stay as they are (Didi, Jija ji, Amma, Boss); never a spelled accent and never a word-for-word line ('everyone must come', not 'everyone comes').
tics: The job that grows: 'Ek kaam karo,' and the one job becomes two or three in the same comma chain ('Ek kaam karo, gate pe raho, sabko andar lo.'). The 'ek' is an idiom, not a count. 'Aur haan' (English mode 'oh, and') carries the run into one more bubble at most once a scene; every bubble ends on a full stop, '?' or '!', never on a trailing comma.

Stacks worry questions about named people and waits only for the last answer: 'Amma ka BP check hua? Dawai? Koi saath hai? Pakka?'. He never answers his own question (Mausi's shape) and never asks how you are (Nani's 'Aur tum.' closes that in the album). Each person in the stack gets a verb or a noun with them ('Amma ka BP check hua?', 'Amma andar hain?'), never a bare kin word. To you, Mummy is 'Tumhari Mummy' ('Tumhari Mummy kaisi hain?'), because 'Didi, kaisi hain?' said aloud, or with a comma, is him calling you Didi, and कैसी then gives you a gender.
Ends a worry stack, or a reassurance he is given, with 'Pakka?' ('Sure?'); at 5.27 it turns round into a statement. Never after a report of harassment or a dowry demand (rule 22).

People first, then business: every vendor gets 'Ghar mein sab theek?' and a question about their own people (a mother's knee, the children's exams) before 'Achha.' and the job. Names, not numbers, are his stock, and he keeps it even when cross ('Aa gaye, bhai? Ghar mein sab theek? Achha. Tent. Abhi.').

Makes everything bigger in words, never in figures: aur, sab, sabko, extra, poora, 'phir aur upar, phir sabse upar'. 'Full' ('full fit') in at most two lines a chapter; the rest of the time 'poora'. The plus-ten is a gesture, the flashed open hand, with no figure said; the only spoken figures in his year are 5.03 and 5.27.
Hands the how to someone else in the same breath: 'Bade Jija ji ko bulao.', 'Credit Jija ji ka.'. He plans nothing; he knows who can.

Credits people out loud by their job, to whoever is near: 'In-charge se miliye!', 'Ghar ke station master se miliye!' (Papa the parcel clerk, promoted in words), and from December 'District scorer se miliye!' (outside any decision beat, guests off the panel).
'Oho!' for good or bad news, by tone: rising with the arm up when a job lands, a falling 'Oho.' with a hand to his forehead at bad news. 'Aaiye' once at the gate, never three times.
Never talks over Nani: he lets her finish, then repeats her last two words back.
Hugs everyone he can reach while he says it out loud (a stage direction, never a word). Never you: household hands never reach towards you (rule 7).
catchphrases: 'Ek kaam karo, ...' | 'एक काम करो, ...' | 'Do one thing, ...' The one job that becomes three before the full stop. 'Ek kaam kijiye' to vendors and elders; in English mode 'Do one thing' once a chapter, otherwise 'One small job,'.
'Pakka?' | 'पक्का?' | 'Sure?' The end of every worry stack. Turned round once, at 5.27: 'Pakka.' | 'पक्का।' | 'For sure.' Never said after a report (rule 22).

'60? 70 kar do!' | 'साठ? सत्तर कर दो!' | 'Sixty? Make it seventy!' His quoted line and his only catchphrase with a number, said once, at 5.03, the chapter's one shout, with the open hand flashed. The owner is asked whether to keep both marked figures (matrix open point).
voice.exclamation: 'Oho!' | 'ओहो!' | 'Oho!' (the same in every mode). For good news and bad, and the tone tells which: a rising 'Oho!' with the arm up when a job lands, a falling 'Oho.' with a hand to his forehead at a delay or a worry. It is a sound with no word in it, so it has no religious sense, and no one else in the cast has it as their exclamation. Guard: never run on into a god-word, and never the city man's reflexes 'Thank God', 'Oh God', 'Oh my God', 'OMG', 'God bless', 'Shukar hai' or 'Bhagwan ka shukar' (rule 3). Each person keeps one exclamation of their own, so he does not use the others' ('Kamaal hai.' Papa, 'Arre waah.' Captain sahab, 'Haaye!' Mausi, 'Had hai!' Mummy, 'Baap re.' Nani, 'Hain?' Mausa ji, 'Uff.' Masterji, 'Gazab!' Tinku, 'Ish.' Mami, 'Badhiya.' you). A plain 'arre' in the middle of a line is free, as it is for anyone. Thanked, he opens on his own sound, 'Oho, no no!', not on Mummy's 'Arre, isme kya'.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: in plain words, out loud, then the blame made bigger: 'Sorry, Didi, poora kasoor mera.' | 'सॉरी, दीदी, पूरा क़सूर मेरा।' | 'Sorry, Didi, it's all my fault.'. Said to whoever he let down, in front of everyone, and to the next person in the same breath ('Jija ji, aapse bhi sorry. Aapki neend kharab ki.'); to you the same, plainly ('Sorry, In-charge, phir last minute. Mera kasoor.'). Mausi's sorry is the tripled 'Sorry, sorry, sorry!' with food held out; his is one 'sorry' and the whole blame. THANKS: a plain 'Thank you' to anyone who helped, with a word for their people: 'Thank you, [Name] bhai! Maa ji ka khayal rakhiye.' | 'थैंक यू, [नाम] भाई! माँ जी का ख़याल रखिए।' | 'Thank you, [Name] bhai! Look after your mother.'. For family, the thank-you is the room hearing what they did: 'In-charge se miliye!' | 'इंचार्ज से मिलिए!' | 'Meet the one in charge!'; for Papa 'Ghar ke station master se miliye!' | 'घर के स्टेशन मास्टर से मिलिए!' | 'Meet our very own station master!'. Thanked himself, he brushes it off with his own exclamation and gives it away: 'Oho, no no! Credit Jija ji ka, Boss ka, sabka!' | 'ओहो, ना ना! क्रेडिट जीजा जी का, बॉस का, सबका!' | 'Oho, no no! Credit's Jija ji's, and Boss's, everyone's!' ('Arre, isme kya' is Mummy's brush-off and 'Hmm. Isme kya.' Mausa ji's, so he does not echo them). To Mami in private, a plain 'Thank you' after what she did, said back to her. LOVE: said in plain words, one to one, with a hug: 'Amma, aapko bahut miss kiya.' | 'अम्मा, आपके बिना एक दिन भी मन नहीं लगा।' | 'Amma, I missed you so much.'; at a parting 'Didi, I'll miss you.' | 'दीदी, आपके बिना मन नहीं लगेगा।' and the worry stack after it; to Mami in private, what she did said back to her ('Aaj poora ghar tumne sambhala. Maine dekha. Thank you.'). Mausi's love is 'Haaye! Bahut yaad aayi.' to the room; his is 'bahut miss kiya' to one face. 'Bahut' is the commonest word in the language and free to both; the phrase 'bahut yaad aayi' is hers, and his Hindi mode keeps 'एक दिन भी मन नहीं लगा', not her 'बहुत याद आई'. FEAR: only to Mami ('Main wahan nahi tha, Boss. Phir se.').

'Don't worry' | 'चिंता मत करो' / 'चिंता नहीं' / 'फ़िक्र मत कीजिए' | 'Don't worry' (to others, never about himself)
'No problem' | 'नो प्रॉब्लम' | 'No problem' (comfort)
'Achha.' | 'अच्छा।' | 'Right.' or 'Good.' (the hinge from people to the job)
'sorted' | 'सेट' | 'sorted' (the word he wants back from you)

'Ghar mein sab theek?' | 'घर में सब ठीक?' | 'All well at home?' (to every vendor, before business)

People and logistics verbs with kar or ho: 'miss kiya', 'call karo', 'book kar dijiye', 'check hua', 'dispatch kar dijiye' | 'मन नहीं लगा', 'फ़ोन करो', 'बुक कर दीजिए', 'चेक हुआ', 'भेज दीजिए' | 'missed', 'ring', 'book', 'checked', 'send'
'Sorry' | 'सॉरी' | 'Sorry' (once, then the blame); 'Thank you' | 'थैंक यू' | 'Thank you' (to whoever helped)
'Oho, no no!' | 'ओहो, ना ना!' | 'Oho, no no!' (when he is thanked, before he gives the credit away)
'credit' | 'क्रेडिट' | 'credit' (always given away; the same loan in Hindi mode, so the Hindi line says what the Hinglish says)
'[job] se miliye!' | '[जॉब] से मिलिए!' | 'Meet the [job]!'
'department' | 'डिपार्टमेंट' | 'department' (his joke at himself: plans are Boss's department)
'arrangement' | 'इंतज़ाम' | 'arrangements'; 'last minute' | 'ऐन वक़्त पर' | 'at the last minute'; 'advance' | 'एडवांस' | 'advance' (5.06)
'bahut miss kiya' | 'एक दिन भी मन नहीं लगा' | 'missed you so much' (his love line)
'Aaiye' | 'आइए' | 'Come in' (guests, once); 'zaroor aaiye' | 'ज़रूर आइए' | 'do come' (his invitation)
'Oho' | 'ओहो' | 'Oho'
Common fillers in the middle of a line, as anyone uses them: arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, bas, theek hai.
Trade words, only outside chapter 5: pressure, flow, site, order, dispatch, pump.
never: Any spoken figure but the two marked beats (5.03 '60? 70 kar do!', 5.27 '60 plates. Pakka.'): no counts, times, prices, ages, 'do din', '60 kursiyaan'; no ordinals, not even 'first job' or 'first class'. The idiom 'ek kaam' is not a count.
A number smaller than his last, or 'kam karo' | 'कम करो' | 'cut it', in public. The one exception is 5.27.
'Nahi' to a guest; 'pata nahi' | 'पता नहीं' | 'I don't know'; 'baad mein dekhenge' | 'बाद में देखेंगे' | 'we'll see later'.

Any doubt of a report of harassment or a dowry demand, or calling one a misunderstanding (rule 22): never 'Pakka?', 'Sach mein?' or any question back after one; he says 'Main aa raha hoon. Abhi.' and moves. No proof words ('saboot', 'likhit', 'proof', 'in writing') anywhere near a report beat.
A bubble that ends on a trailing comma, or more than one 'aur haan' in a scene: on a phone it reads as a bubble cut off, and on every line it turns into a tag.
'Full' in more than two lines a chapter (it becomes the slangy-uncle gimmick); 'poora' does the rest.

Other people's set phrases (owners keep phrases, not fillers): 'Hmm. Ho jayega.', 'So jao.', 'Lo. Aadha.', 'Galti hui.', 'Mazboot.' and a one-word 'Theek.' or 'Lo.' line (Mausa ji); 'Bas.' as a closer, 'Chai piyo.', 'Dandi mat maarna.', 'Sab aayein.' (Nani); 'Suno, suno, suno!', 'Sorry, sorry, sorry!', 'Maine kaha tha na?' (Mausi); 'Haan ji, boliye.', 'Ye mere hisaab mein.', 'Iska bill nahin.' (Mummy); '9:40, aaspaas nahin.', 'Chart ban chuka hai.' (Papa); 'Straight bat. Front foot.', 'Next ball.', 'Dead ball', 'Not out' (Captain sahab); the readback ending 'Correct?' and the status pair 'pending' / 'done', 'Mera item tha.' (Mami); 'Bas abhi.', 'Barabar.' (Masterji); 'Kitaab mein.', 'Mera wicket.', 'Run tumhara.', 'Faisla tumhara.' (Tinku); 'Pehle ___.', 'Maaf kijiye.', 'Sab set.', 'Dikhaiye.' (yours). Single common words are not owned: arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, suno, bas, theek hai, sorry, thank you, tension, fikr, waqt and zaroor are free mid-line.

Other people's shapes: answering his own question or tripling a word (Mausi); the number before the noun (Papa, Tinku); items as 'thing, status' (Mami); closed verbless fragments outside his cross beat (Nani, Mausa ji); tea as his care (Nani's sorry, Masterji's love); a sugar joke about the tea itself (Nani and Papa have one).

Religious words and exclamations (rule 3): 'Thank God', 'Oh God', 'Oh my God', 'OMG', 'God bless', 'Hai Ram', 'Bhagwan', 'Shukar hai', 'Inshallah', 'Mashallah', 'Rab', 'Wahe Guru', 'Jesus'; in English mode also 'Gosh', 'Good Lord', 'Thank goodness', 'Thank heavens', 'Heavens'.
'Main hoon na' as a line of comfort: in his mouth it is heard as the film, so his comfort is 'Don't worry' and a job handed on.
Dowry or ritual words: 'dahej' | 'दहेज', 'lena-dena' | 'लेन-देन', 'kanyadaan', 'vidaai', 'phere', 'mandap', 'shagun', 'baraat'; nothing at all about gifts for the groom's side (rules 22 and 27).
His daughter's name or looks, or 'giving her away'.
'Chhota shehar' | 'छोटा शहर' | 'small town', or any put-down of Nani's town, Mummy's shop or Papa's punctuality; no age joke.

In chapter 5 bubbles (rule 36): 'phone' | 'फ़ोन' or 'call' | 'कॉल' anywhere in the chapter; 'pump' | 'पंप', 'motor' | 'मोटर', 'generator' | 'जनरेटर'; 'gate lights' before 5.07; 'old folks' or 'old ways' before 5.15 and 5.24.

To you: any word that gives you a gender ('beta' | 'बेटा', 'bhanja' | 'भांजा', 'bhanji' | 'भांजी', 'bachcha' | 'बच्चा', 'bhai', 'champ', 'yaar', 'hero'); a kin word standing alone in a bubble to you, or 'Didi' before a verb that agrees with a person ('Didi?' and 'Didi kaisi hain?' read, aloud or with a comma, as calling you Didi, and कैसी then gives you a gender; to you Mummy is 'Tumhari Mummy', and a possessive such as 'Didi ki dukaan' stays); and any Hindi that fails rule 66: 'तुम आ गए?', 'थक गए?', 'करोगे?', 'हमारे इंचार्ज', a participle before रहो, रहना or रहिए ('खड़े रहो', 'बैठे रहो', 'खाते रहो'), or a 'we' that takes you in with a gendered verb ('हम देखते हैं').
Brands of any kind: no phone, car, pump or sweet-shop name (rule 3).
address: NANI: 'Amma' | 'अम्मा'; आप and -इए ('Amma, aap baithiye.'). Short whole sentences; he lets her finish and repeats her last two words. She calls him 'छोटे'.
MUMMY: 'Didi' | 'दीदी'; आप, softened with 'na' ('Didi, rakh lijiye na.'). The first person he rings about anything. She calls him 'Chhote' ('Chhote ji' with आप when she is angry).

PAPA: 'Jija ji' | 'जीजा जी'; आप. To guests, 'Ghar ke station master' | 'घर के स्टेशन मास्टर' | 'our very own station master': the parcel clerk promoted in words. Papa's word for him is for the family address table.
MAUSI: 'Badi Didi' | 'बड़ी दीदी' (plain 'Didi' is Mummy); आप. She calls him 'Munna', तुम.
MAUSA JI: 'Bade Jija ji' | 'बड़े जीजा जी'; आप. He calls him 'Chhote', तुम.
TINKU: 'Tinku'; तुम ('Tinku, ek kaam karo.'). To guests 'our youngest' until December, then 'District scorer se miliye!'. She says 'Mama ji' and आप.
MAMI: 'Boss' | 'बॉस', in front of the family and in private; तुम both ways. Her name is never said on screen; she calls him no name, and 'your Mama ji' to the young ones.
MASTERJI: 'Masterji' | 'मास्टरजी'; आप. CAPTAIN SAHAB: 'Captain sahab' | 'कप्तान साहब'; आप (he greets him 'Catch?').
VENDORS he knows: first name with 'bhai' ('[name] bhai'), आप and -इए ('Ek kaam kijiye'); strangers and guests: 'Bhai sahab', 'Behen ji', 'Aaiye'; आप to all, even when cross.

YOU: तुम, only in rule 66 shapes: commands ('Ek kaam karo', 'gate pe raho', 'batao', 'sambhalo'), 'who should' asks ('Gate pe kaun rahe?' | 'गेट पर कौन रहे?'), and lines where you are not the doer ('Sab tumhare bharose.', where तुम्हारे agrees with भरोसे). To others he names you by your job with no possessive that could agree with you ('In-charge se miliye!', 'Poora week inhone chalaya', never 'हमारे इंचार्ज'); a message to you opens 'In-charge!!'; his sorry to you is 'Sorry, In-charge'. In a bubble to you Mummy is 'Tumhari Mummy' ('Tumhari Mummy kaisi hain?'), and 'Didi' comes only as a possessive ('Didi ki dukaan'), never alone and never before a verb that agrees with a person. No family word for you while rulebook Q7 is open. Your replies: 'Mama ji, sorted.' | 'मामा जी, सब सेट है।' with आप.

Rule 66 checker flags on his lines to or around you, each for a native reader to clear: 'पक्का?' and 'अच्छा।' (words that never change); 'सब तुम्हारे भरोसे।' (भरोसे agrees with भरोसा); 'सबको जगह मिलनी चाहिए।' (agrees with जगह); 'तुम्हारी मम्मी कैसी हैं?' (तुम्हारी and कैसी agree with मम्मी); 'अम्मा अंदर हैं?'; 'पंप भेज रहा हूँ' (about himself); 'नौकरी लगी?' and 'अम्मा ने दवाई ली?' (they agree with नौकरी and दवाई); 'पूरा हफ़्ता इन्होंने चलाया।' (a ने past that agrees with हफ़्ता; but you are the doer, and rule 66 allows तुम-lines only as commands, 'who should' asks and lines where you are not the doer, so this line waits on the owner adding 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' as a fourth shape, or on the native reader clearing it onto the build's cleared list; no wording change is needed if the owner agrees).
All of these go into the one family address table the India review asks for, signed off by the Hindi-first readers and the South Indian reader (rule 65).

Sure?' | HINGLISH: 'Ek kaam karo, gate pe raho, sabko andar lo.' / 'Aur haan, Bade Jija ji ko bulao, chairs bhi nikalwao.' / 'Sabko jagah milni chahiye. Just thought I'd ring, nothing special.' / 'Amma's blood pressure checked? Medicines? Someone with her? Sure?' | HINGLISH: 'Haan, Didi! LOVE, OUT LOUD, to Nani at the blue gate in December, her palm on his bowed head, his arms round her after (short whole sentences: she is the one he slows for). EN: 'Amma, I missed you so much.' | HINGLISH: 'Amma, aapko bahut miss kiya.' | HI: 'अम्मा, आपके बिना एक दिन भी मन नहीं लगा।'

SORRY, plain and then made bigger, to Mummy and then Papa, when his night-before booking has Papa at the station at dawn again. EN: 'Sorry, Didi, it's all my fault.' / 'Jija ji, sorry to you too. I wrecked your sleep.' | HINGLISH: 'Sorry, Didi, poora kasoor mera.' / 'Jija ji, aapse bhi sorry. SORRY, to you, ch 5, when he hands you one more job at the last minute (no gender: a noun line). EN: 'Sorry, In-charge, last minute again. My fault.' | HINGLISH: 'Sorry, In-charge, phir last minute. Mera kasoor.' | HI: 'सॉरी, इंचार्ज, फिर ऐन वक़्त पर। मेरा क़सूर।'

THANKS, plain, to a cook who came through, November, by phone (the writers' ear): the thank-you and a word for his people. EN: 'Thank you, [Name] bhai! Look after your mother.' | HINGLISH: 'Thank you, [Name] bhai! Maa ji ka khayal rakhiye.' | HI: 'थैंक यू, [नाम] भाई! माँ जी का ख़याल रखिए।'

THANKS, credit by job, to the guests at the gate about you (guests off the panel, outside any decision beat; a ने past that agrees with हफ़्ता, so no gender and no possessive that could agree with you; you are the doer, a shape rule 66 does not yet name, so it waits on the owner's ruling in the address table). EN: 'Meet the one in charge! They ran the whole week.' | HINGLISH: 'In-charge se miliye! Poora week inhone chalaya.' | HI: 'इंचार्ज से मिलिए! पूरा हफ़्ता इन्होंने चलाया।'

PRAISE, made bigger in words, to Tinku in December when the scorers' course letter comes (the writers' ear; on screen it is a message, since Tinku speaks only in ch 4). EN: 'District? Oho! Then state, then country, then the world!' | HINGLISH: 'District? Oho! Ab state, phir poora desh, phir duniya!' | HI: 'डिस्ट्रिक्ट? ओहो! अब स्टेट, फिर पूरा देश, फिर दुनिया!'

TO A VENDOR, November, by phone from an auto between sites (the writers' ear for his competence: people first, then 'Achha.' and the job). EN: '[Name] bhai! All well at home? Your mother's knee?' / 'The children's exams? Good.' / 'Now, one small job, please dispatch the order by tomorrow.' | HINGLISH: '[Name] bhai! Ghar mein sab theek? EN: '[Name] bhai, all well at home? Right.' / 'Yesterday it was "just leaving", the day before too.' / 'Today. Now. Here.' | HINGLISH: '[Name] bhai, ghar mein sab theek? Achha.' / 'Kal bhi "nikal raha hoon", parson bhi.' / 'Aaj. Abhi. Yahin.' | HI: '[नाम] भाई, घर में सब ठीक? अच्छा।' / 'कल भी "निकल रहा हूँ", परसों भी।' / 'आज। अभी। यहीं।'

COMFORT, to Nani in the front row, December (short whole sentences). EN: 'Amma, today you just sit. Leave the rest to us.' | HINGLISH: 'Amma, aaj aap sirf baithiye. Baaki hamare zimme.' | HI: 'अम्मा, आज आप सिर्फ़ बैठिए। बाक़ी हमारे ज़िम्मे।'

LOVE, OUT LOUD, to Mami on the Friday night of the wedding week, in private (the writers' ear only, since her tired beat stays wordless on screen). EN: 'Boss, close the list, the rest can wait till morning.' / 'You held the whole house today. I saw. Thank you.' | HINGLISH: 'Boss, list band karo, baaki kal subah.' / 'Aaj poora ghar tumne sambhala. Maine dekha. habits: Device: a big plain black phone in a thick black rubber case with one corner cracked on a site, painted with the screen dark and no logo, every word live text laid on top (rule 30). In chapter 5 it stays in his trouser pocket: never painted, never typed on screen.

Script: English and Roman Hinglish, never Devanagari (Nani's voice-typed Devanagari is the contrast). In the game's Hindi mode his messages show in Devanagari and keep his bursts and marks; where his Hinglish types a whole English phrase ('so proud', 'miss you all'), Hindi mode shows the Hindi a Devanagari typist would use ('बहुत गर्व है', 'सबकी याद आती है'), and single loans he would say anyway stay (बीपी, टेंट, वेटिंग, प्लीज़).
Shape: the run-on typed as a burst. Four or five short messages, each one clause of it, 'aur haan' a message of its own at most once a burst, then 'calling' before you can reply.

The first message is the person's name, capitalised, with his doubled mark ('Didi!!', 'Jija ji!!', 'In-charge!!', '[Name] bhai!!'); everything after it is lowercase, kin names included ('amma', 'nani', 'chhote'), with no full stops. To Mami in private the name comes with no mark at all ('Boss').
Marks: '!!' is his; a worry question takes one '?', because '??' is Mausi's; never '!!!'.

Numbers: his bigness is typed in words (sab, everyone, extra), never as figures and never as the plus-ten. A digit appears only when a fact someone must act on cannot be said another way, and then he would rather ring.

Emoji: 🎉 for good news, ‼️ for worry, and 🤗 (a face with no person, gender or skin tone) for love typed in words ('miss you all 🤗'): he is the only one in the family who types love. Never a person emoji; no folded hands until the owner rules (realism notes).
Capitals once a year, for joy (Tinku's course letter), never in anger: all caps reads as shouting, the 'aggro uncle' trap (realism notes).

Voice notes from the back of an auto between sites, starting mid-word because he presses record late; shown as a voice-note strip with their words as live text, and they run on like his speech ('...aur haan, ek kaam aur,').

Forwards: only weather warnings for Nani's district, each with one line of his own ('amma ko andar rakhiye na!!'), the warning painted blank. Never politics, religion, gods, famous faces or false news (rule 3; caricature traps).

When: just before his eight o'clock call to Nani, at red lights, and late at night after Mami's list. He replies in seconds or not at all, because he rings instead, and never reads a long message to the end ('ok ok call me').

Short forms: 'pls', 'ok ok', 'msg'. English verbs with kar come into his typing as into his talk ('book kar dijiye pls'); 'ok ok call me' stays as it is, because the readers marked it true. No spelled accent and no typo played for laughs.
Thanks and sorry are typed plainly too ('thank you', 'sorry didi'), never as a code.
In private with Mami, and only there, his asks come down, in words: 'sabko?' becomes 'ok sab nahi' becomes 'tumhari list'.
The game has no group chat (owner, 23 Oct). On screen he is single messages on a painted blank phone or a message card under a panel, and a message on the player's own phone waits on rulebook Q9.
