changed: COMMON FILLERS FREED (cast-wide 1): the never list no longer takes common words from him or gives them away. Arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, suno, bas, theek hai, sorry, thank you, tension, fikr, waqt and zaroor are free in the middle of a line; only set phrases stay with their owners ('Arre waah.', 'Kamaal hai.', 'Suno, suno, suno!', a one-word 'Theek.', 'Bas.' as a closer, and the rest listed). 'Achha' and 'Pakka' are no longer his alone; what stays his is the place they sit: 'Achha.' as the hinge from people to the job, 'Pakka?' at the end of a worry stack.

THE SHAPE, NOT A TAG (real India 1): 'aur haan' now comes at most once a scene and every bubble ends on a full stop, '?' or '!', so nothing looks cut off on a phone. In the test set 'aur haan' is in 1 line of 12 (it was 8) and no bubble ends on a comma. His long run now shows inside one bubble as the job that grows ('Ek kaam karo, gate pe raho, sabko andar lo.') and the worry stack that waits on 'Pakka?', which still reads apart from Papa's ordered sentences, Masterji's wander and Mausi's triple.

ENGLISH VERB WITH KAR OR HO ALLOWED (cast-wide 2): 'miss kiya', 'call karo', 'book kar dijiye', 'check hua', 'dispatch kar dijiye'. He is told apart from Mummy by what he turns into a verb (people and logistics) against hers (home things in counter English). 'ok ok call me' is kept as it was, because the readers marked it true.

SORRY AND THANKS IN PLAIN WORDS (cast-wide 3): sorry is a plain 'Sorry, Didi, poora kasoor mera.' and, to you, 'Sorry, In-charge, phir last minute. Mera kasoor.'; thanks is a plain 'Thank you, [Name] bhai! Maa ji ka khayal rakhiye.', a 'Thank you' to Mami in private, and when he is thanked his own brush-off, 'Oho, no no!', before the credit is given away (it was 'Arre, isme kya!', Mummy's brush-off in the same moment). Credit by job stays for family, as his way of letting the room hear it, not as a trade code.

CONGRATULATIONS (cast-wide 4): 'Badhaai ho' is off his never list (rule 3 does not bar everyday phrases); it and 'Congratulations' are left for Mummy and Mami if the owner allows them, and he cheers by making the news bigger ('Ab promotion, phir aur upar, phir sabse upar!').

RULE 22 GUARD ADDED (Hindi and rules note 2, cast-wide 5): never 'Pakka?', 'Sach mein?' or any question back after a report of harassment or a dowry demand, and no proof words near a report beat. A believe-first sample is added: 'Didi, main aa raha hoon. Abhi.' / 'Aap unke saath rahiye.' The register says it too.

LOVE LINE (real India 2): 'Amma, I missed you. Roz.' became 'Amma, aapko bahut miss kiya.' | 'अम्मा, आपके बिना एक दिन भी मन नहीं लगा।' | 'Amma, I missed you so much.', as a city son says it. 'Roz' was bending the line only because 'bahut' had been given to Mausi; 'bahut' is the commonest word in the language and is his again, while Mausi keeps her phrase 'bahut yaad aayi' (the matrix strike of his 'Bahut' is undone for this line). Typed love in Hinglish became 'chhote roz miss karta hai'.
RUMOUR LINE (real India 3): moment 8 is now 'Oho. Band? Mithai wale bhai theek toh hain? Pakka?', a reaction first and the shopkeeper himself, not a jump to his mother.

'FULL' CUT DOWN (real India 5): 'full' is in one test line ('Full fit!') and at most two lines a chapter; the sorry is 'poora kasoor', the tea is no longer 'full meethi', the gate order no longer says 'full'.

LONE KIN WORD TO YOU FIXED (Hindi and rules note 1): moment 10's bare 'Didi?' became 'Tumhari Mummy kaisi hain?' | 'तुम्हारी मम्मी कैसी हैं?' | 'How's your Mummy?' (9 counted words). 'Didi kaisi hain?' was tried first, but said aloud, or with a comma, it is him calling you Didi, and the feminine कैसी gives you a gender. The tics, never list and address table now bar a kin word alone, or 'Didi' before a verb that agrees with a person, in a bubble to you; 'Didi ki dukaan' in moment 9 is a possessive and stays.

HINDI MODE TYPING (Hindi and rules note 3): 'सो प्राउड 🤗' became 'बहुत गर्व है 🤗' and 'मिस यू ऑल 🤗' became 'सबकी याद आती है 🤗'; Hinglish keeps 'so proud' and 'miss you all'. The mix now says Hindi mode never spells a whole English phrase in Devanagari.
टिकट ONE GENDER (Hindi and rules note 4): the Papa tease is now 'अगले साल का टिकट भी बुक कर लिया? / मेरा भी कर दीजिए।', masculine like Papa's file, so it cannot read as a slip.

ENGLISH MODE DE-TRANSLATED (cast-wide 10, real India 4): 'everyone comes!!' became 'everyone must come!!' (Hinglish 'sabko aana hai!!'); 'Meet the family's railway!' became 'Meet our very own station master!' (Hindi 'घर के स्टेशन मास्टर', which also settles the open question on the gender of रेलवे, and promotes the parcel clerk in words, his habit of making things bigger); 'Meet the in-charge!' became 'Meet the one in charge!'; the chairs joke reads 'Short of chairs? People stand, dinner's over sooner.'; 'All on you.' became 'It's all in your hands.'.

HINDI MODE FOR LOW-ENGLISH READERS (cast-wide 11): he keeps the loans most readers know (नो प्रॉब्लम, सेट, एक्स्ट्रा, प्रमोशन, बीपी, टेंट, वेटिंग) but Hindi mode says 'भेज दीजिए' for 'dispatch'. 'Credit' stays क्रेडिट in Hindi mode, a loan the Hindi reader knows, because 'सारा काम' made the Hindi drift from the Hinglish.

SHARED BITS SPLIT (cast-wide 6): moment 11's 'Paani hi tha', one of four 'only water' lines, became 'Lagi toh nahi?', his worry going to the child; moment 4 no longer jokes about the sugar in the tea (Nani and Papa share that joke) but at himself ('Boss ko mat bataiye').
URDU-ROOTED WORDS SHARED (cast-wide 8): he now says 'zaroor aaiye', 'fikr mat kijiye', 'kasoor' and 'ain waqt' as everyday town words; a new inviting sample carries the first two.
VERBS BACK IN (cast-wide 9): his comfort and worry lines keep 'hai' and 'hoon' ('Amma andar hain?', 'Pump bhej raha hoon', 'Sabko jagah milni chahiye').

RULE 66 FLAG (cast-wide 0): the never list now bars any participle before रहो, रहना or रहिए ('खाते रहो' as well as 'खड़े रहो', 'बैठे रहो') and a 'we' that takes you in with a gendered verb; the credit line about you is a ने past ('इन्होंने चलाया').
WARMTH ADDED: a plain thank-you to Mami after what she held together, a word for the cook's mother after the thank-you, the invitation that asks for everyone, and a sorry to Papa for his lost sleep.

KEPT AS THE READERS MARKED IT TRUE: 'Pakka?'; 'Oho!'; 'Boss' for his wife; 'Ghar mein sab theek? Maa ji ka ghutna?' to every vendor; 'Aa gaye, bhai? Ghar mein sab theek? Achha. Tent. Abhi.' word for word; the chairs joke, now with the verb it was missing ('Kursiyaan kam padin toh log khade-khade khaayenge. Jaldi niptega!'); 'Didi!!', 'ok ok call me' and 'DISTRICT LEVEL!! 🎉🎉'. Also kept: his essence, want, fear and contradiction (worries about everything, plans nothing; makes anyone come); 'Ek kaam karo'; the stacked worry questions he never answers himself; people before business; the cross tell; slowing only for Nani; fear said only to Mami; the two marked figures; the address table.

CHAIRS JOKE MENDED (Hindi and rules): 'log khade-khade, khaana jaldi niptega' had no verb after 'khade-khade' and read as broken Hindi, not as his run-on. It is now 'Kursiyaan kam padin toh log khade-khade khaayenge. Jaldi niptega!' | 'कुर्सियाँ कम पड़ीं तो लोग खड़े-खड़े खाएँगे। जल्दी निपटेगा!' (9 words); the future agrees with लोग, not with you.

THANKED, HIS OWN SOUND (Hindi and rules): moment 7 opened on 'Arre, isme kya!', Mummy's brush-off in the same moment, and its Hindi said 'सारा काम' where the Hinglish said 'Credit'. It is now 'Oho, no no! Credit Jija ji ka, Boss ka, sabka!' | 'ओहो, ना ना! क्रेडिट जीजा जी का, बॉस का, सबका!' | 'Oho, no no! Credit's Jija ji's, and Boss's, everyone's!' (8 words).

'JUST CHECKING IN' OUT (real India): it is American office English. The worry call to Mummy now opens 'Haan, Didi! Bas aise hi phone kiya, kuch khaas nahi.', as the Hindi mode already had it; English mode 'Didi! Just thought I'd ring, nothing special.'

RULE 66, THE ने PAST (cast-wide): 'Poora week inhone chalaya' | 'पूरा हफ़्ता इन्होंने चलाया' marks no gender, since the verb agrees with हफ़्ता, but you are the doer, and rule 66 names only three shapes. No wording change; it waits on the owner (see OPEN).

OPEN, for the owner and readers: may rule 66 add a fourth shape, 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' (here 'Poora week inhone chalaya'; the same shape sits in Tinku's, Mausi's, Papa's, Mummy's and Mausa ji's files), or should the native reader clear each such line onto the build's cleared list? Keep both marked figures (5.03 and 5.27)? May 'Badhai ho!' and 'Congratulations.' go to Mummy and Mami? A Hindi-first reader checks 'घर के स्टेशन मास्टर', 'फ़ुल फ़िट', 'नो प्रॉब्लम', 'एकदम मिठाई', 'वेटिंग भी चलेगा' and 'Kursiyaan kam padin'; 🤗 is proposed as his and no other file claims it; every joke still waits on rulebook Q5.

voices.name: Tinku (टिंकू), 21

voice.register: Quick, warm and teasing: the fastest young voice in the house, and the one that sounds most like a 21-year-old at a small-town college. She talks in short, quick lines, mostly three to eight words, with the verb kept in more often than not, and many of them are questions. Her own shapes: (1) the tally tease, someone's habit counted to their face and softened with 'haan?' ('Papa aaj 4 baar tok chuke. Record.', 'Achha Mami, aaj ye 4 baar, haan?'); (2) the quick English question when something happens again ('Seriously? Phir se?'), which is also how her cross run starts; (3) the dodge: asked about herself, she answers with somebody else's count; (4) now and then, once a chapter at most, a live commentary aside from the commentator she wanted to be at nine ('Aur ye gaya!'). Feelings come in plain words, often English ones, and the joke comes after, never instead ('Sorry, meri galti. 14 nahin, 15.', 'Thank you.', 'Jaldi aana, yaar. Main din ginungi.'). Cricket is how she sees the lane cup and how she talks with Captain sahab, who gave her the book; with everyone else it shows only in her counting. In chapter 4 her questions are the decisions themselves, asked plainly with no tag (rule 37), crisp and warm, never the comic one. To Nani she slows into whole, careful, polite Hindi sentences with -इए, no English and no tag. Moved, she goes very short and plain ('March. Jawaab: haan.'). Cross, she gets faster but not louder (Mausi is the one who gets louder): flat and exact, she reads out the record in two or three chained bubbles, then the book snaps shut and the ear cups go on. She talks most to you, as an equal and a rival; then to Nani, in polite Hindi.
voice.mix: Young small-town Hinglish, the way a final-year commerce student talks at home: a Hindi frame with short English clauses dropped in ('Seriously?', 'Wait, wait', 'not now', 'No way') and the everyday English verb with kar or ho ('call kiya', 'miss karungi', 'try karo', 'relax kijiye'). Her counting words are a scorer's (baar, ginti, score, total, record); the cricket words (run, over, wicket, keeper, innings) come out on cup day and with Captain sahab, never as a code for a feeling. Commerce words stay out of her speech (stock, bill, balance, hisaab, profit), so the shop family's talk does not tip into the trader idiom; 'tally' and 'total' stay because a scorer uses them. No trending slang ('literally', 'vibe', 'bestie'): her quickness is in the teasing and the counting (realism notes, section 7). The common fillers are hers as much as anyone's (arre, achha, chalo, bas, theek hai, haan), and so is everyday Hindustani (fikr, zaroor, waqt). With Nani: plain polite Hindi, आप, every word in full, no English except Nani's own nouns (doctor, BP) and the one '80, not out, Nani.' at the homecoming. With Mummy, Papa and the other elders: the same Hinglish with आप and ji, her English kept to a word or two ('Seriously, Mama ji?', 'Papa, please, not now.'); her teasing rides on counts, so it never needs a familiar 'you' to an elder. With you: तुम and 'yaar', in commands, 'who should' questions and lines where you are not the doer (rule 66). Hindi mode: natural Hindi that a reader with little English follows easily. Her English clauses turn into Hindi ('Seriously?' is 'सच में?', 'Wait, wait' is 'रुकिए, रुकिए', 'Relax' is 'आराम से'); only the loans every Hindi reader knows stay (सॉरी, थैंक यू, स्कोर, रिकॉर्ड, पार्टी, स्पीकर, and रन, विकेट on cup day), and she says तीन-ज़ीरो, not the formal तीन-शून्य (Hindi-first readers confirm). Hinglish mode: every number is a figure ('3 baar', '4 chammach'), so a number is never misread as a word. English mode: plain young Indian English, numbers as words, 'haan?' and 'yaar' kept, and 'zero' rather than the British 'nil'.
tics: The tally tease: counts someone's habit out loud, to their face, then 'haan?': 'Achha Mami, aaj ye 4 baar, haan?' | 'अच्छा मामी, आज ये चार बार, हाँ?' | 'Okay, Mami, that's four times today, haan?' Only counts, scores and totals, never an ordinal, a clock time or a price.
Ends a tease with 'haan?' | 'हाँ?', in every mode. Not on a moved line, not to Nani, and not on a chapter 4 question.
The quick English question when something happens again: 'Seriously? Phir se?' | 'सच में? फिर से?' | 'Seriously? Again?' It is how her cross run starts.
The dodge, her contradiction: asked about herself (her marks, her plans, the form), she answers with somebody else's count, a different person each time: 'Main? Papa aaj 4 baar tok chuke. Record.'
Says 'Kitaab mein.' when anyone makes a promise: it is written down now. Never after a report of harassment or a dowry demand (rule 22).
Hands a choice over with 'Faisla tumhara.' It is a test, not a shrug: she scores what you do with it.

The commentary aside, at most once a chapter: calls a small household moment live, in the present tense, like a commentator: 'Aur ye gaya!' | 'और ये गया!' | 'And there it goes!'; 'Aur Mama ji gate par! Kya entry!'
Says the feeling first, in plain words, then the joke or the fact: 'Sorry, meri galti.' before the corrected count; 'Thank you.' before the thing she is thanking you for.
When cross: faster and flatter, never louder; the record in two or three chained bubbles, then the book shut and the ear cups on.
catchphrases: 'Kitaab mein.' | 'किताब में।' | 'In the book.' (when anyone promises something; verbless, so it marks no gender)
'Seriously? Phir se?' | 'सच में? फिर से?' | 'Seriously? Again?' (new, from the readers' note; the start of her cross run, most often at Mama ji)
'Faisla tumhara.' | 'फ़ैसला तुम्हारा।' | 'Your call.' (you are not the doer; the rule 66 checker flags तुम्हारा at a sentence end and a native reader clears it, since it agrees with फ़ैसला)
voice.exclamation: 'Gazab!' | 'ग़ज़ब!' | 'Brilliant!' Kept: the readers marked it as ringing true, and it sounds like UP, which suits a junction town. Nobody else in the cast takes it as their exclamation. Bright for a good surprise (a cousin's job, a phone call, the last ball); flat and ironic for a bad one (the lights going out: 'Gazab! Batti gul, khel band.'). Typed, it stretches: 'gazabbb'. Religious meaning: none in everyday Hindi, where it means 'amazing' or 'unbelievable'. Guard: never in 'ग़ज़ब ख़ुदा का' or 'ख़ुदा का ग़ज़ब' ('God's wrath'), and never followed by any name. The English 'Brilliant!' avoids every mild word that hides a holy name (Gosh, Blimey, Crikey, Goodness). A Hindi-first and an Urdu-speaking reader confirm; fallback 'Zabardast!' | 'ज़बरदस्त!' | 'Terrific!'.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: plain and at once, in English, then the fact put right on the spot, because she never fudges a count, her own included: 'Sorry, meri galti. 14 nahin, 15.' | 'सॉरी, मेरी ग़लती। चौदह नहीं, पंद्रह।' | 'Sorry, my mistake. Fifteen, not fourteen.' To an elder, the same words with the name ('Sorry, Papa. Meri galti.'). To Nani, in Hindi only: 'Nani, galti ho gayi. Abhi theek karti hoon.' | 'नानी, ग़लती हो गई। अभी ठीक करती हूँ।' | 'My mistake, Nani. I'll put it right now.' One sorry and no food in her hand, so it never sounds like Mausi's 'Sorry, sorry, sorry!' with a plate held out. To Captain sahab, the same plain words turned round: 'Galti meri, Captain sahab.' | 'ग़लती मेरी, कप्तान साहब।' | 'My fault, Captain sahab.' THANKS: a plain 'Thank you', then the thing she is thanking for: to you, 'Thank you. Kal raat ki dawai tumne sambhali.' | 'थैंक यू। कल रात की दवाई तुमने सँभाली।' | 'Thanks. You handled last night's medicines.' (the ने past agrees with दवाई, so it gives you no gender). To an elder, 'Thank you, Mausa ji.' with the name. To Nani, in Hindi: 'Nani, aapne bacha liya.' | 'नानी, आपने बचा लिया।' | 'Nani, you saved me.' WHEN SHE IS THANKED: she brushes it off and puts the credit in someone else's column, which is her contradiction again: 'Arre Masterji, kuch nahin. Bas gin liya.' | 'अरे मास्टरजी, कुछ नहीं। बस गिन लिया।' | 'Oh, it's nothing, Masterji. I only counted.' When Captain sahab thanks her for the book, a question back and the credit in his column: 'Thank you kis baat ka, Captain sahab?' / 'Kitaab aapne hi di thi.' | 'थैंक यू किस बात का, कप्तान साहब?' / 'किताब आपने ही दी थी।' | 'Why thank me, Captain sahab?' / 'You gave me the book.' LOVE: plain and short, never in a cricket code. To you at a parting: 'Jaldi aana, yaar. Main din ginungi.' | 'जल्दी आना, यार। मैं दिन गिनूँगी।' | 'Come back soon, yaar. I'll be counting the days.' (a real idiom in both languages, her counting turned tender). After a hard week: 'Baitho, yaar. Tumne bahut kiya.' The one love line in cricket is the birthday saying everyone in India knows, once a year, when Nani comes home: '80, not out, Nani.' | 'अस्सी, नॉट आउट, नानी।' | 'Eighty, not out, Nani.'

Short English clauses: 'Seriously?', 'Wait, wait', 'not now', 'No way', 'Okay'
An English verb with kar or ho: 'call kiya', 'miss karungi', 'try karo', 'relax kijiye'
Counting words: baar, ginti, ginna, score, total, tally, record | बार, गिनती, गिनना, स्कोर, रिकॉर्ड

the book, meaning her scorebook: 'kitaab' | 'किताब'; 'Kitaab mein.'
'Faisla tumhara.'; and, when an elder thanks her, 'Thank you kis baat ka?' with the credit put in their column

'Ji nahin' for a polite no to an elder
The everyday fillers, like everyone in the house: arre, achha, chalo, bas, theek hai, haan; and everyday Hindustani such as fikr and zaroor
Real everyday idioms, never proverbs (those are Nani's): 'batti gul', 'din ginna'
never: bhai, bro, didi, bhaiya, beta or any word that gives you a gender (rule 8)

'yaar' or 'oye' to an elder

With Captain sahab cricket is the talk itself (the trial, cup day), never a stand-in for sorry or thanks. '80, not out, Nani.' is the real birthday saying, not a code

the bare call 'Not out.', 'Next ball', 'Well played', 'Well fielded', 'Front foot', 'Straight bat', the toss call or any umpire's verdict (all Captain sahab's); 'not out' only after a total, and only for Nani

other people's set phrases, tags and exclamations (the common fillers are everyone's and are not on this list): Mausi's 'Suno, suno, suno!', 'Sorry, sorry, sorry!', 'hai na?' and 'Haaye'; Captain sahab's 'Arre waah.'; Nani's 'Bas.' as a closing word and 'Baap re'; Mausa ji's one-word 'Theek.'; Mama ji's 'Pakka?' at the end of a worry and 'Oho'; Mami's 'Correct?' or 'Sahi?' tag and 'Ish'; Mummy's 'Had hai'; Papa's 'Reached?'; your 'Pehle ___', 'Badhiya.' and 'Sab set.'
'Badhai ho' (Mummy's, if the owner allows it) and 'Mubarak ho' (left unused, so the congratulation leans to no community); her congratulation is 'Gazab! Party kab hai?'
any religious word or exclamation (rule 3; the list in matrix 2.13), any caste word, any brand
slang or English to Nani, apart from Nani's own nouns and the one '80, not out'
trending slang such as 'literally', 'vibe', 'delulu' or 'bestie'; her quickness is in the teasing and the counting (realism notes, section 7)
'the youngest' about herself, except to refuse it
'captain' as a job word on a chapter 4 card or question (rule 36: in Hindi the word is Captain sahab's title)
'sharp', already worn out by three askers
'too emotional', 'drama', 'bossy', 'argues', or any note word read as sexist on sight; nothing about women or men in general (rule 22)
the name, or a note word, of anyone on a decision's cards before or during that decision (rule 36)

any doubt of a report of harassment or a dowry demand, the word 'misunderstanding', or any ask for proof ('saboot', 'proof', 'likhit mein', 'in writing') near a report beat (rule 22); she writes it down exactly as it was said, and she believes it
'well done', 'oops', 'sorry' or 'please' in a chapter outcome line (rule 64)
a year on screen (rule 2)
a spoken bubble over 10 words (rule 62); a long run becomes more bubbles
address: Nani: 'Nani' | 'नानी', आप, polite Hindi only, -इए forms. Nani calls her 'Tinku', and 'scorer' | 'स्कोरर' only when the scorebook proves her right (Nani's note).

Mummy: 'Mummy' | 'मम्मी', आप, the same as to Papa, so respect is equal between the parents (realism notes 1.1, source [6]). When Mummy is cross she calls her 'Tinku ji', with आप, and Tinku knows at once that she is in trouble.
Papa: 'Papa' | 'पापा', आप.
Mama ji: 'Mama ji' | 'मामा जी', आप. Mami: 'Mami' | 'मामी', आप.
Mausi: 'Mausi' | 'मौसी', आप. Mausa ji: 'Mausa ji' | 'मौसा जी', आप.
Masterji: 'Masterji' | 'मास्टरजी', आप. Captain sahab: 'Captain sahab' | 'कप्तान साहब', आप.

You (the player): mostly no address word. When she wants one, 'yaar' | 'यार', the everyday word that young women and men all over north India use to a sibling or a friend, which marks no gender (the owner and the readers clear it under rules 8 and 66). 'oye' | 'ओए' only now and then, mostly typed, never to an elder. तुम, because 'elder' in her file means a generation up (Hindi-first readers settle it). Her Hindi to you is only commands (उठो, चुनो, बैठो, आना), 'who should' questions (कौन देखे?) and lines where you are not the doer (फ़ैसला तुम्हारा, दवाई तुमने सँभाली). Never बेटा, भैया or दीदी. You call her 'scorer'.
People on the cards: first names only, and only in rule 38's fixed line after a pick, never before or during a decision.
While rulebook Q7 is open, nobody calls Tinku 'beta' either, so you are not the only one without a pet name.

Tumne bahut kiya.' / 'Aaj raat ginti meri.' | Hindi 'बैठो, यार। तुमने बहुत किया।' / 'आज रात गिनती मेरी।' (किया agrees with बहुत and मेरी with गिनती; both flagged, both cleared)

habits: Her phone: a plain phone in a plain dark case, one corner of the screen protector cracked. It is painted with a blank screen and every message is live text (rule 30). No brand, app name, app look or 'forwarded' label (rule 3).
Two thumbs, fast. A one-word holding reply within seconds ('k', 'ok'), and the real reply comes later.

Roman Hinglish, all in lowercase, with no full stops: a new line for each thought, one question mark at most and never two. Never all capitals, which people her age read as shouting (realism notes 2.1).
More English than her speech: whole short English phrases sit here that she would say only in part aloud ('called u again', 'form sent', 'miss u').
Her numbers, typed: always digits, and only counts, scores and totals, in shorthand (3-0, 14/14, 1 mein 0, 2x). No clock times, durations or prices, in typing as in speech.

Stretched letters for warmth and for her exclamation: 'yesss', 'nooo', 'thank youuu', 'gazabbb'. Short forms: k, ok, idk, u, ur, pls, lol, no. for 'number'. To elders she types 'aap' and 'aapne', never 'u'.
Plain sorry and thanks type the way she says them: 'sorry yaar', 'thank youuu', then the reason on the next line.

Emoji: few, and only faces and objects: 🙂 😐 😂 😅 🏏. No thumbs-up: to people her age it reads as cold. No person emoji, since one carries a gender and a skin tone. Stickers go only to her college friends, and only drawn objects (a cup of tea, a duck for out-for-nil), never a famous face (rule 3).
To Nani she switches to the Hindi keyboard: Devanagari, whole words, the full stop (।), no emoji and no English. Then she calls anyway. Nani is the only person she does this for.
To Papa she copies his layout of one fact a line, but keeps her lowercase and drops his full stops, as a tease. She is the one who tells the family that his full stops do not mean he is cross.
Voice notes: never to elders (realism notes 2.3), only to friends. She plays Mausi's long voice notes at double speed.
When: late at night and between lectures. Never at the table while Nani is speaking; she is not a phone addict (the cast map's caricature guard).
She never forwards anything. She sends a photo of a total instead (painted blank, with the figures as live text). Almost no typos, and her numbers are always right.
The family group can be mentioned but never shown (owner, 23 Oct; rule 47). If the story needs her post, it becomes a single message card.

voices.name: Mausi (मौसी), about 55, chapter 1 voice

voice.register: Hindi-first; the loudest and fastest voice in the cast, warm and bossy like a front-room tuition teacher with her Class 3. She talks in bursts: two to four bubbles of short closed sentences, most ending on ! or ?, the first bubble starting over the end of yours. Her shape: she says a word twice to push the room along ('Chalo, chalo!', 'Na, na!'), asks a question and answers it herself before anyone can, and tags a statement 'hai na?' and moves on before anyone replies. A triple is kept for a peak, at most once a scene, and 'Suno, suno, suno!' is the one the family quotes back. Her long run is a string of short loud sentences, never a comma chain (Mama ji's run-on) and never a list (Mummy's jobs, Mami's statuses). The common fillers come and go in her lines as in anyone's (arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, suno, bas, theek hai); what marks her is the shape and the classroom and kitchen her words come from, never a word she owns. Pace quick and rising. When cross she gets louder and faster, the only one in the family who does; when moved she goes silent, the only time she does. No numbers at all, not even ordinals. One shout bubble a chapter at most (rule 35, which is 1.09), and never a whisper, because she cannot whisper. Each bubble is at most 10 words (rule 62), so a longer thought becomes more bubbles. She is never the asker (rule 37) and never reacts to who was picked (rule 39).
voice.mix: A Hindi frame with single English words in it, the older speakers' pattern in the realism notes (1.1). Her English carries feeling and school, not trade: sorry, tension, first class, topper, homework, copy (exercise book), class, teacher, fail, late mark; in chapter 1 also the travel nouns berth and chart. The everyday English verb with kar or ho comes to her as it does to any schoolteacher, with school verbs: 'top kiya', 'check karo', 'fail ho gayi', 'pass ho gaya' (of you only as a command, since a past said of you would mark a gender). Mummy is told apart by what she turns into counter English, not by owning the pattern. She never switches a whole clause into English (Mama ji's and Mami's way). Her Hindi is everyday small-town Hindustani with a teacher's words in it (inaam, bujho, copiyan, 'kaan pakdo', 'khaali pet'), and the town's ordinary words fikr, waqt and zaroor come to her plainly too; never spelled to sound funny. The tag 'hai na?' is a habit of hers, not a word she owns; in English mode it becomes the Indian English 'right?'. In Hinglish mode she reads as Roman Hindi with those English words (how a Hinglish bubble looks waits on rulebook Q6). A Hindi-first reader reads every line aloud (rule 65).
tics: Says a word twice to hurry, refuse or soothe, the way real Hindi does: 'Chalo, chalo!', 'Na, na!', 'Aao, aao.', 'Sorry, sorry!', or a name twice ('Munna, Munna!', 'Bhabhi, Bhabhi!'); to elders 'Chaliye, chaliye!'. The triple is saved for a peak, at most once a scene: 'Suno, suno, suno!' to call the room (the one the family quotes back), or 'Na, na, na!' at news she will not have. 'Haay' is never doubled or tripled, because हाय-हाय is a lament and a protest chant.

Asks a question and answers it herself, like the riddle-setter she is every morning, blurting the answer before anyone can guess: 'Kiski? Hamari!', 'Main padosan hoon? Nahin!', 'Andhera? Koi baat nahin!', 'Chai ya halwa? Halwa!'. The one question in the year she cannot answer herself is 'Kisne karwaayi?' at the lower berth, and then she goes silent.
Ends a statement with 'hai na?' and is gone before anyone answers; in English mode, 'right?'. Not on every line: a few a scene at most.
Quotes people back word for word: 'Pichhle saal tumne kaha tha…'. Her memory is exact; she never misquotes.
Says what she feels, out loud, to the whole room: love ('Bahut yaad aayi'), hurt ('Amma pehle Chhoti ko bulaati hain!'), sorry. Silent only when moved, palm to her chest.

Runs the room like her class: marks the late ('Late mark!'), sets the classroom's punishment in fun ('Kaan pakdo!', to Munna or Tinku), grades a favour ('Ekdum first class!', at most once a chapter), now and then fails herself when she is wrong ('Aaj teacher fail!'), and measures a loss by her pupils ('meri class ka inaam'). Her teaching is in her mouth, not only in one wordless picture, so she is more than the loud aunt who feeds. But the classroom is one of her two sources, never her stamp: about one line in four reaches for it at most, and the kitchen and her exact memory of what people said carry the rest (the flood is 'Achaar ke martbaan upar!', not her pupils' exercise books; being wrong is 'Galat kaun nikla? Main!').
Worries in quick questions about the body and the belly, and answers for you if you are slow: 'Kuch khaya bhi? Nahin?', 'Chot toh nahin lagi?'.

Food as punctuation: 'Pehle khao' (the only 'Pehle' that is hers; 'Pehle ___' as a courtesy is yours), 'Khaali pet baat nahin!', 'Muh meetha karo!', and something held out as she says it, her face in the frame. 'Haay' never comes just before she holds out food.
Report-card verdicts on habits, never on character, in all her judging notes ('Never sits still for long.').
'Hamara, hamari' (ours) for anyone she is proud of ('hamari topper'), but never of you, since it would mark your gender.
She always has an answer and almost never says 'pata nahin', which is why 'Kisne karwaayi?' silences her.
When cross: louder and faster, hand on hip, the basket bag set down hard, and her own catchphrase fails ('Koi sunta bhi hai? Nahin!').
catchphrases: 'Suno, suno, suno!' | 'सुनो, सुनो, सुनो!' | 'Listen, listen, listen!' (her opener and the line people quote back; her one regular triple. Anyone may say 'suno' or 'chalo'; the tripled call to the room is hers)
'Maine kaha tha na?' | 'मैंने कहा था न?' | 'Didn't I tell you?' (whenever something she predicted comes true, good news above all)

'Pichhle saal tumne kaha tha…' | 'पिछले साल तुमने कहा था…' | 'Last year you said…' (the quote-back; it marks no gender, because with तुमने the verb agrees with what was said; you are the doer, though, so it waits on the owner's rule 66 question in address 0). None of the three has a number in it.
voice.exclamation: 'Haay!' | 'हाय!' | English mode 'Haay!' too, the way Mami keeps 'Ish'. Spelled short, the way the cry sounds in a Hindi-belt town, not the film spelling 'Haaye' that makes her the screen's Punjabi aunty. For sympathy, surprise and delight, and just before she says a feeling ('Haay! Bahut yaad aayi.'). At most once a scene, and never just before she holds out food. Nobody else in the cast uses it. It has no religious meaning on its own; the guard is that it is never followed by a name of any kind or by 'Maa': no 'Hai Ram', 'Haay Ram', 'Haay Rabba', 'Haay Allah', 'Haay Maa', 'Ui Maa'. Never doubled or tripled (हाय-हाय is a lament and a protest chant). Keeping it in English mode also ends the old mix-up of her 'Oh!' with Mama ji's 'Oho!'.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: plain and doubled, food held out as she says it, her face in the frame: 'Sorry, sorry! Pehle khao.' | 'सॉरी, सॉरी! पहले खाओ।' | 'Sorry, sorry! Eat first.' To an elder: 'Sorry, sorry! Pehle khaiye.' Tinku and you now say a plain 'sorry' too; hers is told apart by the double and the food, not by owning the word. Wrong in front of everyone, she says so first and loudest, her own question answered at once: 'Galat kaun nikla? Main! Sorry, sorry! Pehle khao!'; now and then she fails herself as a teacher instead ('Aaj teacher fail, hai na?'). THANKS, GIVEN: plain words, out loud, to the whole room: 'Bahut achha kiya!' | 'बहुत अच्छा किया!' | 'So nice of you!'; and her teacher's grade 'Ekdum first class!' | 'एकदम फ़र्स्ट क्लास!' | 'First class!' at most once a chapter, so the grade stays a treat and never turns into a code. 'Thank you' is not her habit at home, as it is not for most of her generation; she says it to a stranger like anyone. WHEN SHE IS THANKED: she wants it heard: 'Achha? Zor se kaho! Amma bhi sunein!' | 'अच्छा? ज़ोर से कहो! अम्मा भी सुनें!' | 'Really? Say it louder! Let Amma hear too!' Only Amma's thanks, in December, makes her silent. LOVE: said out loud, to the whole room: 'Haay! Bahut yaad aayi.' | 'हाय! बहुत याद आई।' | 'Haay! I missed you so much.' At a parting, the same key: 'Abhi se yaad aa rahi hai!' | 'अभी से याद आ रही है!' | 'Missing you already!' Mama ji's love is warm and one to one, with a hug; hers is loud and to the room, with food.

never: Any doubt of a report of being followed or harassed, or of a dowry demand: no 'sach mein?', 'pakka?', 'galatfehmi', 'misunderstanding', 'imagined', 'chhodo', 'jaane do', 'hota rehta hai' about it. She is the first to believe, and the hard topic never reaches a bubble or a story panel anyway (rule 26); she has no line in the lead-in or settle of a hard decision. Her 'Na, na!' and 'Ye nahin chalega!' are for harmless news only.

Any religious word or exclamation (rule 3): no Hai Ram, Haay Ram, Haay Rabba, Bhagwan, Allah, Rab, Wahe Guru, Ishwar, Jesus, tauba, 'shukr hai', 'Ui Maa', 'Mata ji' as a goddess; in English mode no Gosh, Golly, Goodness, Oh my, Heavens, Lord, Thank God. No caste word, no brand.
Any number in speech: no figures, no counts, no years (rule 2), no ordinals ('teesri class' is struck), no 'ek-ek', 'teen baar' or 'sau mein sau'. 'First class' stays as an idiom of praise.

Any word that gives you a gender: beta, bachcha, bhaiya, didi, raja, rani; 'hamara/hamari' of you; any verb or adjective that agrees with you: kitne/kitni bade/badi ho gaye, aa gaye/aa gayi, thak gaye/gayi, -oge/-ogi, khaate/khaati raho (rules 8 and 66). 'How grown up you've got' becomes 'Chehre pe thakaan.'

Other people's set phrases, so the blind sort can tell her apart. These are phrases, not fillers: arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, suno, bas and theek hai are everyone's. Kept out: 'Arre waah' and 'Arre!' as an exclamation on its own (Captain sahab's, matrix 2.15; hers is 'Haay!'), 'Ek-ek karke' and 'Pehle ___' as a courtesy (yours; she keeps only 'Pehle khao'), 'Lo. Aadha.' and a one-word 'Theek.' bubble (Mausa ji's), 'aur haan' as a joiner, 'Oho!', 'full' and a one-word 'Roz.' (Mama ji's), 'Kamaal' and 'Reached?' (Papa's), 'Had hai!', 'Ye mere hisaab mein' and 'Iska bill nahin' (Mummy's), 'Gazab!' and the 'haan?' tag (Tinku's), 'Not out', 'Next ball', 'Well played' (Captain sahab's), 'Baap re', a closing 'Bas.', 'Chai piyo', 'Main yahin hoon', 'Khush raho' (Nani's), 'Uff' and 'Jeete raho' (Masterji's), 'Hain?', 'Mazboot', 'Galti hui', 'Ho jayega' (Mausa ji's), 'Ish', 'Tick', 'Correct?', 'pending', 'Congratulations' (Mami's), 'Badhiya' as a one-word verdict and 'Shukriya' (yours), 'Badhai ho' (Mummy's, if the owner allows it), and 'Mubarak ho' (left unused, so the congratulation leans to no one community).
A whole English clause (Mama ji's and Mami's way): her English stays single words, and school verbs with kar or ho.
A comma chain or a list: her long run is short closed sentences, never Mama ji's run-on or Mummy's and Mami's lists.

Character words or verdicts on anyone: aalsi, kaamchor, raub, besharam, badchalan, chalu; nothing on anyone's morals, marriage or dress; no sentence about ladkiyan, ladke, aurtein or mard in general (rule 22). Her talk is energy and care, never gossip about people.
The stock aunty's questions to you: shaadi, rishta (a match), salary or 'kitna kamate', weight, looks, skin colour (gori, kaali, saanwli) for anyone, 'naukri kab'.
A joke at her own body or age, or at her loudness as mockery: she laughs first and the strip laughs with her ('Meri class aise hi sunti hai'), never at her.
Film lines or famous catchphrases (rule 3): never 'Main hoon na'.
A second shout in a chapter; any whisper (rule 35).
More than one triple in a scene, or 'Haay' more than once in a scene or just before she holds out food.

Any card person's name, or any word from a decision's card notes, in a bubble before or during that decision, in either language (rule 36). In chapter 1 that rules out, until the decision that carries them: phone, tea, water, blanket, trip, 'last', bag, sari, tiffin, food (खाना), coach (डिब्बा), seat, window, family, everyone (सबके), पास, साथ, बार, तरह, joke, bus (and बस), platform, town (शहर), maths, coaching, teaches, and बोल. The test-set lines below are not panel lines; any line placed in a panel re-runs the build's note-word check.
address: To you: तुम, only in commands ('Ab batao', 'Idhar baitho', 'Pehle khao', 'Jaldi aana'), 'who should' asks, and lines where you are not the doer ('Chehre pe thakaan', 'Bahut yaad aayi', 'Tumhari khabar'); no address word, or her opening 'Suno, suno, suno!'. The first time in a chapter she names Mummy to you she says 'tumhari Mummy' | 'तुम्हारी मम्मी', and 'Chhoti' after that, since 'Chhoti' alone is opaque to a new reader (Nani's note). Never beta (rulebook Q7 is open, and it stays out until then), bachcha, bhaiya, didi. Lines rule 66's checker flags where you are not the doer, which a native reader clears: आई (agrees with याद), लगी (with चोट), मुझे (a pronoun). OWNER QUESTION (rule 66): in some of her lines you are the doer of a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing done and so marks no gender: 'Pichhle saal tumne kaha tha' (catchphrase 2, sample 5), 'Kuch khaya bhi?' (sample 8), 'khana khaya??' (typing 1), 'Parathe rakhe, hai na?' (test moment 6), and her thanks 'Bahut achha kiya!' whenever it is said to you. Rule 66 allows तुम in only three shapes (commands, 'who should' asks, lines where you are not the doer), and this is none of them. Either the owner adds 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' to rule 66 as a fourth shape, or the native reader clears each line and the build puts it on its cleared list. No wording changes if the owner agrees. The same question covers Tinku's, Papa's, Mummy's, Mausa ji's and Mama ji's lines of this shape.
To Nani: 'Amma', आप and -इए ('Amma, bujhiye kaun?', 'Pehle khaiye'). Never 'Ammi' (leans towards one community; realism 1.3).
To Mummy: 'Chhoti', तुम. In English mode, 'your Mummy' when she speaks of her to you.
To Papa: no address word, आप ('Chaliye, chaliye!', 'Jaldi kijiye!'); to you, 'tumhare Papa'. Never 'Tinku ke Papa' (a wife's way of naming her own husband).
To Mama ji: 'Munna', तुम (his childhood pet name; readers confirm).
To Tinku: 'Tinku' or 'hamari topper', तुम.

To Mausa ji: 'Aji' | 'अजी', with आप ('Abhi khaiye!'), since a wife who calls her husband 'Aji' says आप to him. The note asks for आप from him to her too; his file now has तुम both ways and no word for her, so the readers settle it in the one family address table. READERS' QUESTION: 'Aji' with आप is real, but it can sound like the 1970s film wife; many small-town teachers of her age say 'Suniye' | 'सुनिए' or no word at all. If the Hindi-first readers hear the film in it, her lines to him take 'Suniye' or no address word, still with आप, and nothing else changes, since her shape marks her without it.
To Mami: 'Bhabhi', तुम.
To Masterji and Captain sahab: their titles and आप.
To strangers: 'Bhaiya' to the stall man, 'Sahab' to the ticket checker, आप; neither is ever a card person.

What they call her: Nani 'Badi' (तुम); Mummy and Papa 'Didi' (आप); Mama ji and Mami 'Badi Didi' (आप); Tinku and you 'Mausi' (आप, with -इए); Mausa ji no word ('tumhari Mausi' to you); Masterji 'Behenji' (आप), what a neighbour of about sixty says to a schoolteacher of about fifty-five (Masterji's file has 'Mausi ji', which borrows the household's word, and is to be matched to 'Behenji'); Captain sahab and her old pupils 'Madam ji'. All for readers to confirm (rule 65), in the one family address table.

habits: Device: a big-screen Android phone in a plain flip case with no markings (rule 3). She reads it held a hand's width from her nose, since she is short-sighted and wears no glasses; that distance is her phone trait (six files share 'font at its largest', so it is not). Painted blank; every word on it is live text (rule 30).

Mostly voice notes, long ones, the phone held flat under her chin like a plate and spoken at full volume so the whole room hears. They open 'Haan suno....' and close '....chalo, khana kha lena 😊'. On screen a voice note is a live-text card: a play mark, a long bar and her first words, with no length figure, so no number reaches her lines.
When she types: Roman Hinglish, all lowercase except 'OK', spelled the way she says it ('haay', not 'haaye') and always in full, never short forms like 'h' or 'k' (Masterji's and Tinku's).

Punctuation: four dots '....' between every phrase instead of full stops or commas; double question marks '??', which are hers (Mama ji keeps '!!'). One long message, never a burst of short ones (Mama ji's), never one item a line (Papa's), never a list (Mami's); the one exception waits on the owner, if message cards are held to the 10-word cap (habit 9). She types her doubles too, with no commas ('jaldi jaldi', 'abhi abhi'), the one triple the family quotes ('suno suno suno'), and her self-answered question ('kaun jeeta?? hamari topper').
No figures, even typed: no times, no counts, no prices. Her daily send is a riddle, not a sum.

Emoji: 😊 at the end of nearly everything, even bad news (the family knows to read past it); 😋 for food. Never 👍 (Mummy's), never a person emoji (it carries a gender and a skin tone), and 🙏 not at all until the owner decides (realism 2.2).

Her one daily send is her own: 'aaj ki paheli' (today's riddle), a traditional children's riddle in words to the family group early each morning, whose answers she marks by voice note at night. Never a good-morning flower (Papa's), never gods, politics, a famous face, false news or a home remedy (rule 3; realism 2.2).
Timing: replies within seconds all day, answers a one-word message with a long voice note, and is sending from four in the morning. No reply means she is cooking.
Typos: autocorrect turns her Hinglish into English words and she sends it anyway; it is never shown as a joke on her.

The family group is mentioned, never shown (owner, 23 Oct). A message reaches the player as one message card. OWNER QUESTION (rule 62): the rulebook does not yet say whether a message card counts as a spoken line, with the 10-word cap, or as sign words. Four of her messages are over 10 words (samples 0, 3, 5 and 7). If the cap applies, each splits at her '....' into cards of 10 words or fewer, written out in that sample's note; no message changes until the owner answers. Split, every card still ends on her '....', '??' or 😊, so it never reads as Mama ji's burst of short '!!' messages.

How others' typing meets hers: Mummy answers 'ok 👍' within a minute in shop hours and never after nine; Papa replies with one full-stopped sentence; Tinku replies 'mausi 😂'; Mausa ji sits beside her and does not need to.
samples: To you, the evening before the train (a message card on the painted blank phone): 'suno suno suno....kal raat wali train....tum bhi saath ho na?? apni baatein seedha mujhe batana....tumhari mummy se nahi 😊' (listen listen listen....tomorrow night's train....you're with us, right?? tell me your news yourself....not through your Mummy). Gender-free: 'saath ho' and a command; 'tumhari mummy' because it is the first time she names her to you. If it is shown in chapter 1 it is a sign, so the note-word check applies (साथ). If the owner holds message cards to the 10-word cap (habit 9), it goes as three cards: 'suno suno suno....kal raat wali train....' / 'tum bhi saath ho na??' / 'apni baatein seedha mujhe batana....tumhari mummy se nahi 😊'.

To you, after any trip: 'khana khaya?? kya kya khaya?? 😋' (eaten?? what did you eat??). Kept, rings true. About food only: 'Reached?' is Papa's. Gender-free: खाया follows खाना; you are the doer, so it waits on the owner's rule 66 question (voice, address 0).
Voice note to you before dawn, a live-text card: '▶ Haan suno.... neend nahi aayi....toh socha....' (Yes, listen.... couldn't sleep....so I thought....). No length figure on the card.

Family group, early morning (mentioned, or shown as a single card): 'aaj ki paheli....ek thaal moti se bhara, sabke sir par aundha dhara....kya hai?? jawab shaam tak....tinku tum mat batana 😊' (today's riddle....a plate full of pearls, held upside down over everyone's head....what is it?? answers by evening....Tinku, don't you answer). Kept, rings true. The answer is the night sky; a traditional children's riddle, where 'ek' is the article 'a', not a count. If the owner holds message cards to the 10-word cap (habit 9), it goes as three cards, the riddle whole on the middle one: 'aaj ki paheli....' / 'ek thaal moti se bhara, sabke sir par aundha dhara....' / 'kya hai?? jawab shaam tak....tinku tum mat batana 😊'.
To Mausa ji at night: 'aji....bp ki goli ka waqt....abhi khaiye 😊' (aji....time for your BP pill....take it now). आप, as in her speech to him.

To Mummy before dawn on the ward night, from Nani's house: 'chhoti....amma se baat hui....unko bhi neend nahi....fikr mat karo....subah aati hoon....tum so jao 😊' (Chhoti....spoke to Amma....she can't sleep either....don't worry....I'll come in the morning....you go to sleep). Mummy, who never messages after nine, reads it in the morning. If the owner holds message cards to the 10-word cap (habit 9), it goes as two cards: 'chhoti....amma se baat hui....unko bhi neend nahi....' / 'fikr mat karo....subah aati hoon....tum so jao 😊'.

To you, after your good news: 'haay....maine kaha tha na?? ekdum first class....mithai kab?? 😋' (haay....didn't I tell you?? first class....when are the sweets??). Gender-free: no verb agrees with you.

To Mummy, her hurt typed and then smiled over: 'amma ne aaj bhi pehle tumhe bulaaya....koi baat nahi....main toh hoon hi 😊' (Amma called you first again today....never mind....I'm always here anyway). The 😊 is why nobody hears it. If the owner holds message cards to the 10-word cap (habit 9), it goes as two cards: 'amma ne aaj bhi pehle tumhe bulaaya....' / 'koi baat nahi....main toh hoon hi 😊'.

changed: Triples cut back to doubles by default ('Chalo, chalo!', 'Na, na!', 'Aao, aao.', 'Sorry, sorry!', 'Munna, Munna!'), the way real Hindi repeats a word; a triple is kept for a peak, at most once a scene, and 'Suno, suno, suno!' stays the one the family quotes back. The test set now opens with a triple twice in twelve (moments 3 and 8, and 8 is a line the readers marked true) instead of eight times. Why: the real-India note, too many triples.

'Haaye' is now spelled 'Haay' in Roman letters (हाय is unchanged) and kept in English mode too, replacing 'Oh!'. It comes at most once a scene and never just before she holds out food, so the worry line and the good-news line lose it. Why: 'Haaye' is the film spelling of the Punjabi aunty, the very type the comics review named; keeping 'Haay' in English also ends the blur with Mama ji's 'Oho!'.

'Aji' now goes with आप: 'Aji, goli khaayi? Nahin? Haay! Abhi khaiye!', the typed 'abhi khaiye', and moment 4 with no तुम command ('Mujhe phiki chahiye.'). Why: a wife who calls her husband 'Aji' says आप to him. Mausa ji's file still has तुम both ways, which the note wants matched, so the family address table settles it.
The order to Papa and Mausa ji is now 'Chaliye, chaliye! Bade wale upar! Jaldi kijiye!'. Why: the Hindi note, चलो to a jija reads as a step down.

English tags are now 'right?' across her English lines ('Amma calls your Mummy first! Right?'), and 'Didn't I say so?' is now 'Didn't I tell you?', 'Absolutely first class' is now 'First class!', 'No tension!' is now 'Don't take tension!', and 'copybooks' is now 'notebooks'. Why: Indian English says 'right?' or 'na?', and the English-mode readers heard the rest as translated.

Common fillers are no longer banned for her: she says 'Achha?' (moment 7), 'arre' may come mid-line as anyone's filler (as an exclamation it stays Captain sahab's, matrix 2.15), and the never list now keeps out only other people's set phrases. The bans on arre, dekho, achha, bas, theek, chalo/suno as anyone else's, 'please', 'pata nahin', 'mausam' and 'barsaat' are gone ('pakka?' stays out only as doubt after a report). Why: cast-wide note 1. Fillers belong to everyone, and she is told apart by shape and word sources.

The English verb with kar or ho is now hers when it suits a schoolteacher: 'Phir se top kiya, hai na?', and 'check karo', 'fail ho gayi' in her uses. She still never switches a whole clause. Why: cast-wide note 2. It is the most common Hinglish pattern, and Mummy is marked by her counter English, not by owning the pattern.

Sorry and thanks are plain words. Sorry is 'Sorry, sorry! Pehle khao.', and since Tinku and you now say a plain 'sorry' too, hers is told apart by the double and the food. Thanks is now the everyday 'Bahut achha kiya!', with the teacher's grade 'Ekdum first class!' at most once a chapter. Why: cast-wide note 3, no thanks or sorry in a code more than once a chapter.

The town's words reach her plainly: 'fikr mat karo' to Chhoti, 'goli ka waqt' to Aji, and 'Jaldi aana. Zaroor!' in a new parting sample. Why: cast-wide note 8, so fikr, waqt and zaroor are not one tailor's badge.

Moment 2 drops the cold food ('Khana thanda!') for 'Ab aaye ho? Late mark! Kaan pakdo!', the classroom's own punishment said in fun. Moment 11 now worries ('Koi baat nahin! Chot toh nahin lagi?') instead of a second class joke. Why: cast-wide note 6, where five people reached for cold food in moment 2; the change also keeps her school words from becoming a gimmick.

The first time she names Mummy to you in a chapter, she says 'tumhari Mummy' and then 'Chhoti' ('Tumhari khabar, tumhari Mummy se? Kyon?'; the typed 'tumhari mummy se nahi'). Why: Nani's note, 'Chhoti' alone is opaque to the player-reader.

Lines get more of their verbs ('Abhi se yaad aa rahi hai!', 'Bachche aaj bhi tumhari benchon par baithte hain!'), and the shout ends 'Ye nahin chalega!' instead of 'Kabhi nahin!'. Why: cast-wide note 9 on verbless telegrams, and 'Kabhi nahin!' did not answer her own question the way a Hindi-belt aunt would.

Moment 3 keeps her own congratulation ('Naukri lag gayi! Maine kaha tha na?', now 'lag gayi' as it is said); 'Badhai ho' is left for Mummy if the owner allows it, and 'Mubarak ho' unused. Why: cast-wide note 4.

Kept word for word, as the readers marked true: 'Bahut yaad aayi'; 'Rishta main laayi thi. Berth bhi main laaun?'; 'Kaisi hoon? Batati hoon! Ghutna dukhta hai, dil nahin!'; 'Chehre pe thakaan! Kuch khaya bhi?'; 'Na, na, na! Band? Toh meri class ka inaam?'; 'Late mark!'; 'Ekdum first class!'; the riddle 'ek thaal moti se bhara'; the '....' typing with 😊; 'khana khaya?? kya kya khaya??'. Also kept: her essence, want, fear, contradiction, year arc, the shout's place, the lower-berth silence, the December silence, every never-rule on harassment and dowry reports, and the note-word limits.

Open points for readers and the owner: whether Mausa ji says आप back to her (his file says तुम); whether 'Meri class aise hi sunti hai' and 'Kaan pakdo!' to a grown brother sound right to a Hindi-first reader; whether 'Badhai ho' is allowed (owner); rule 66's fourth shape and rule 62 for message cards (owner, the entries below); whether 'Aji' sounds like the film wife (readers, the entry below).

Moment 9 is now 'Gali mein nadi? Haay! Achaar ke martbaan upar! Chalo, chalo!' | 'गली में नदी? हाय! अचार के मर्तबान ऊपर! चलो, चलो!' | 'Lane's a river? Haay! Pickles up! Come on, come on!'. Why: the Hindi note, where 'Arre' worked as an exclamation, which matrix 2.15 gives to Captain sahab, so her own 'Haay' takes its place; and the real-India note, where the classroom had become her stamp, so the flood reaches for the courtyard's pickle jars instead of her pupils' exercise books.

Moment 5 is now 'Galat kaun nikla? Main! Sorry, sorry! Pehle khao!' | 'ग़लत कौन निकला? मैं! सॉरी, सॉरी! पहले खाओ!' | 'Who got it wrong? Me! Sorry, sorry! Eat first!'. Why: the same real-India note; it was the third school line of four in the test set. Now two of twelve reach for school ('Late mark! Kaan pakdo!' and 'meri class ka inaam', both marked true and kept), and the rest come from the kitchen, her questions answered at once and her exact memory. 'Aaj teacher fail' stays a now-and-then habit (tic 5, sorry), and tic 5 now says the classroom is one of her two sources, never her stamp.

Rule 66: address 0 now sets out the owner's question on pasts with ने where you are the doer ('Pichhle saal tumne kaha tha', 'Kuch khaya bhi?', 'khana khaya??', 'Parathe rakhe, hai na?', and 'Bahut achha kiya!' said to you): add it to rule 66 as a fourth shape, or have the native reader clear each line onto the build's cleared list. The lines' notes point there, and the cleared list now holds only lines where you are not the doer. No wording changed. Why: the Hindi note, rule 66 names only three shapes for तुम and the file had cleared these as 'a ने past', which the rule does not name.

Rule 62 and typed messages: typing habit 9 now asks the owner whether a message card is held to the 10-word cap, and samples 0, 3, 5 and 7 carry their split at her '....' into cards of 10 words or fewer, ready if the cap applies. No message changed. Why: the Hindi note, four of her messages run to between 13 and 20 words.

Masterji's word for her stays 'Behenji' (आप), and address 10 now says why and that Masterji's file, which has 'Mausi ji', is to be matched to it. Why: the two address tables disagreed, and 'Behenji' is what a neighbour of about sixty says to a schoolteacher of about fifty-five.

'Aji' now carries a readers' question (address 6, uses 28): if the Hindi-first readers hear the 1970s film wife in it, her lines to Mausa ji take 'Suniye' or no address word, still with आप. Why: the real-India note.

voices.name: Mausa ji (मौसा जी), about 58, chapter 2's voice

voice.register: Low, slow and plain: the quietest voice in the cast, with long gaps his hands fill. Most bubbles are two to four counted words and none is more than six (names and kin words not counted, as in rule 62; his own cap, well inside rule 62's ten), usually in two short pieces: an opener ('Hmm.', 'Hain?', 'Lo.' or the thing itself), then the state of a thing. His usual sentence is about a thing, not a person: the wire, the bench, the board, the food, the job, given a state or a verdict. Verdicts on things are often bare ('Taar dheela.', 'Board theek.') and sometimes keep their verb ('Bench theek hai.'); comfort and kind lines always keep their 'hai' ('Achha hai.', 'Amma ji mazboot hain.'), so he never talks in telegrams. His own jobs come with the pronoun dropped ('Aata hoon.', 'Garam karta hoon.', 'Ho gaya.'). His orders are small and practical: rest ('So jao.'), hands off live current ('Switch mat chhoona.'), and the next little job as he hands something over ('Lo, Mausi se baat karo.', 'Haath dho lo.'). He answers more than he asks; his few questions are about sleep, water or a drip. Nearly every bubble is followed by something his hands do, and when a beat needs more he speaks again after a deed, so a run is two bubbles with an action between them. He talks most to whoever should be resting (you, at the ward). His few words are kind and busy, never the silent head of the house. Told apart from the other short voices by shape and source, not by owned words: Nani gives people orders and counter proverbs; Captain sahab makes a cricket call, then gives the reason; Tinku gives a score with a tag; Mummy lists jobs; Mami reads things back; you name the listener. He reports on things, names almost nobody, counts nothing and leaves himself out.
voice.mix: Bare, plain Hindi, the plainest in the cast after Nani's, with no proverb or image of his own (that is Nani's and Masterji's ground). The common fillers are his as much as anyone's: achha, haan, chalo, arre and theek hai come in mid-line, sparingly, as they would from any man of 58; so do everyday Urdu-rooted words such as waqt, fikr and zaroor ('Waqt lagega.'). English comes in from his work. First, the lineman's nouns, used as Hindi nouns: current, line, fuse, load, meter, earthing, board, switch, wiring, joint. Second, now and then, the everyday Hinglish English verb with ho or kar, and his is always about what the line or the current did, with the thing as the subject ('Line trip ho gayi.', 'Short hua hai.', 'Wiring check ho gayi.'). That is how a lineman really talks, and it keeps his thing-first shape; Mummy's English verbs are counter jobs she hands to people ('ye cup return karo'), his are what the current did. The hospital words everyone uses: BP, drip, ward, X-ray. Where everyday Hindi has its own word he takes it: 'bijli' for power, 'taar' for wire, जोड़ for a joint in Hindi mode. No whole English clause (Mama ji's and Mami's), and no English feeling words such as tension, relax or chill. Never 'main switch' or 'mains' in Hinglish, because 'main' reads as मैं. Hinglish mode is Roman Hindi with those nouns. English mode is plain, natural British English, as short as the Hindi: the thing first and himself left out wherever English allows it ('Board's fine. Open the shutter.', 'Lights on, then.'), with the full everyday phrase wherever a clipped one would sound translated ('Get any sleep?', 'It'll take time.', 'No harm done.'). One English word for each work verdict, so the English sort still hears him: mazboot is 'solid' of work and 'strong' of a person, dheela is 'loose', theek is 'fine'.
tics: The thing first, then its state: 'Taar dheela.' | 'Board theek hai.' | 'Fuse ud gaya.' Most of his sentences have a thing as the subject, and none passes a judgement on a person.

'Hmm.' | 'हम्म।' before an answer, or as the whole answer, in at most one bubble in three and never two running; otherwise one slow nod. In chapter 2's three or four bubbles that is once. When he is moved, the 'Hmm' becomes a cleared throat and a look at the window.
Himself left out: first-person verbs only for plain jobs, with the pronoun dropped ('Abhi aaya.', 'Aata hoon.', 'Dekh liya.'). The only 'my' in any mode is the fixed English sorry, 'My mistake.'.

One-word verdicts: 'Theek.' | 'ठीक।' (fine; the bare one-word line is his, while 'theek hai' mid-line is everyone's), 'Mazboot.' | 'मज़बूत।' (solid, of work; strong, of a person; his highest word), 'Dheela.' | 'ढीला।' (loose, sloppy: of a joint, a wire or a job, never of cloth, which is Masterji's, and never of a person), 'Chalega.' | 'चलेगा।' (it'll do: his kind word for a thing that is not quite right).
'Lo.' | 'लो।' as he sets something down or hands it on (half a sweet lime, his shoulder towel, the phone), sometimes with the one small job that goes with it ('Lo, Mausi se baat karo.').

His orders are small and practical: rest ('So jao.'), live current ('Switch mat chhoona.', 'Board mat chhoona.'), and the next little job ('Haath dho lo.'). In English mode the current order is always 'Leave the ___.'.
His exclamation 'Hain?' | 'हैं?' always stands alone at the start of a bubble, with its own question mark.
When thanked he says only 'Hmm.' | 'हम्म।' as he stands up, and leaves the room.
He leaves before a goodbye is over: from a room when he is thanked, from a platform before the train moves. He never waits out the last coach (that vigil is Papa's).

When cross he goes quiet, picks up the nearest job and does it twice as hard (re-tightening a screw that was already tight). If a word comes, it is one flat order about a thing ('Andar rakho.'), with no address word.
Until May a job that can wait is 'Kal.' | 'कल।'; from May on it is 'Abhi.' | 'अभी।', and he never says 'kal' about a job again.
He drops address words with everyone his own age or younger; the only name he says is 'Tinku'. With an elder he never drops the 'ji' ('Abhi, Amma ji.').
catchphrases: 'Hmm. Ho jayega.' | 'हम्म। हो जाएगा।' | 'Hmm. It'll get done.' (his comfort and his promise; no person in it)
'So jao.' | 'सो जाओ।' | 'Go to sleep.' (to whoever should be resting, you most of all)
'Lo. Aadha.' | 'लो। आधा।' | 'Here. Half.' (the half he sets down beside you; a share, not a count, and the only time 'aadha' is in his mouth)
voice.exclamation: 'Hain?' | 'हैं?' | 'Eh?' A nasal sound of surprise with no word in it and no religious sense (matrix 2.13). Said low, for a good or a bad surprise alike. It always stands alone at the start of the bubble with its own question mark, so the Hinglish 'Hain?' is never read as the verb 'hain' (are). A plain 'arre' mid-line is anyone's, his too, but 'Arre waah' is Captain sahab's cry and never his; never a god-word, never another person's cry.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: 'Galti ho gayi.' | 'ग़लती हो गई।' | 'My mistake.' Plain everyday north Indian Hindi, still with no subject, and then his hands put the thing right in front of whoever saw. THANKS, GIVEN: plain words, 'Achha kiya.' | 'अच्छा किया।' | 'Good of you.' (the past with ने agrees with the deed, so it gives you no gender; rule 66 does not yet name that shape, so it waits on the owner, as the address notes say). His work verdict as thanks ('Silai mazboot hai, Masterji.' | 'That's solid stitching, Masterji.') comes at most once a chapter, so it stays a compliment and never becomes a code. THANKS, RECEIVED: just 'Hmm.' | 'हम्म।' | 'Hmm.' as he stands up, and he leaves the room; the leaving is the rest of his answer. LOVE: never said as a feeling; a deed with his hands, here and now: 'Lo. Aadha.' | 'लो। आधा।' | 'Here. Half.' as he sets half a peeled sweet lime down beside you; the steel chairs kept outside the ward all night; the lit back step that nobody mentions.
uses: Pet words, Hinglish | Hindi | English: hmm | हम्म | hmm; ho jayega | हो जाएगा | it'll get done; theek, alone | ठीक | fine; mazboot | मज़बूत | solid, strong; dheela | ढीला | loose; chalega | चलेगा | it'll do; abhi | अभी | now; lo | लो | here; ho gaya | हो गया | done; dekh liya | देख लिया | checked; galti ho gayi | ग़लती हो गई | my mistake; achha kiya | अच्छा किया | good of you; kaam | काम | the job.
Everyone's fillers, used sparingly and mid-line: achha, haan, chalo, arre, theek hai; and everyday Urdu-rooted words: waqt, fikr, zaroor.

His trade, as Hindi nouns: bijli, taar, joint (जोड़ in Hindi mode), current, line, fuse, load, meter, earthing, board, switch, wiring; trade verbs with ho or kar about what the line did: trip ho gayi, short hua, check ho gayi, ud gaya (of a fuse); and the ward's BP, drip, ward, X-ray.
Things in the house he reports on: khana, paani, cheeni, bench, kursi, gate, light, seedhi (the back step).
'Ji.' | 'जी।' to the doctor, the night nurse and ward staff, standing up to say it; 'Amma ji' with आप to Nani.

Card notes stay short work verdicts, how someone does a job as a lineman would judge it (slow, rushed, never checks twice), never temper, looks, dress or character, and never said in a bubble (rule 36). The four proposed chapter 2 notes are unchanged.
never: मैं, 'main', 'I', 'me', मेरा, मुझे, 'mera', 'mujhe'; 'my' only in the fixed English sorry 'My mistake.' (a script can check these).
A judgement on a person as the subject of his sentence. People come into his lines only in small practical orders, an address word, or comfort ('Amma ji mazboot hain.').
More than six counted words in one bubble; two of his bubbles back to back with no deed between them.
Any figure or count in speech: no hours, minutes, prices, head-counts or 'dobara'; 'aadha' only in 'Lo. Aadha.'.

'sorry', 'thank you', 'please', 'dhanyavaad' or 'shukriya' (your word for a stranger who has helped): not because anyone owns them, but because his Hindi is plain and older and his sorry and thanks are 'Galti ho gayi.' and 'Achha kiya.'.

Another person's exclamation: 'Baap re' (Nani), 'Had hai' (Mummy), 'Kamaal hai' (Papa), 'Oho' (Mama ji), 'Gazab' (Tinku), 'Haaye' (Mausi), 'Uff' (Masterji), 'Arre waah' (Captain sahab), 'Ish' (Mami), 'Badhiya' (yours).

Another person's phrase (phrases stay owned; the common fillers do not): 'Pehle ___' for someone else first (yours), 'phir se naap' (Masterji's re-measuring), 'Iska bill nahin', 'Theek hai, toh' and 'Isme kya' as a brush-off of thanks (Mummy's), 'Next ball', 'Not out', 'Well fielded' (Captain sahab's), 'Tick' and 'Correct?' (Mami's), 'Reached?', 'Pahunche?' and 'Aakhri dibbe tak' (Papa's), 'Suno, suno, suno!', 'Shabaash' and 'bahut yaad' (Mausi's), 'Bas.' as a closing line and 'Khush raho' (Nani's), 'Jeete raho' (Masterji's), 'haan?' as a tag (Tinku's), 'Don't worry' (Mama ji's).
'Chhote' (Mummy's word for her brother).
A proverb, an idiom or an image of his own (Nani's and Masterji's ground); English feeling words such as tension, relax, chill.
Tea as his way of caring (Nani, Masterji and Mama ji already carry it); at home he pours it without a word.
'kal' about a job, from May on.
Any word on anyone's character, temper or looks in speech; any word on a woman's dress, looks or morals.
Any doubt of a report of harassment or a dowry demand, or calling one a misunderstanding (rule 22); no word about one in a bubble at all.
'beta', 'bhaiya', 'didi', a pet name or any word that gives you a gender (rules 8 and 66; rulebook Q7); 'sister' or 'doctor sahab' for the ward staff.
Any religious word or exclamation (the matrix 2.13 list), any caste word or trade-caste name (so 'mithai ki dukaan', never 'halwai'), any brand (rule 3).
A speech, a lecture or unasked advice; a raised voice, except the one time current is live; a joke at anyone's expense but his own; a feeling word about himself.
address: These follow the cast map's one address table once it settles them, checked by the Hindi-first readers and the South Indian reader (India review; rule 65).
NANI: 'Amma ji' | 'अम्मा जी' and आप, always; she says आप to him.
MAUSI: no name and no address word; तुम both ways; to you and Tinku she is 'tumhari Mausi' | 'तुम्हारी मौसी', and to a nephew or niece on the phone just 'Mausi' ('Lo, Mausi se baat karo.').
MUMMY: no address word, तुम (his wife's younger sister); she says 'Jija ji' and आप.
PAPA: no address word, आप; Papa says 'Bhai sahab' and आप.
MAMA JI: no address word, तुम; Mama ji says 'Bade Jija ji' and आप.
TINKU: 'Tinku', with तुम, the only name he says; she says 'Mausa ji' and आप.
MAMI: no address word, आप; she says 'Jija ji' and आप.
MASTERJI and CAPTAIN SAHAB: 'Masterji', 'Captain sahab', with आप both ways.
THE DOCTOR, THE NIGHT NURSE AND STAFF: 'Ji.' and आप, standing; never a word that gives them a gender.

YOU: no address word, and तुम rarely; only rule 66 shapes: commands ('So jao.', 'Switch mat chhoona.') and lines where you are not the doer ('Neend aayi?', 'Ho jayega.', 'Lo. Aadha.'). One line is outside the three shapes: 'Achha kiya.', where you are the doer and the past with ने agrees with the deed, so it marks no gender; it waits on the owner (RULE 66 NOTES). You say 'Mausa ji' with आप and -इए ('Aap so jaiye, Mausa ji.' | 'आप सो जाइए, मौसा जी।'); your thanks, 'Thank you, Mausa ji.' | 'थैंक यू, मौसा जी।' | 'Thanks, Mausa ji.' (your own file keeps 'shukriya' for a stranger who has helped), gets one 'Hmm.' and sends him out of the room.

RULE 66 NOTES: the checker will flag 'हो जाएगा' and 'वक़्त लगेगा' (futures), 'नींद आई?', 'आधा', 'मत छूना' and 'हाथ लगाना', 'हो गया', 'अच्छा किया' and 'कुछ नहीं हुआ' (an ending at a sentence's end), and 'करता हूँ' and 'जलाता हूँ' (an ending before हूँ). Each agrees with a thing (the job, the time, नींद, कुछ), is an infinitive command, is a past with ने that agrees with the deed, or is himself. A native reader clears each. OWNER QUESTION: rule 66 lets तुम lines through in only three shapes (commands, 'who should' asks, lines where you are not the doer), and 'अच्छा किया' is none of them: you are the doer, and it is clean only because a past with ने agrees with the thing done. Tinku's, Mausi's, Papa's, Mummy's and Mama ji's files have the same shape. Either the owner adds 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' to rule 66 as a fourth shape, or the native reader clears the line and the build puts it on the cleared list. The wording stays either way.

SAYING NO, 2.17, when you offer to take the night chair, a run of two bubbles (kept; between them he turns his chair to face the ward door): EN 'No.' / 'Go to sleep.' | Hinglish 'Nahin.' / 'So jao.' | Hindi 'नहीं।' / 'सो जाओ।'

BEING THANKED, by anyone (changed from 'Kaam tha.', which is made up, and then from 'Hmm. Isme kya.', which four voices shared and which is now Mummy's alone; the one word as he stands up, and then he leaves the room): EN 'Hmm.' | Hinglish 'Hmm.' | Hindi 'हम्म।'

SORRY, to Mausi, when the new fan in her tuition room turns the wrong way (changed to the spoken form; then he rewires it on the spot): EN 'My mistake.' | Hinglish 'Galti ho gayi.' | Hindi 'ग़लती हो गई।'

A BLUNT VERDICT, to Mama ji's hired lighting men at the wedding (the matrix sample; then he tightens the joint himself): EN 'Hmm. Loose joint.' | Hinglish 'Hmm. Joint dheela.' | Hindi 'हम्म। जोड़ ढीला।'

THE WEDDING LIGHTS TRIP, to Mama ji (new: the English trade verb with ho, the line as its subject; then he unplugs the second heater and resets the line): EN 'Too much load. Line's tripped.' | Hinglish 'Load zyada. Line trip ho gayi.' | Hindi 'लोड ज़्यादा। लाइन ट्रिप हो गई।'

THE ONE SHOUT, at a painted person's hand reaching for a live switch (kept as a voice reference only: it goes in a panel only where he may speak (Q11), where that chapter's one shout is free (rule 35; Nani holds chapter 2's), and where the hand's owner has a face in frame (rule 7)): EN 'Hands off! It's live!' | Hinglish 'Haath hatao! Current hai!' | Hindi 'हाथ हटाओ! करंट है!'

habits: DEVICE: an old phone in a plain grey cover, in his right shirt pocket on vibrate; it comes out only to answer. Painted, its screen is always blank and his words are live text (rule 30). No font-size trait: six files claimed the largest font, and it is not his.
SCRIPT: Roman Hindi with his few trade nouns. Never English sentences (Papa types English) and never Devanagari (Nani's voice typing); the game shows each language mode's version.

SHAPE: a log-book line, from 34 years of night-shift entries: the thing first, then its state ('Board theek.', 'Kursiyan lag gayin.'), one to five words, a capital at the start and one full stop at the end. Never a question mark, never a figure, never a greeting, a name or a sign-off.
ACKNOWLEDGING: 'Ok.', with its capital and full stop, about an hour late. Papa's is 'Noted.' inside a minute, Tinku's is a lowercase 'ok' inside seconds, Masterji's is 'ok ji'.

HIS TELL: the missed call. For 'reached', 'coming' or 'yes' he rings once and hangs up, a habit from the years when every call cost money (readers confirm it reads true for a man of 58). On screen it is a message card reading 'Missed call: Mausa ji' | 'मिस्ड कॉल: मौसा जी', with no app look.
SPEED: about an hour, because the phone is in his pocket and his hands are busy; inside a minute for anything about current, a board or the lights going.

CALLS: he would rather call than type, and never sends a voice note. His calls last under a minute: 'Haan.' at the start, 'Theek.' at the end, and no goodbye. To a nephew or niece with news: 'Achha hai. Lo, Mausi se baat karo.', and the phone goes to Mausi. To his own two grown children, 'Haan. Sab theek hai.', and the phone goes to their mother.
EMOJI: none, ever; no stickers, no forwards, no good-morning pictures (Papa's). The thumbs-up is Mummy's.
One slow right thumb; never a typo, because there are too few words, and never a short form ('h' for 'hai' is Masterji's).

THE FAMILY GROUP: Mausi added him; he posts once or twice a year and reacts to nothing, and knows what is in it because Mausi reads it out. On screen a group message is one message card on the painted blank phone, never a group chat, with no app look and no 'forwarded' label (owner, 23 Oct; rule 3).

test_lines.moment: 2. Someone everyone was waiting for arrives two hours late. (To Mama ji, in from the city. Nobody is scolded: no greeting, no address word, no figure, only the next job. Then he takes the pan off the shelf and warms the food himself.)
test_lines.en: Wash your hands. Warming it up.
test_lines.hinglish: Haath dho lo. Garam karta hoon.
test_lines.hi: हाथ धो लो। गरम करता हूँ।

test_lines.moment: 3. A cousin phones to say they have got their first job. (Into the phone; the cousin's gender stays open. Handing the phone to Mausi is the deed, and then he goes back to the fuse box he was mending.)
test_lines.en: Good. Here, talk to your Mausi.
test_lines.hinglish: Achha hai. Lo, Mausi se baat karo.
test_lines.hi: अच्छा है। लो, मौसी से बात करो।

test_lines.moment: 4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it. (To Tinku, who made it. The plain verdict, then his kind word, then he drinks every drop.)
test_lines.en: Too much sugar, Tinku. It'll do.
test_lines.hinglish: Cheeni zyada hai, Tinku. Chalega.
test_lines.hi: चीनी ज़्यादा है, टिंकू। चलेगा।

test_lines.moment: 5. In front of the family, someone shows that they had a fact wrong. (He had said the new socket was wired right. To everyone; then he kneels and rewires it while they watch.)
test_lines.en: My mistake. Wired it backwards.
test_lines.hinglish: Galti ho gayi. Taar ulta hai.
test_lines.hi: ग़लती हो गई। तार उल्टा है।

test_lines.moment: 6. Someone they love is leaving, and they say goodbye on a railway platform. (To one of his grown children at the junction. He thumbs the peel off a sweet lime, sets half on the seat by the window, and walks off down the platform before the train moves, the way he leaves a room when thanked.)
test_lines.en: Here. Half. For the journey.
test_lines.hinglish: Lo. Aadha. Raste ke liye.
test_lines.hi: लो। आधा। रास्ते के लिए।

test_lines.moment: 7. Someone thanks them for something they did. (The one word as he stands up; then he leaves the room.)
test_lines.en: Hmm.
test_lines.hinglish: Hmm.
test_lines.hi: हम्म।

test_lines.moment: 8. A neighbour passes on a rumour that the corner sweet shop is closing. (To Papa on the step. Nothing about the owner, only about work he has seen; then back to the cricket with the sound off.)
test_lines.en: It was only just rewired.
test_lines.hinglish: Wiring abhi nayi lagi thi.
test_lines.hi: वायरिंग अभी नई लगी थी।

test_lines.moment: 9. Heavy rain floods the lane outside the house. (To the household. Then he kneels at the switchboard with the power off, and nobody touches a switch until he nods.)
test_lines.en: Power's off. Leave the board.
test_lines.hinglish: Bijli band. Board mat chhoona.
test_lines.hi: बिजली बंद। बोर्ड मत छूना।

test_lines.moment: 10. Someone asks them how they are. (Asked by you, late at night. No figure and nothing about himself: his one word, then your rest. Then he pulls the ward door to.)
test_lines.en: Fine. Go on, off to sleep.
test_lines.hinglish: Theek. Chalo, ab so jao.
test_lines.hi: ठीक। चलो, अब सो जाओ।

test_lines.moment: 11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table. (To the child. He sets the cotton towel from his shoulder down on the spill and lifts the phone charger's wire clear of the water.)
test_lines.en: Here. No harm done.
test_lines.hinglish: Lo. Kuch nahin hua.
test_lines.hi: लो। कुछ नहीं हुआ।

test_lines.moment: 12. A phone call brings good news. (Then he goes out and switches on every light on the gate: a lineman's joy.)
test_lines.en: Eh? Really? Lights on, then.
test_lines.hinglish: Hain? Sach? Light jalaata hoon.
test_lines.hi: हैं? सच? लाइट जलाता हूँ।
