voices.name: Masterji (मास्टरजी), about 60, the tailor next door; chapter 3's voice

voice.register: Slow, warm and unhurried: the station road's slow measurer, one of the cast's four long runners (Papa speaks in exact whole sentences, Mausi fast and tripled, Mama ji in one run-on). SHAPE: a verdict first, short and sure, said as a whole sentence with its verb and its 'hai' (he is the house's slow full-sentence speaker, never one more clipped voice); then, in about one run in two, a turn to cloth or weather, often hinged on 'Waise'. The other runs stop at the verdict, so the turn stays a habit and never a stamp. What tells him apart is this shape and where his words come from (cloth, weather, the garment calendar), not any word he owns: 'waise', 'dekhiye', 'achha', 'arre', 'chalo', 'bas' and 'theek hai' are everyone's. A run is two or three bubbles, budgeted as pairs so a turn is never the line that gets cut; in a single bubble the verdict shows, and the turn too when that line has one. Full stops throughout, even after 'Uff.'; no exclamation marks; he asks a question only when he wants the answer, and never answers his own the way Mausi does (the fixed ending's 'Whose drain? Let the lane cup decide.' hands the question on to the cup). NUMBERS: none in speech. Time is only 'bas abhi' (right away, which means an hour), and he blames the trains; the past is dated by what was on his machine ('the year of Bhai sahab's jacket'), never a year or a count of years. A measure by feel ('ungli bhar', 'baal bhar', 'baalisht') comes at most once in a run. His exactness shows in plain verdicts: straight, crooked, level, loose, tight (of cloth, never of a person). FEELING: said sideways, in cloth and weather pictures a Hindi-first reader follows at once ('Geela kapda sookh jaata hai. Fikr phate ki hoti hai.'), with plain warmth in his thanks ('Sukhi raho.', 'Ehsaan raha.'); never the plain feeling words Mausi and Mama ji own. HUMOUR: kind and whimsical, and rationed: at most one picture a run that gives the sky, the clouds, the mud or the drain a mood (the sky sulks, the clouds sit 'munh phulaaye', the mud sleeps late, the drain is stubborn), and none in a cross line. The joke is at the road, the sky, his own trade or himself, never at a person's body or a woman's clothes, and he is never its butt. WHEN CROSS (at things only: the drain, the sky, cheap cloth): the turn stops. One short verdict, silence, and he straightens out of his stoop. He never raises his voice; Mummy, his chapter's other voice, gets more polite instead, so their tells never match. TALKS MOST TO whoever stands still long enough (you, most of all), Mummy over the wall, and Captain sahab across the drain.
voice.mix: Ordinary station-road Hindustani: a Hindi frame with the everyday words any old bazaar in the Hindi belt shares (fikr, farq, mausam, mizaaj, waqt, zaroor, khair, afwaah, astar). These are the town's words, not his badge: others in the cast say fikr, waqt and zaroor too, so his speech marks the town and never a community, and he is never played for comedy. Tailoring English comes as Hindi nouns (fitting, trial, size, finish, pattern, shutter, and 'ready-made', said with a sniff). His working verbs are the Hindi ones the old master taught him at fourteen (naapna, kaatna, silna, kholna for let out, kasna for take in), and at the counter, as at any tailor's counter, the shop pattern of an English word with ho or kar comes out too ('kandhe ka alter ho jaayega', 'trial ho gaya'); never a whole English clause, which is Mama ji's and Mami's shape. No markedly Urdu courtesy forms (the list is in 'never'), so the register reads as an old bazaar; a Hindi-first and an Urdu-speaking reader confirm (rule 65). In Hinglish mode his lines are Roman Hindi with those nouns. In English mode he speaks unhurried, slightly old-fashioned Indian English: 'Look,' for 'Dekhiye'; 'By the way,' or 'Then again,' for 'Waise', alternating, at most once a run, chosen by sense (a side remark or a counterweight); 'Uff.' kept as it is, since Indian English speakers say it; 'right away' for 'bas abhi'; 'Spot on.' for 'Barabar.'; 'Please don't mind.' for 'Bura mat maaniye.'; and the cloth and weather pictures intact. Never 'Mind you,' or 'Ugh.' (the first read as translated, the second is a teenager's disgust). No accent is ever spelled out (the funny-shopkeeper trap in the realism notes).
tics: Verdict first, as a whole sentence with its verb; then, in about one run in two, a turn to cloth or weather, often on 'Waise' (English 'By the way,' or 'Then again,'). The other runs end at the verdict. 'Waise' itself is anyone's word; the shape is his.

Opens with 'Dekhiye' / 'Look,' to everyone, Tinku and you included: a counter habit, not a respect form. At most one line in three, so it stays a habit. A plain 'dekho' is as free to him as to anyone.

Gives the sky, the clouds, the mud and the drain a mood, at most once a run and never when cross: 'Aasmaan rootha hai', 'Baadal din bhar munh phulaaye the', 'Keechad abhi so raha hai', 'Naali ziddi hai'. Only pictures a Hindi-first reader follows without help.
Reads the weather from the feel of cloth (limp means rain, stiff or crisp means sun) and is right; the chapter uses his forecasts. Asked how he knew: 'Kapde se pata chalta hai.'
Dates the past by what was on his machine ('Bhai sahab ki jacket wala saal', 'Mama ji ki interview wali kameez'); never a year, never a count of years.
Gives every time as 'bas abhi', which means an hour, and blames the trains when he is late; never a clock time.
A measure by feel at most once in a run: 'ungli bhar' (a finger's width), 'baal bhar' (a hair's breadth), 'baalisht' (a hand span). Never a figure, because his tape lost its marks.

Tailoring pictures for whatever he cannot say straight: a person is an old garment relined, the stitching stays home wherever the cloth goes, a city kurta only looks good in photos. Never a picture of anyone's body.

A real idiom from his own trade or weather when one fits, at most one a run, never a coined line dressed as a saying: 'paani sir se upar' at the drain, 'bakhiya udhedna' when he is caught out, 'baal ki khaal nikaalna' of Nani's checking, 'afwaah udna', 'munh phulaana' of the clouds. Proverbs stay Nani's register.

Thanks plainly and warmly: the young get an elder's good wish and the reason ('Sukhi raho. Us chai ne bachaa liya.'), a neighbour gets 'Ehsaan raha.'; sorry is plain too ('Bura mat maaniye.', 'Aap sahi hain.'), and his re-measuring comes at most once a chapter.
Holds his right thumb and forefinger a finger's width apart while he talks.
'Uff.' with a full stop is his only exclamation, at things, never at a person.
When cross, the turn stops: one short verdict, silence, and he straightens out of the stoop.
catchphrases: 'Bas abhi.' | 'बस अभी।' | 'Right away.' His only way of giving a time; it means an hour. (No figure.) Every player has a tailor who says it.

'Barabar.' | 'बराबर।' | 'Spot on.' His one-word praise of work, then a tug of the tape ends. In Hindi it also means 'equal', a quiet echo in a fairness game that nobody ever points out. (English mode was 'Level.', which no English speaker says as praise.)

'Kapde se pata chalta hai.' | 'कपड़े से पता चलता है।' | 'The cloth tells you.' His plain answer when anyone asks how he knew the weather would turn: a remark, not a saying. (It replaces 'Kapde ka bhi mizaaj hota hai.', which read as a coined saying.)
voice.exclamation: 'Uff.' | 'उफ़्फ़।' | English mode 'Uff.' as well, since Indian English speakers say it ('Ugh.' is struck: it is a teenager's disgust, not an old tailor's sigh). A sound with no religious meaning, for exasperation at things: the drain, the sky, cheap cloth, a power cut. Always a full stop, never an exclamation mark; it is his alone among the cast's exclamations, and it fills the place where an elder might reach for a religious word (rule 3). For joy he has no cry: he says 'Achha?' and claims the good news was in the cloth all along.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY, in plain words first: 'Bura mat maaniye, Bhabhi ji.' | 'बुरा मत मानिए, भाभी जी।' | 'Please don't mind, Bhabhi ji.' (to Tinku or you, 'Bura mat maanna.', a command that marks no gender). When he is shown wrong in front of people he says so, then makes the joke at himself: 'Aap sahi hain. Feeta purana hai, main bhi.' | 'आप सही हैं। फ़ीता पुराना है, मैं भी।' | 'You're right. My tape's old, and so am I.' His trade sorry, at most once a chapter, is to re-measure out loud: 'Bura mat maaniye. Chaliye, phir se naap lete hain.' He never says 'I'm late' (the trains were). THANKS, plain and warm: to the young, an elder's good wish and the reason: 'Sukhi raho. Us chai ne bachaa liya.' | 'सुखी रहो। उस चाय ने बचा लिया।' | 'You're a gem. That tea saved me.' To Tinku 'Jeeti raho, Tinku.', and to a young man such as his son 'Jeete raho.'; never जीते रहो or जीती रहो to you, because the form fixes a gender (rule 66's fourth flag), so you get 'Sukhi raho.', where सुखी never changes. To a neighbour or an elder: 'Bhabhi ji, aapki chhat ne bachaa liya. Ehsaan raha.' | 'भाभी जी, आपकी छत ने बचा लिया। एहसान रहा।' | 'Bhabhi ji, your roof saved my cloth. I owe you.' When he is thanked, he makes the favour small: 'Kinari hi toh thi. Isme kaunsi badi baat hai.' | 'Only an edge. Think nothing of it.' Never a 'no charge' thanks (Mummy's 'Iska bill nahin.'). The owner and the Hindi-first readers confirm that 'Jeete raho' and 'Sukhi raho' pass rule 3 (good wishes with no religious word in them). LOVE: his time, said out loud: the tumbler set down beside you, 'Chai yahin rakh di hai. Abhi garam hai.', then a story offered, 'Bhai sahab ki jacket wali baat sunaaoon?' At a parting it is said sideways in cloth: 'Kapda kahin bhi jaaye, silai yahin ki rehti hai.' | 'कपड़ा कहीं भी जाए, सिलाई यहीं की रहती है।' | 'Wherever the cloth goes, the stitching's from here.' Never 'yaad aayi', 'I missed you' or 'love' (Mausi's and Mama ji's plain words).

dheela, kasa, kadak | ढीला, कसा, कड़क | loose, tight, crisp (of cloth or work, never of a person's body)
seedha, tedha, barabar | सीधा, टेढ़ा, बराबर | straight, crooked, level
mausam, mizaaj, barsaat, aasmaan, baadal, dhoop | मौसम, मिज़ाज, बरसात, आसमान, बादल, धूप | weather, mood or temper, monsoon, sky, clouds, sunshine
rootha, ziddi, so raha, munh phulaaye | रूठा, ज़िद्दी, सो रहा, मुँह फुलाए | sulking, stubborn, asleep, pouting (said of the sky, the drain, the mud, the clouds; one a run at most)
keechad, naali, daraar | कीचड़, नाली, दरार | mud, drain, crack
fikr, farq, waqt, zaroor, khair | फ़िक्र, फ़र्क़, वक़्त, ज़रूर, ख़ैर | worry, difference, time, surely, anyway (the town's everyday words, shared with others in the cast)
waise | वैसे | by the way, then again (his usual hinge; anyone's word)
dekhiye | देखिए | look (his counter opener)
bas abhi | बस अभी | right away (an hour)
ready-made | रेडीमेड | ready-made, with a sniff, never as praise
gharwali | घरवाली | his wife, whose hands made the buttonholes
uff | उफ़्फ़ | his one exclamation

real idioms, one a run at most: paani sir se upar, bakhiya udhedna, baal ki khaal nikaalna, afwaah udna, munh phulaana | पानी सिर से ऊपर, बखिया उधेड़ना, बाल की खाल निकालना, अफ़वाह उड़ना, मुँह फुलाना | gone too far, to take apart (said of himself), to split hairs, a rumour flies, to sulk

plain sorry and thanks: bura mat maaniye, aap sahi hain, sukhi raho, jeeti raho (Tinku), jeete raho (a young man), ehsaan raha, isme kaunsi badi baat hai | बुरा मत मानिए, आप सही हैं, सुखी रहो, जीती रहो, जीते रहो, एहसान रहा, इसमें कौन सी बड़ी बात है | please don't mind, you're right, you're a gem, you're a star, I owe you, think nothing of it

JUDGING NOTES (chapter 3's cards only, with his face chip; unchanged by this pass): his idiom is how people are as customers (fidgets through every fitting, never collects the stitching, has every seam redone, wants everything by tomorrow), landing on women and men equally; punctuality stays off his notes (rule 20).
never: Any figure in speech: no inches, minutes, hours, prices, scores, ordinals, years or counts of years (rule 2); no 'sharp', no 'about', 'roughly' or लगभग for a measure. The number leaners are Papa and Tinku.
A measure by feel more than once a run.
A turn to cloth or weather on every run, more than one mood picture a run, or any mood picture in a cross line.

A picture a Hindi-first reader cannot follow ('Barsaat mein ghadi bhi phoolti hai' and 'Ab ye tumhari chai wali barsaat', both struck), or a coined line dressed as a saying ('Kapde ka bhi mizaaj hota hai' and 'Jo waqt par aaye, use kuch chahiye', both struck). Idioms only real ones; proverbs left to Nani.
'Pehle ___' as someone-else-first (yours).
A 'no charge' or bill-free thanks (Mummy's 'Iska bill nahin.').

Another person's phrase or tag, which is not the same as a common word: Captain sahab's 'Arre waah.' and bare cricket calls; Mausa ji's one-word 'Lo.' and 'Theek.'; Nani's closing 'Bas.' and 'Khush raho'; Mausi's 'Suno, suno, suno!', 'Shabaash' and 'bahut yaad'; Papa's 'Kamaal hai' and 'Aakhri dibbe tak'; Mama ji's 'Don't worry'; your 'Badhiya'; the tags 'hai na?' (Mausi), 'haan?' (Tinku) and 'Correct?' (Mami). The common fillers (arre, achha, chalo, suno, dekho, bas, theek hai, haan, waise) are everyone's, and he says them mid-line like anyone.
A whole English clause (Mama ji's and Mami's shape). An English word with ho or kar only in counter talk.
जीते रहो, जीती रहो or any -ते or -ती word before रहो, रहना, रहिए or रहें in a line to you (rule 66's fourth flag); to you it is 'Sukhi raho'.
Hurrying anyone, 'jaldi' about his own work, or 'I'm late'.
Any word on a woman's dress, its length, tightness or modesty (no छोटा or तंग of clothes on a woman, no शर्म, इज़्ज़त, 'decent', 'modern'), or on anyone's body size (no मोटा, पतला).
'Bossy', 'argues', रौब, बहस, or any note about women or men in general.
'Ready-made' as praise.

Markedly Urdu courtesy forms (janaab, aadaab, farmaiye, huzoor, tashreef, khuda hafiz) and any religious word: no god's name, blessing, festival word, 'shukr hai', 'tauba', 'Khuda', 'Rab', 'Bhagwan'; in English mode no 'Goodness', 'Heavens', 'Good grief', 'Lord', 'Oh my', 'Bless you' (rule 3).
English mode 'Mind you,' and 'Ugh.' (struck as translated and as a teenager's word).
Beta, beti, bhaiya, didi or any gendered word for you; any future or helper-verb past that changes with your gender in a line to you (rule 66).
A card person's name, or any word from a note on that decision's cards, in a bubble (rule 36).

Any doubt of a report of harassment or bullying, or of a dowry demand, or calling one a misunderstanding (rule 22). His 'Afwaah hai' is for sweet-shop talk only and never sits in a chapter beat near a report twin.
An exclamation mark, a raised voice, or temper at a person.
address: Nani: 'Nani ji', आप ('Ab dhoondhiye'). She calls him 'Master'.
Mummy: 'Bhabhi ji', आप ('Bura mat maaniye, Bhabhi ji.'). She calls him 'Masterji', आप.
Papa: 'Bhai sahab', आप. Papa says 'Masterji', आप.
Mama ji: 'Mama ji', आप, now that he is a grown customer. Mama ji says 'Masterji', आप.
Tinku: 'Tinku', तुम; his thanks to her is 'Jeeti raho, Tinku.' She says 'Masterji', आप.
Mausi: 'Behenji', आप, as her own file has it: what a neighbour of 60 says to a schoolteacher of 55, while 'Mausi' stays the household's word. Mausa ji: 'Mausa ji', आप both ways. Mami: 'Mami ji', आप.
Captain sahab: 'Captain' (कप्तान), dropping the sahab, with आप; thirty monsoons of familiarity, not rudeness. Captain sahab calls him 'Master', आप.
Customers and strangers: 'Dekhiye' and आप, every time; 'Chaliye', not 'Chalo', when he re-measures for them.

YOU (rule 66): no address word at all. तुम only in commands ('वो ईंट लाओ। सिरे पर रख दो।'), 'who should' asks ('थान छत पर कौन ले जाए?'), and lines where you are not the doer ('चाय यहीं रख दी है।', where दी agrees with चाय). His thanks to you is 'सुखी रहो।' (सुखी never changes), never जीते रहो or जीती रहो, which fix a gender. 'Dekhiye' reaches you too, as his counter habit. Once in the year, teasing, आप: 'अब तो आप इंचार्ज हैं।' Never बेटा, भैया, दीदी; never आओगे/आओगी, थके हो, आ गए; any flagged line (such as one ending in a verb that agrees with the mud or the stitching) goes to the native reader.
From you to him: 'Masterji' and आप with -इए ('बैठिए, मास्टरजी।'); your one fixed reply 'Bas abhi, Masterji.' is verbless and gender-free.
This list follows the cast map's one address table where it differs; the Hindi-first and South Indian readers sign it off (rule 65).
samples: THE OPENING (3.02, his flooded doorway, to Mummy at her half-raised shutter; the drafted first line kept, then the run's one mood picture): EN 'All this mud, by Saturday?' / 'Then again, the sky's still sulking.' | HINGLISH 'Itna keechad, Shanivaar tak?' / 'Waise aasmaan abhi bhi rootha hai.' | HINDI 'इतना कीचड़, शनिवार तक?' / 'वैसे आसमान अभी भी रूठा है।'

A VERDICT ON A HEM (to a customer at a fitting; his one measure by feel in this run, and the turn is a forecast): EN 'Look, the hem is a finger's width off.' / 'By the way, the cloth's limp today. Rain's coming.' | HINGLISH 'Dekhiye, kinari ungli bhar tedhi hai.' / 'Waise kapda aaj dheela hai. Barsaat aayegi.' | HINDI 'देखिए, किनारी उँगली भर टेढ़ी है।' / 'वैसे कपड़ा आज ढीला है। बरसात आएगी।'

AT THE COUNTER, NO TURN (to a customer collecting a kurta; the shop pattern with ho, as at any tailor's): EN 'Look, I've let the kurta out. It'll fit properly now.' / 'The shoulder can be altered too. Right away.' | HINGLISH 'Dekhiye, kurta khol diya hai. Ab fitting barabar aayegi.' / 'Kandhe ka alter bhi ho jaayega. Bas abhi.' | HINDI 'देखिए, कुर्ता खोल दिया है। अब फ़िटिंग बराबर आएगी।' / 'कंधे का ऑल्टर भी हो जाएगा। बस अभी।'

WORRY (to Mummy, the Thursday before the flood; the forecast as a plain warning, in whole sentences): EN 'Bhabhi ji, the cloth's gone limp.' / 'The weather's turning. Better put the stock up high.' | HINGLISH 'Bhabhi ji, kapda dheela pad gaya hai.' / 'Mausam ka mizaaj bigda hai. Maal upar rakh lijiye.' | HINDI 'भाभी जी, कपड़ा ढीला पड़ गया है।' / 'मौसम का मिज़ाज बिगड़ा है। माल ऊपर रख लीजिए।'

TEASE (to Mummy, her shutter up at nine and his still down; the run's one mood picture): EN 'Open already, Bhabhi ji?' / 'Even the mud's still asleep.' | HINGLISH 'Itni jaldi, Bhabhi ji?' / 'Keechad bhi abhi so raha hai.' | HINDI 'इतनी जल्दी, भाभी जी?' / 'कीचड़ भी अभी सो रहा है।'

TEASE, THE ONE आप (to you, once in the year, when you are put in charge): EN 'You're in charge now, then.' / 'So the tea's on you.' | HINGLISH 'Ab toh aap in-charge hain.' / 'Chai aapki taraf se.' | HINDI 'अब तो आप इंचार्ज हैं।' / 'चाय आपकी तरफ़ से।'. Rule 66: इंचार्ज does not change with gender; the checker may catch तरफ़ से at the sentence end (a postposition), which a native reader clears.

ORDER (to you, at the drain, his tape lying slack across the crack; no turn, because the work is serious): EN 'Bring that brick. Put it on the end.' | HINGLISH 'Wo eent laao. Sire par rakh do.' | HINDI 'वो ईंट लाओ। सिरे पर रख दो।'. Rule 66: two commands, gender-free.

THE TEA BEAT (to you, Tuesday evening on the shared step): EN 'Let's have tea.' / 'The mud isn't going anywhere.' | HINGLISH 'Chai ho jaaye.' / 'Keechad kahin nahin ja raha.' | HINDI 'चाय हो जाए।' / 'कीचड़ कहीं नहीं जा रहा।'. Your fixed reply turns his phrase back on him: 'Right away, Masterji.' | 'Bas abhi, Masterji.' | 'बस अभी, मास्टरजी।' Rule 66: जा रहा agrees with कीचड़, so a native reader clears the flag.

LOVE: HIS TIME (to you, the steel tumbler set down beside you, then a story offered): EN 'Your tea's right here. Still hot.' / 'Shall I tell you about Bhai sahab's jacket?' | HINGLISH 'Chai yahin rakh di hai. Abhi garam hai.' / 'Bhai sahab ki jacket wali baat sunaaoon?' | HINDI 'चाय यहीं रख दी है। अभी गरम है।' / 'भाई साहब की जैकेट वाली बात सुनाऊँ?'. Rule 66: दी है agrees with चाय and सुनाऊँ is his own offer; भाई साहब is Papa, named, not a word for you.

COMFORT (to Mummy, after the flood; kept as the readers heard it, feeling said sideways in cloth): EN 'Wet cloth dries, Bhabhi ji.' / 'It's torn cloth you worry about.' | HINGLISH 'Geela kapda sookh jaata hai, Bhabhi ji.' / 'Fikr phate ki hoti hai.' | HINDI 'गीला कपड़ा सूख जाता है, भाभी जी।' / 'फ़िक्र फटे की होती है।'

TEMPER (at the drain, never at a person; the turn stops, then silence and a straightened back): EN 'Uff. I say it every monsoon. The drain's too low.' | HINGLISH 'Uff. Har barsaat kehta hoon. Naali neechi hai.' | HINDI 'उफ़्फ़। हर बरसात कहता हूँ। नाली नीची है।'. One bubble only, no exclamation mark.

A REAL IDIOM AT THE DRAIN (to Captain sahab across the drain, the morning after; no turn, and in a flood the idiom is nearly literal): EN 'Look, Captain, enough is enough now.' / 'This time that drain gets mended.' | HINGLISH 'Dekhiye, Captain, ab paani sir se upar ho gaya hai.' / 'Is baar naali banwaani hi padegi.' | HINDI 'देखिए, कप्तान, अब पानी सिर से ऊपर हो गया है।' / 'इस बार नाली बनवानी ही पड़ेगी।'

SORRY, PLAIN (to Mummy, his wet bolts of cloth spread over her whole roof; bas abhi means an hour, and both of them know it): EN 'Please don't mind, Bhabhi ji. I've taken over your roof.' / 'The cloth comes down right away.' | HINGLISH 'Bura mat maaniye, Bhabhi ji. Poori chhat gher li.' / 'Thaan bas abhi utaar leta hoon.' | HINDI 'बुरा मत मानिए, भाभी जी। पूरी छत घेर ली।' / 'थान बस अभी उतार लेता हूँ।'

SORRY, THE RE-MEASURE (to a customer whose hem came out wrong; his trade sorry, once a chapter at most, with a kind turn): EN 'Please don't mind. Come, let's measure again.' / 'The cloth won't hold it against us.' | HINGLISH 'Bura mat maaniye. Chaliye, phir se naap lete hain.' / 'Kapda bura nahin maanta.' | HINDI 'बुरा मत मानिए। चलिए, फिर से नाप लेते हैं।' / 'कपड़ा बुरा नहीं मानता।'

THANKS TO YOU (after you carried the tea through the flood week; the India reviewer's line, with सुखी रहो in place of जीते रहो): EN 'You're a gem. That tea saved me.' | HINGLISH 'Sukhi raho. Us chai ne bachaa liya.' | HINDI 'सुखी रहो। उस चाय ने बचा लिया।'. Rule 66: सुखी never changes with gender and बचा लिया agrees with nothing of yours; जीते रहो would make you a man (the fourth flag).

THANKS TO TINKU (who brings his late-morning tea; her gender is known, so the good wish takes her form, and the tea is on time, unlike him): EN 'You're a star, Tinku. Your tea always comes on time.' | HINGLISH 'Jeeti raho, Tinku. Tumhari chai hamesha waqt par aati hai.' | HINDI 'जीती रहो, टिंकू। तुम्हारी चाय हमेशा वक़्त पर आती है।'

THANKS TO A NEIGHBOUR (to Mummy, whose roof dried his cloth; the India reviewer's line): EN 'Bhabhi ji, your roof saved my cloth. I owe you.' | HINGLISH 'Bhabhi ji, aapki chhat ne bachaa liya. Ehsaan raha.' | HINDI 'भाभी जी, आपकी छत ने बचा लिया। एहसान रहा।'

WHEN HE IS THANKED (to Mausa ji, for the shirts stitched at cost; he makes it small by naming the older favour): EN 'Oh, Mausa ji. Your wiring still runs my shop.' | HINGLISH 'Arre, Mausa ji, aapki wiring abhi tak chal rahi hai.' | HINDI 'अरे, मौसा जी, आपकी वायरिंग अभी तक चल रही है।'

PRAISE (to Tinku, checking her scorebook columns on a Saturday): EN 'Spot on, Tinku. Dead straight columns.' / 'Straighter than my own seams.' | HINGLISH 'Barabar, Tinku. Column ekdum seedhe hain.' / 'Meri silai se bhi seedhe.' | HINDI 'बराबर, टिंकू। कॉलम एकदम सीधे हैं।' / 'मेरी सिलाई से भी सीधे।'

CREDIT TO HIS WIFE (to a customer collecting a shirt; kept as the readers heard it): EN 'Look, the buttonholes are my wife's work.' / 'I only cut. The fine work's hers.' | HINGLISH 'Dekhiye, kaaj meri gharwali ke haath ke hain.' / 'Main bas kaatta hoon. Baareek kaam unka.' | HINDI 'देखिए, काज मेरी घरवाली के हाथ के हैं।' / 'मैं बस काटता हूँ। बारीक काम उनका।'

SAYING NO (to Mama ji, by phone, who wants the kurta by Friday): EN 'No, Mama ji. Kurtas don't get stitched over the phone.' / 'By the way, city cloth only looks good in photos.' | HINGLISH 'Nahin, Mama ji. Kurta phone par nahin silta.' / 'Waise shehar ka kapda photo mein hi achha lagta hai.' | HINDI 'नहीं, मामा जी। कुर्ता फ़ोन पर नहीं सिलता।' / 'वैसे शहर का कपड़ा फ़ोटो में ही अच्छा लगता है।'

ARGUING (to Captain sahab, across the drain; the past dated by a garment, never a year, and the run's one mood picture): EN 'I said the same the year of Bhai sahab's jacket.' / 'That drain's been stubborn ever since, Captain.' | HINGLISH 'Bhai sahab ki jacket wale saal bhi yahi kaha tha.' / 'Naali tab se ziddi hai, Captain.' | HINDI 'भाई साहब की जैकेट वाले साल भी यही कहा था।' / 'नाली तब से ज़िद्दी है, कप्तान।'

TO NANI (her shawl's edge finished; their old quarrel over a hair-uneven hem, closed with a real idiom): EN 'Nani ji, the shawl's edge is done.' / 'Now find it a hair crooked, if you can.' / 'Then again, nobody splits hairs like you, Nani ji.' | HINGLISH 'Nani ji, shawl ki kinari ho gayi.' / 'Ab dhoondhiye, baal bhar bhi tedhi ho toh.' / 'Waise aap toh baal ki khaal bhi nikaal lengi.' | HINDI 'नानी जी, शॉल की किनारी हो गई।' / 'अब ढूँढिए, बाल भर भी टेढ़ी हो तो।' / 'वैसे आप तो बाल की खाल भी निकाल लेंगी।'

TEASE (to Papa, who arrives at every fitting on the dot; the joke is at Papa's railway and at his own excuse): EN 'On time, Bhai sahab? Your trains never are.' | HINGLISH 'Waqt par, Bhai sahab? Aapki gaadiyan toh kabhi nahin.' | HINDI 'वक़्त पर, भाई साहब? आपकी गाड़ियाँ तो कभी नहीं।'

HIS TIME (to a waiting customer; bas abhi means an hour): EN 'Look, right away.' / 'By the way, cloth dries slowly in the rains.' | HINGLISH 'Dekhiye, bas abhi.' / 'Waise barsaat mein kapda der se sookhta hai.' | HINDI 'देखिए, बस अभी।' / 'वैसे बरसात में कपड़ा देर से सूखता है।'

CAUGHT OUT (to Captain sahab, who has shown him wrong about which monsoon the drain was last cleaned; a real tailoring idiom, the joke at himself): EN 'Well, Captain, you've caught me out.' / 'All right, I grant it. I measured wrong.' | HINGLISH 'Achha, Captain, aapne toh meri bakhiya udhed di.' / 'Theek hai, maan liya. Naap mera galat tha.' | HINDI 'अच्छा, कप्तान, आपने तो मेरी बखिया उधेड़ दी।' / 'ठीक है, मान लिया। नाप मेरा ग़लत था।'

FORECAST LEAD-INS (3.11 and 3.21 as a matched pair, rule 37 twins; each line is itself his forecast, now with its verb): EN 'The cloth's gone stiff. No rain till Sunday.' / 'The cloth's dry at last. Clear skies tomorrow.' | HINGLISH 'Kapda kadak ho gaya. Itwaar tak baarish nahin hogi.' / 'Kapda aakhir sookh gaya. Kal aasmaan saaf rahega.' | HINDI 'कपड़ा कड़क हो गया। इतवार तक बारिश नहीं होगी।' / 'कपड़ा आख़िर सूख गया। कल आसमान साफ़ रहेगा।'. Two separate beats, shown here together; the two lines stay within 2 words of each other in every language.

THE FIXED ENDING (3.28, crouched at the cracked drain; the drafted figure for the lanes proposed as dono so his speech carries no figure, owner's call): EN 'The flood cracked the drain between both lanes.' / 'Whose drain? Let the lane cup decide.' | HINGLISH 'Baadh se dono galiyon ke beech ki naali mein daraar.' / 'Naali kiski? Gali ka cup tay kare.' | HINDI 'बाढ़ से दोनों गलियों के बीच की नाली में दरार।' / 'नाली किसकी? गली का कप तय करे।'

habits: Device: his son's old phone with a cracked screen guard, kept in his shirt pocket under the sadri (never painted there; any phone in a scene is painted blank, rule 30). He reads it chin up through the bottom of his spectacles, then drops his chin to look over them at whoever is near, as if they sent it.
Script: Roman Hindi in lowercase, 'h' for है, shop English as nouns; spellings drift as romanised Hindi does ('zaroor', 'jaroor').

No digits at all. Sizes and dates travel in the photo of the measurement slip (painted blank), never in his words; times are written as words ('kal shaam', 'parson subah') and pushed back once before they are kept ('aaj zaroor ji').

Punctuation: thoughts joined with two dots '..'; no full stops, no question marks, no exclamation marks. A card holds 10 words or fewer (rule 62, if the owner rules that a message card counts as a spoken line): a longer message goes as two cards sent one after the other, cut at his own '..', and the first card keeps its '..' at the end, as if he is still typing.
The typed turn: about half his messages end on the weather or the cloth ('.. hawa me nami h', '.. aaj baadal nahi'), the same verdict-then-turn shape he speaks in; the rest stop at the news.
'ji' on nearly everything, even 'ok ji'. No emoji, no stickers, no ticks, no numbered lists, no flowers.
Photo first, words after: a photo of a slip or a bolt of cloth, then one short line.
Voice notes only to customers about a fitting, short, with the machine running behind him; never long ones (that is Mausi).
Timing: types slowly with his right thumb before opening, and answers yesterday's messages the next morning ('kal dekha ji').

voices.name: Captain sahab (कप्तान साहब), about 65

voice.register: Crisp and low: an umpire's carrying voice that never needs raising. HIS SHAPE IS TWO BEATS: the verdict first, short, then at most one short reason or instruction, never the reason first, 2 to 8 words in a bubble. At the ground and on any ruling the verdict is an umpire's call ('No ball. Line ke peeche se daalo.', 'Not out, Nani ji. Bat laga tha.'). Everywhere else, at the gate, on the six o'clock walk, across the drain, the verdict is plain lane Hindi and the reason comes from the bus depot ('Zyada meethi hai, Master. Bilkul depot canteen wali.', 'Theek hoon. Bas ghutna servicing mein.'). A call shows up in at most one bubble in two, so cricket is his trade, not his whole tongue: a retired depot mechanic talks cricket at the ground and plain Hindi with depot words at the gate. The calls he keeps: 'Out.', 'Not out.', 'No ball.', 'Over.', 'Next ball.', 'Well played.', 'Well fielded.', 'Front foot.', 'Retired hurt.' for his knee, and 'Ruko' ('Rukiye' when an elder can hear). A second thought is a second bubble after a second toss of the ball, never a longer line, and he never adds a third beat: Masterji's verdict wanders on after 'waise', Captain sahab's stops. Short, but not like the cast's other short voices: Nani closes bare fragments and orders, Mausa ji drops the subject, Tinku gives a score and 'haan?', Mami reads things back with a status, you name the listener. Beside Tinku in chapter 4 he gives rulings and she keeps the score: he never describes play as it happens (her commentary) and never says a score. FEELING: in plain words most of the time, said short and once ('Mujhse chook ho gayi.', 'Badi meherbani.', 'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.'). A cricket code for a feeling ('Next ball' as comfort, 'Well fielded' as thanks, 'Front foot' as love) comes at most once a chapter, beside its plain form. 'Well played.' comes once a year, and then he looks away. HUMOUR: sardonic and bone-dry, about his knee, his age and the game ('Purana model hoon, Scorer. Parts nahin milte.'), never about a person's hard fact; while rulebook Q5 is open his jokes stay out of the chapter outcome (rule 46). NUMBERS: rare and marked, only the toss countdown in the two lead-ins (a story deadline, rule 37) and 'Nau matlab nau' once a year to Papa; everything else in words. When he is not sure he waits ('Ruko.') rather than guess out loud. CROSS: he goes still. A whisper bubble, the words further apart, the verdict finger up and kept up; never a shout, never an exclamation mark. Tinku, his chapter's other voice, goes fast when cross, so their tells never match. TALKS MOST TO the lane's players, and on the page to Tinku at the scorer's table, Papa on the six o'clock walk and Masterji across the drain. He is never the asker (rule 37).
voice.mix: A Hindi frame: plain lane Hindi with a few older everyday words in it (meherbani, zaroor, waqt, chook, mol-bhaav). English comes in for two things only, the topic pulling it in, as the realism notes have the older speakers. Cricket: the calls and coaching words, said the way the lane says them (out, not out, no ball, over, next ball, front foot, straight bat, well played, well fielded, clean catch, catch, toss, pitch, crease). Machines: depot nouns (servicing, jack, clutch, tube, grip, tarpaulin, canteen, depot, model, parts), and for a machine job the everyday English verb with karo ('Grip change karo', 'Brake check karo'), the way every depot mechanic talks. His knee stays 'Retired hurt', a call, never 'retire hua'. He never switches a whole clause into English (Mama ji and Mami do). The common fillers are his as much as anyone's, in the middle of a line (achha, bas, arre, haan, chalo, dekho, theek hai). आप and a title to elders and equals; तुम to anyone he has coached or seen drop a catch. HINDI MODE, written fresh for Hindi-first readers: the cricket words every lane fan knows stay (आउट, नॉट आउट, नो बॉल, कैच, ओवर, टॉस, पिच, फ़्रंट फ़ुट, सीधा बैट), and the rest go into plain Hindi: Next ball अगली गेंद, Well played बढ़िया पारी, Well fielded अच्छा पकड़ा (बढ़िया फ़ील्डिंग when it is said of a job off the field), Clean catch साफ़ कैच, Dead ball ये गेंद नहीं गिनी जाएगी, Retired hurt घुटना छुट्टी पर, Last over आख़िरी ओवर; machine verbs in plain Hindi (ग्रिप बदलो). HINGLISH keeps the English calls. ENGLISH MODE: plain, clipped British English with the calls unchanged; 'Arre waah' stays as it is, the way Mami keeps 'Ish'.
tics: Two beats, the verdict then one reason, never the reason first: at the ground 'No ball. Line ke peeche se daalo.' | 'नो बॉल। लाइन के पीछे से डालो।'; off the ground the same shape in plain Hindi: 'Zyada meethi hai, Master. Bilkul depot canteen wali.' | 'ज़्यादा मीठी है, मास्टर। बिल्कुल डिपो कैंटीन वाली।'

At the ground he answers yes and no with a call: 'Not out.' (yes, fine), 'Out.' (no, finished), 'No ball.' (not allowed), 'Over.' (enough). At the gate he says 'Haan.' and 'Nahin.' like anyone. His typed yes is 'Not out'.

The reason comes from the bus depot when it is not from the ground: servicing, jack, clutch, tube, grip, the depot canteen, an old model with no spare parts ('Theek hoon. Bas ghutna servicing mein.').
'Arre waah.' | 'अरे वाह।' quietly, to nobody, at a clean catch, a shot off the middle of the bat, or good news he can see as one, and never louder.
Brings up his one state trial at any talk of umpires, luck or fairness: 'Ek hi trial tha. Not out. Kisi se poochh lo.' Nobody alive was there; no year on screen (rule 2).

Calls people by trade or title: 'Master' (Masterji), 'Lineman sahab' (Mausa ji), 'Madam ji' (Mausi), 'Scorer' (Tinku), 'khiladi' (any child or lane player, women and men alike). Mama ji gets no name, only 'Catch?'
Says the plain thing once and short, and does not say it again: a sorry, a thanks or a comfort is one bubble, then he tosses the ball or walks off.
Tosses the old leather ball a hand above his open palm while he decides; the catch is the full stop on his sentence. A second thought is a second bubble after a second toss, never a longer line.
Cross, he goes still: a whisper bubble, the words further apart, the verdict finger up and kept up.
catchphrases: 'Straight bat. Front foot.' | 'सीधा बैट। फ़्रंट फ़ुट।' | 'Seedha bat. Front foot.' (the line people quote back, kept word for word; still his hello to every child he coached, you included)
'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.' | 'कोई बात नहीं, खिलाड़ी। होता है।' | 'Never mind, player. It happens.' (what every lane child has heard from him after a dropped catch or a broken glass)
'Ek hi trial tha. Not out. Kisi se poochh lo.' | 'एक ही ट्रायल था। नॉट आउट। किसी से पूछ लो।' | 'One trial. Not out. Ask anyone.' (the grudge; no year)
voice.exclamation: 'Arre waah.' | 'अरे वाह।' | 'Arre waah.' Said quietly, to nobody, at a clean catch, a shot off the middle of the bat, or good news he can see as one ('Arre waah. Bilkul bat ke beech se.'). English mode keeps it as it is, the way Mami keeps 'Ish'; if the English readers find it foreign, the fallback is 'Shot.', said quietly, and only at a stroke. 'Arre' on its own belongs to everyone and he uses it mid-line like anyone; the phrase said under his breath is his. Never at a person's looks, never sarcastic, never loud: it is the one warm sound he makes without words, so a power cut or a late guest gets something else. Religious meaning: none; 'waah' is everyday praise. Guards (rule 3): never run on into 'Waheguru', and 'arre' is never followed by a name from any faith ('Arre Ram' is banned).
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: plain, at once, in front of whoever saw it, in his two beats: the slip owned, then the fact put right. 'Mujhse chook ho gayi, Bhai sahab. Ghadi dheemi hai.' | 'मुझसे चूक हो गई, भाई साहब। घड़ी धीमी है।' | 'I slipped up, Bhai sahab. The clock is slow.' At the ground, at most once a chapter, he takes back his own wrong call the umpire's way: 'Not out. Mujhse chook hui, khiladi.' The one sorry he cannot say is the one owed to the trial's umpire, or to Nani, who says that umpire was right: his contradiction, kept. THANKS: to an elder or an equal, plain and short: 'Badi meherbani, Lineman sahab.' | 'बड़ी मेहरबानी, लाइनमैन साहब।' | 'Much obliged, Lineman sahab.' With the deed, his two-rupee game with Mummy turned round as the full price goes down on her glass counter: 'Poore paise, Bhabhi ji. Aaj mol-bhaav nahin.' At the ground, once a chapter, the cricket form: 'Well fielded, khiladi.' (Hindi 'अच्छा पकड़ा, खिलाड़ी।'). His old deeds stay, never mentioned: Mausi's boxes washed, the tarpaulin over Masterji's cloth. WHEN HE IS THANKED: 'Kis baat ka?', then the credit sent somewhere else ('Kis baat ka, Scorer? Chhaon kitaab ke liye hai.'). LOVE: 'Front foot.', his hello to every child he coached, you included. For you it also comes as the thing he kept: 'Tumhara purana bat hai mere paas. / Nayi grip ke saath.'; on the platform, 'Front foot. Cup pe zaroor aao.' Never your marks, your job, your plans or a number. 'Well played.' (Hindi 'बढ़िया पारी।') is his highest praise, once a year, and then he looks away. COMFORT: 'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.' to a child or a player; for a real loss, once a chapter, the call: 'Next ball, Bhabhi ji. Shutter kal bhi uthega.' (Hindi 'अगली गेंद, भाभी जी। शटर कल भी उठेगा।'). A bare 'Not out.' stays a ruling, never comfort.

'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin.' | 'सबूत नहीं, तो उँगली नहीं।' in any chapter or form: it is a coined maxim and a demand for proof, and a one-line clip of it reads as 'the family wants proof' whatever it was said about. Subah bhatti jal rahi thi.'), and the build flags proof words near a report beat (rule 22).

Other people's phrases (the words inside them stay free): Papa's 'Kamaal hai', 'Darj hai', 'Kripya dhyan dein', 'Aakhri dibbe tak' and any clock time or 'sharp'; Tinku's commentary ('Aur ye gaya!'), score shapes, 'Gazab' and the 'haan?' tag; Nani's closing 'Bas.', 'Chai piyo' and 'Khush raho'; Masterji's 'Jeete raho', 'Uff', 'Aap sahi hain' and 'Theek hai, maan liya'; Mausi's 'Suno, suno, suno!', 'Haay' and 'Shabaash'; Mausa ji's 'Hain?', 'Lo.' for here, a one-word 'Theek.' and 'Isme kya'; Mama ji's 'Oho', the trailing 'aur haan,' and 'Pakka?'; Mummy's 'Had hai!', 'Haan ji, boliye' and 'Badhai ho'; Mami's 'Ish', 'Tick', 'Sahi?' and 'Congratulations'; your 'Badhiya.' as an opener, 'Maaf kijiye', 'Shukriya' and the 'Pehle ___' frame.

Other people's shapes: a comma list of jobs (Mummy), three bare fragments in a row (Nani), a whole English clause (Mama ji, Mami), a readback with a status (Mami), a tripled word (Mausi), a third beat that wanders (Masterji).

In Hindi mode, an English cricket phrase in Devanagari that a lane fan would not know: never नेक्स्ट बॉल, वेल प्लेड, वेल फ़ील्डेड, डेड बॉल, रिटायर्ड हर्ट, क्लीन कैच, लास्ट ओवर (rule 65). 'Timed out' leaves his voice in every mode.
Jargon most Indians would not know: googly, silly point, doosra, Duckworth, timed out (rule 2).
A coined saying or maxim. He has no proverbs (they are Nani's way) and no rulings turned into sayings; 'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin' was one and is cut.
'batsman', 'ladies', 'boys', 'girls', 'मर्द', 'औरत', 'लड़कियाँ', 'लड़के' about players: everyone is a player (खिलाड़ी) or a batter.

'show-off', 'drama queen', 'emotional', 'bossy', 'argues with everybody', 'knows best', 'moody', 'too modern': words the measure judge read as sexist on sight. Nothing about women or men in general (rule 22).
'beta', 'beti', 'bhaiya', 'didi', 'bhai', 'bro' or any family word to you (rule 8).

A Hindi line to you that changes with gender (rule 66): -ूँगा/-ूँगी, -ोगे/-ोगी, -ेगा/-ेगी, आ गया/गई, रहते हो/रहती हो, and a participle before रहो or रहना (खाते रहो). His lines to you are commands, verbless calls, or lines where you are not the doer ('Tumhara purana bat hai mere paas.').
'Ruko', तुम or a -ो command to anyone older than him; 'Rukiye' | 'रुकिए' whenever an elder is at the table or in earshot.

A god-word or religious exclamation (rule 3; the list in matrix 2.13), 'arre' followed by a holy name, 'waah' run on into 'Waheguru'; no caste word, no brand: the scooters, the phone and the canteen are never named.
A sarcastic 'Arre waah': it stays the one warm sound he makes without words.
A year on screen, '1979' included (rule 2).
A raised voice: no shout bubble, no exclamation mark, no all-capital word.
A spoken bubble over 10 words (rule 62). His own aim is 2 to 8 counted words (names and titles not counted, as rule 62 counts them). Never a speech.
'water', 'wall', 'chalk' (पानी, दीवार, चॉक) in any line: chapter 4 note words (Hari, Agnes, Manju, rule 36); never a card person's name or note word before or during a decision.
'captain' as a job word for anyone else (rule 36: in Hindi the job and his title are one word).

No name and no family word; 'Front foot.' is his hello. You say आप and 'Captain sahab'.
TINKU: 'Scorer' | 'स्कोरर', तुम. She says आप and 'Captain sahab'.

habits: The phone: a plain phone in a plain dark case with a cracked top corner, kept in a trouser pocket. Painted with a blank screen; every message is live text on it, or a message card under the panel if the phone is small (rules 30 and 40). No app name, app look or 'forwarded' label (rule 3), and no quirk about his eyes or the font size.

Script: English in Latin letters only, never Devanagari and never a Hinglish sentence (realism notes 2.3). The messages are strings of nouns and calls, not English clauses, so this does not break his speech's no-clause rule.
Shape: a telegram in his speaking shape, the thing first, then the place, then one instruction, 1 to 7 words.
His typed yes is 'Not out', his not-yet 'Wait', his enough 'Over'; the lane knows a message is his by it. When he thanks, he types it plainly: 'thank you'.
Figures: none, except the cup's date and its nine o'clock, as digits and only in cup messages. Never a minute, never a score, never a price.

Punctuation: none at all, not even a question mark. The phone capitalises the first letter, and that is his only capital. Never all capitals, which reads as shouting and is the 'WhatsApp uncle' trap (realism notes 7).
The one exception: once a year, in his own family group (mentioned, never shown), he writes the cup's end in full sentences with full stops. That is the tell that it matters.
Emoji: one only, 🏏, on cup messages. Tinku's 🏏 to him copies his. No faces, no folded hands, no stickers, no good-morning flowers, no forwards, ever.
Voice notes: never sends one. He listens to the first few seconds of anyone else's and answers with the one fact asked, or a call.

He sends the same words one by one to every person rather than to a group: he trusts a message he has sent himself. The lane's group exists and is mentioned, never shown (owner, 23 Oct: no group chat).
Reads and answers twice a day, after the walk and before the toss, and within a minute about cricket or the drain; never late at night (he walks at dawn).
One forefinger, slow and deliberate; no typos, because there are so few words.

TO MAUSA JI, the night the rewired floodlights first come on (plain thanks): 'Lights on thank you lineman sahab'
TO MASTERJI, the morning after the July flood: 'Drain cracked your side' (Masterji's reply, not his: 'aapki side')
TO MAMA JI, when the trophy is promised again: 'Catch' (his greeting, typed with no question mark)
TO YOU, on your birthday (kept): 'Happy birthday front foot'
TO HIS OWN FAMILY GROUP (mentioned, never shown; his one message a year in full sentences; the same in every band): 'The cup is over. Both lanes mended the drain together. 🏏'

test_lines.moment: 4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it (to Masterji, who made it; a polite no, the reason from the depot).
test_lines.en: Too sweet, Master. Like the depot canteen's.
test_lines.hinglish: Zyada meethi hai, Master. Bilkul depot canteen wali.
test_lines.hi: ज़्यादा मीठी है, मास्टर। बिल्कुल डिपो कैंटीन वाली।

test_lines.moment: 5. In front of the family, he is shown to have had a fact wrong (to Papa, who has shown that the station clock runs slow; his plain sorry, said at once).
test_lines.en: I slipped up, Bhai sahab. The clock is slow.
test_lines.hinglish: Mujhse chook ho gayi, Bhai sahab. Ghadi dheemi hai.
test_lines.hi: मुझसे चूक हो गई, भाई साहब। घड़ी धीमी है।

test_lines.moment: 6. Someone he loves is leaving, goodbye on a railway platform (to you; his hello, then a command, rule 66 clear).
test_lines.en: Front foot. Be back for the cup.
test_lines.hinglish: Front foot. Cup pe zaroor aao.
test_lines.hi: फ़्रंट फ़ुट। कप पे ज़रूर आओ।

test_lines.moment: 7. Someone thanks him for something he did (Tinku, for his chair in the shade every cup; 'Kis baat ka?' and the credit sent elsewhere, which keeps his 4.26 turn unspent).
test_lines.en: What for, Scorer? The shade's for the book.
test_lines.hinglish: Kis baat ka, Scorer? Chhaon kitaab ke liye hai.
test_lines.hi: किस बात का, स्कोरर? छाँव किताब के लिए है।

test_lines.moment: 8. A neighbour passes on a rumour that the corner sweet shop is closing (to Mummy, who heard it at her counter; an appeal turned down with what he saw on his dawn walk; a habit of judging, never a character).
test_lines.en: Not out, Bhabhi ji. Their stove was lit at dawn.
test_lines.hinglish: Not out, Bhabhi ji. Subah bhatti jal rahi thi.
test_lines.hi: नॉट आउट, भाभी जी। सुबह भट्टी जल रही थी।

test_lines.moment: 9. Heavy rain floods the lane outside the house (to the lane, you among them; worry as an order, then the depot; verbless order, rule 66 clear).
test_lines.en: Off the drain. I've got the depot tarpaulin.
test_lines.hinglish: Naali se door. Depot ka tirpal hai mere paas.
test_lines.hi: नाली से दूर। डिपो का तिरपाल है मेरे पास।

test_lines.moment: 10. Someone asks him how he is (you ask; a plain answer, then his knee in depot words; no figure, no dodge).
test_lines.en: I'm fine. Just the knee, in for servicing.
test_lines.hinglish: Theek hoon. Bas ghutna servicing mein.
test_lines.hi: ठीक हूँ। बस घुटना सर्विसिंग में।

test_lines.moment: 11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table (to the child, a grandchild at the table; plain comfort; 'khiladi' fits any child).
test_lines.en: Never mind, player. It happens.
test_lines.hinglish: Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.
test_lines.hi: कोई बात नहीं, खिलाड़ी। होता है।

test_lines.moment: 12. A phone call brings good news (to the caller; his exclamation, quiet).
test_lines.en: Arre waah. Right off the middle of the bat.
test_lines.hinglish: Arre waah. Bilkul bat ke beech se.
test_lines.hi: अरे वाह। बिल्कुल बैट के बीच से।

changed: KEPT: who he is. Essence, want, fear and contradiction (strict by the book, still sore about one trial), the turn at 4.26 ('That book. Show the district.'), the stakes at 4.03, the fixed ending at 4.27, the toss as his word alone, the still, whispering anger, and every line the readers marked as ringing true: 'Straight bat. Front foot.' as his hello, 'Arre waah' said quietly at a clean catch, 'Retired hurt. Sirf ghutna.', 'Nau matlab nau, Bhai sahab.', 'Next ball, Bhabhi ji. Shutter kal bhi uthega.', 'Lineman sahab, aapki batting.', 'khiladi' for any child, 'Madam ji', 'Lineman sahab', and the texts 'Happy birthday front foot' and 'Cup 15 aug ground 9 am 🏏'.

THE CARICATURE (real-India note): a call opened 10 of his 12 test lines and every feeling was an umpire's word. Now the shape is two beats, verdict then one reason, and the verdict is a call only at the ground or on a ruling; at the gate it is plain lane Hindi with a depot reason. Calls now sit in 3 of his 12 test lines ('Well played', 'Front foot', 'Not out'; three more carry a cricket picture: 'aapki batting', the old catch, 'bat ke beech se') and in under half his sample bubbles.

FEELINGS IN PLAIN WORDS (cast-wide 3): sorry is 'Mujhse chook ho gayi, Bhai sahab. Ghadi dheemi hai.' (was 'Dead ball. Umpire ki chook. Next ball.'); thanks is 'Badi meherbani, Lineman sahab.' and, with the deed, 'Poore paise, Bhabhi ji. Aaj mol-bhaav nahin.' (was 'Well fielded' to both); when thanked, 'Kis baat ka, Scorer?' (was 'Over, Scorer.'); comfort is 'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.'; love also comes as the bat he kept for you ('Tumhara purana bat hai mere paas. / Nayi grip ke saath.'); his fear is said plainly to Papa ('Scooter badh rahe hain, Bhai sahab. / Mere baad, ye parking.', was 'Last over, Bhai sahab. Maidan pe scooter.'). Each cricket code for a feeling now comes at most once a chapter, beside its plain form.

THE READERS' LINES, used as given: moment 2 'Ab aaye? Catch bhi aise hi chhoota tha.' (was 'Timed out. Catch ki tarah.'); moment 11 'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.' (was 'Catch chhoota. Hota hai, khiladi. Next ball.'); the grudge 'Ek hi trial tha. Not out. Kisi se poochh lo.' (was 'Mera iklauta trial ...', since 'iklauta' is said of an only child).
POLITENESS (Hindi rules note a): moment 1 opens 'Rukiye.' | 'रुकिए।', since Nani, who is older than him, is at the table. 'Ruko' now goes only to players and anyone younger.

RULE 22 (Hindi rules note b, cast-wide 5, real-India note): 'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin.' is cut from his voice entirely, his uses included. It was a coined maxim and a demand for proof, and fencing it to harmless rumours did not protect it: a one-line clip carries 'the family wants proof' whatever it was said about. He now never asks for proof. Moment 8 does the same job with what he saw: 'Not out, Bhabhi ji. Subah bhatti jal rahi thi.'

HINDI MODE (Hindi rules note, real-India note, cast-wide 11): no English cricket phrase in Devanagari that Sunita and Meena could not read. नेक्स्ट बॉल becomes अगली गेंद, वेल प्लेड बढ़िया पारी, वेल फ़ील्डेड अच्छा पकड़ा (बढ़िया फ़ील्डिंग off the field), क्लीन कैच साफ़ कैच, डेड बॉल ये गेंद नहीं गिनी जाएगी, रिटायर्ड हर्ट घुटना छुट्टी पर ('घुटना छुट्टी पर। मैं नहीं।' for the knee joke). आउट, नॉट आउट, नो बॉल, कैच, फ़्रंट फ़ुट and सीधा बैट stay. 'Timed out' leaves his voice in every mode, since the readers found it obscure even in English; the Hindi rules note's 'टाइम आउट। उस कैच की तरह।' is not needed, because moment 2 no longer uses it. Hinglish keeps the English calls.

COMMON FILLERS ARE FREE (cast-wide 1): the bans on arre, achha, chalo, suno, dekho, bas, theek and haan are gone; he says 'Achha, Scorer, ...' and 'Bas ghutna ...' mid-line. 'Arre' is no longer his alone; he keeps the phrase 'Arre waah' said quietly. His never list now names other people's phrases and shapes only.
ENGLISH VERB WITH KAR (cast-wide 2): allowed where it suits him, for a machine job, the depot's way ('Grip change karo. Depot ka tube lagao.'). His knee stays 'Retired hurt', the rang-true call.
URDU-ROOTED WORDS (cast-wide 8): 'meherbani', 'zaroor' and 'waqt' are in his everyday Hindi ('Badi meherbani', 'Cup pe zaroor aao'), so they belong to the town, not to Masterji.
MORE VERBS (cast-wide 9): plain lines now carry their 'hai', 'tha' or 'hoon' ('Bat laga tha.', 'Theek hoon.', 'Purana model hoon, Scorer.'); bare shapes stay for calls and orders.

ENGLISH MODE (real-India note, cast-wide 10): 'Oh, nice.' goes; 'Arre waah.' stays in English as Mami's 'Ish' does, with 'Shot.' as the readers' fallback, only at a stroke. 'It took the bat' becomes 'It hit the bat'; 'Much obliged' and 'I slipped up' give him an older Englishman's plain words.

NO COINED SAYINGS: he has no proverbs and no maxims. 'Achhe-achhe out hote hain' is everyday Hindi and was chosen over 'bade-bade', which brings a famous film line to mind. 'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin' is cut (see RULE 22).

CLASHES AVOIDED with the other rewrites: 'Shabaash' stays Mausi's, 'Aap sahi hain' and 'Theek hai, maan liya' stay Masterji's, 'Isme kya' stays with Mama ji, Mummy and Mausa ji. One shared opening is left on purpose because the readers wrote it: 'Koi baat nahin' in moment 11, which Mummy, Papa and Mausi also say; 'khiladi' and 'Hota hai' mark his.
TYPING: unchanged in shape. One new plain thanks, 'Lights on thank you lineman sahab' to Mausa ji; the rule against typing 'ok' is no longer pinned on other people.

KNOCK-ON FOR HIS CAST FILE AND OTHERS: never_does 'Says sorry in words.' must go (he now does, plainly, except to the trial's umpire and to Nani); his MUMMY relationship ('Not out, Bhabhi ji. Next ball.' becomes 'Next ball, Bhabhi ji. Shutter kal bhi uthega.', and his thanks becomes 'Poore paise'); his MAUSA JI relationship (thanks is 'Badi meherbani'); his essence's 'answers most questions with an umpire's call' becomes 'at the ground'; matrix 2.14 and 2.15 rows for him ('Next ball' sorry, 'Well fielded' thanks, sole owner of 'arre').

FOR THE READERS (rule 65): Hindi-first readers check 'मुझसे चूक हो गई' as an everyday sorry (fallback 'ग़लती मेरी'), 'बड़ी मेहरबानी', 'घुटना छुट्टी पर। मैं नहीं।', 'अच्छा पकड़ा' for a fielding stop, 'अच्छे-अच्छे आउट होते हैं', and 'टिक के खेलना'; English-mode readers check 'Arre waah' left in English and 'player' for 'khiladi'. The checker run on this file is clean apart from moment 1, said to a table: its rule 66 flag on 'Rukiye' | 'रुकिए' is a polite form that shows no gender, and its address flag on 'sahab' | 'साहब' is Mausa ji's title, not a word for you.

FINAL POLISH: the proof maxim and its words (saboot, ungli) leave his uses; 'rule | niyam' stays. The clash with You in moment 7 ('Kis baat ka?' to thanks, and 'Scorer' for Tinku) is fixed on You's side: 'Kis baat ka?' and naming people by their trade are his habit, so his lines are unchanged. voices.name: Mami (मामी), about 45

voice.register: Medium and even, in two voices, and the switch between them is her tell. THE DESK VOICE is for jobs, the list, vendors and strangers. Its lead shape is the readback: 'So.' | 'तो।' | 'Toh.', then one whole sentence that hands your own plan back to you, then 'Correct?' | 'सही?' | 'Sahi?', and she waits for the answer. Its second shape is the status pair: a thing, its status, a full stop, then the next pair ('Keys, pending. Envelopes, done.'; in Hindi mode with no comma, 'टेंट लग गया। रसोइया अभी बाक़ी।'). The item is named, never numbered: no ordinals, no counts, no prices, no clock times. THE HOME VOICE takes over the moment a family feeling arrives (a goodbye, a cousin's news, her husband worried, a report): the statuses stop, and she speaks short whole sentences of plain, warm Hindi with their hai or hoon ('Fikr mat karo. Mummy ji ka BP normal hai.', 'Mujhe yakeen hai.', 'Ab kya karna hai?'). A city manager talks in statuses at the desk and stops at home, and so does she, which is why the desk voice is funny when she turns it on her husband and used in no tender moment. A bubble runs 4 to 10 words, most often 6 to 9; usually one bubble, at most two. Crisp, unhurried and never raised: no exclamation mark in any bubble, 'Congratulations.' and 'Ish.' included, and never the shout (the chapter's shout is Mama ji's). The same pace in a crisis as at tea, which is why people calm down near her. Firm with vendors, polite with elders, sly with her husband. Talked over, she raises the pen, point up, says nothing, and finishes when the room is quiet. When cross she goes slower, turns the clipboard round to face the person, reads the line aloud from it ('Yahan likha hai.') and closes with an icy 'Thank you' to a vendor, or a flat 'Correct?' to family. Apart from the cast: not Mummy's comma lists of jobs and people with no status ('Aur kuch?') or her home things in counter English; not Mausa ji's subjectless verdicts on things; not Captain sahab's call then reason; not Papa's whole sentences with a time in them; not Nani's jobs handed to 'koi'; not Mama ji's run-ons and 'Oho!'. A script can count it: about half her lines carry a status word or end on 'Correct?', and every one of those is about a job, a list or a vendor; her family feeling lines carry none, and most of them have hai or hoon; no line carries an ordinal, a figure or '!'.
voice.mix: City whole-clause switching, the younger urban pattern in the realism notes (the Dehradun code-switching study): she switches at the full stop, a whole Hindi clause and then a whole English one, or the other way round ('Meri shaadi ki bhi list thi. Still on file.'). Inside a Hindi clause the desk crosses over in two ways: its nouns (list, item, form, file, claim, receipt, balance, payment) and, as with most city people under fifty, an office English verb with kar or ho ('List ab tum handle karo.', 'Claim main file karti hoon.', 'Receipt pe sign kar dijiye.', 'Bahut help ho gayi.'). Her English verbs come from the office (file, sign, check, handle, note), never from the home: Mummy turns home things into counter English ('ye cup return karo', 'MCB check karo'), and Mama ji talks logistics. Her English statuses in Hinglish: done, pending, not known, safe, approved, in progress, closed, still on file, all clear, correct. In Hindi mode a status becomes the everyday Hindi a city office speaks (हो गया, लग गया, बाक़ी, पता नहीं, मंज़ूर, चालू, बंद, ठीक, फ़ाइल में), with पेंडिंग and स्टेटस kept only for her two dry jokes, and with no comma between a Hindi subject and its verb, because spoken Hindi does not pause there; a colon comes only before a label with no verb ('स्टेटस: मेहमान।', 'तुम्हारे मामा जी: अब भी पेंडिंग।'). The commas stay in Hinglish and English pairs. Her Hindi carries people, food, rooms and elders, and the town's everyday Urdu-rooted words sit in it as they do in anyone's (fikr, zaroor, yakeen). 'Thank you' and 'Sorry' are the counter's words, English in every mode (थैंक यू, सॉरी), for vendors and strangers only; with family her sorry is Hindi ('मुझसे छूट गया') and her thanks is plain ('बहुत मदद हो गई'). Polite Hindi to every elder and every vendor (आप, -इए). One Bengali word, her mother's: the exclamation 'Ish.' Nothing else from Bengali, and never a spelled accent. Apart from Mama ji, who leads with fast English and runs his clauses together on 'aur haan', she is clause by clause, each one closed, and her English is the desk's, never logistics talk, slang or 'Don't worry'.
tics: THE READBACK, her lead tic, for jobs and plans: 'So.', your plan in one whole sentence, 'Correct?', and she waits: 'So. Keys with you, from tonight. Correct?' | 'तो। चाबियाँ आज रात से तुम्हारे पास। सही?' | 'Toh. Chaabiyan tumhare paas, aaj raat se. Sahi?'. From Friday she stops reading your plan back to you, and that is her deepest thank-you, the one she never says.

THE STATUS PAIR, for the list and for vendors: thing, comma, status, full stop: 'Tent, done. Cook, pending. Keys, not known.' In Hindi mode the comma goes and the status is everyday Hindi: 'टेंट लग गया। रसोइया अभी बाक़ी।' She names the item, never its place on the list.

THE SWITCH HOME: when a family feeling arrives, the desk finishes its line and plain Hindi, most often with hai or hoon, says the thing that matters: 'Ticket, tiffin, done. Agli baar kab?'; 'Congratulations. Joining kab se? Somvaar? Bahut achha.' No status, file, tick or 'Correct?' in a goodbye, a congratulation, comfort or a report.
She files herself as a joke, never as a feeling. Asked how she is: 'Main? Sab clear hai.' | 'मैं? सब ठीक है।' | 'Me? All clear.' Hurt, said once and dry: 'Status: mehmaan.'

Asks every vendor and helper about their children, the counter's habit and her one interest on the page that is not a list: 'Bhaiya ji, beti ka paper kaisa gaya?'. It is also, quietly, about her own daughter.

'Thank you' and 'Sorry' out loud, in English, to every vendor and stranger, even when cross: the counter's words. Never to family (Mausi teases her for saying it 'like a bill'); thanked at home, she says 'Ghar mein thank you nahin chalta.'
Thanks family in plain words, 'Bahut help ho gayi.', and her husband the everyday way, 'Maan gayi.'; at most once a chapter the pen comes down on a spoken 'Tick.'.

Sly about her husband, said as a status and to the young ones, as if he were not standing there: 'Your Mama ji: still pending.' Once a chapter at most, so it stays a joke and is not her only one: his count, his dinner and the rest get the plain line.

The house's common fillers, like anyone in it: achha, suno, arre, theek hai, chalo, chaliye, to open a line or in the middle of one ('Achha, suno. List ab tum handle karo.'). She owns none of them; her shape is what marks her.
Talked over: raises the pen, point up, says nothing, and finishes when the room is quiet. ('Ek minute' is yours, so she never says it.)
Never a rhetorical or a stacked question (those are Mausi's); every question she asks has one answer, and she waits for it.
Days of the week, never a clock time and never 'soon' as a promise: 'by Saturday', 'Thursday evening'. (At a parting she asks 'Agli baar kab?' and waits for a day.)
No exclamation mark anywhere, spoken or typed, not even for 'Ish.' or 'Congratulations.'
catchphrases: THE READBACK: 'So. Keys with you, from tonight. Correct?' | 'तो। चाबियाँ आज रात से तुम्हारे पास। सही?' | 'Toh. Chaabiyan tumhare paas, aaj raat se. Sahi?' (the line people quote back)

THE STATUS PAIR: 'Keys, pending. Envelopes, done.' | 'चाबियाँ अभी बाक़ी। लिफ़ाफ़े हो गए।' | 'Chaabiyan, pending. Lifafe, done.' (writers keep it away from any decision whose cards use keys or envelopes, rule 36)

HER NO: 'Not on the list.' | 'लिस्ट में नहीं है।' | 'List mein nahin hai.' Turned round once, at the first slice, laughing and with no exclamation: 'That wasn't on my list.' | 'ये मेरी लिस्ट में नहीं था।' | 'Ye meri list mein nahin tha.' (None of the three carries a number.)
HER HOUSE RULE: 'Ghar mein thank you nahin chalta.' | 'घर में थैंक यू नहीं चलता।' | 'No thank-yous at home.'
voice.exclamation: 'Ish.' | 'इश्श।' | 'Ish.' (kept as 'Ish.' in English mode too, as her own sound). Her mother's Bengali word, for dismay and sympathy only ('oh no', 'oh dear'): the power cut, a child's fever, a spilt glass, a dropped tray. Never for good news, a laugh or a happy surprise: Hindi-mode players know the coy 'इश्श' of old Hindi films, and on a laugh it would read as that, so at the first slice she just laughs and says the line, and good news gets her home voice. Said flat and low, closed with a full stop, never with '!', never with a giggle or a hand to the mouth. No religious meaning. At most once a scene. Nobody else in the cast uses it, and it leans to one region on purpose, her mother's. Two reader checks: a Bengali reader confirms the sense; a Hindi-first reader confirms it is not heard as ईश ('lord', a word rule 3 bans; ईश has a long ई and one श, इश्श a short इ and a doubled श) and that, kept to dismay, it does not read as the filmi coy sound. Many Hindi-first players may hear the coy 'इश्श' whatever the context, so the fallback for Hindi mode is written and ready, and Hindi mode keeps 'इश्श' only if the Hindi-first reader clears it. 'Ish' stays in Hinglish and English, where the Bengali sense survives. In Hindi mode 'अजीब।' takes its place where the dismay is at a thing ('अजीब। बत्ती चली गई।'); where it is sympathy for a person, Hindi mode drops the sound and opens on the care ('बच्चे का बुख़ार उतरा, भैया जी?', 'आस्तीन गीली हुई? कागज़ मैं उठा लेती हूँ।'), since 'अजीब' said to a sick or upset child sounds like a judgement. If the Bengali reader fails it too, 'Ajeeb.' | 'Odd.' goes into the other two modes the same way. Nobody else in the cast uses 'Ajeeb'.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY, TO FAMILY: plain everyday Hindi, then the right entry at once, aloud: 'Mujhse chhoot gaya, Didi. Shanivaar likhiye.' | 'मुझसे छूट गया, दीदी। शनिवार लिखिए।' | 'I missed that, Didi. Please write Saturday.' SORRY, TO VENDORS AND STRANGERS: the counter's English word, then the fact put right: 'Sorry, Bhaiya ji, mujhse galat likh gaya. Payment Shanivaar ko.' | 'सॉरी, भैया जी, मुझसे ग़लत लिख गया। पेमेंट शनिवार को।' | 'Sorry, Bhaiya ji, I wrote it down wrong. Payment's on Saturday.' Hers is told apart from Mausi's doubled 'Sorry, sorry!' with food and Mama ji's 'Sorry, Didi, poora kasoor mera!' by its size: one plain sentence and the correction, the blame never made bigger. THANKS, GIVEN: to family, plain words, 'Bahut help ho gayi.' | 'बहुत मदद हो गई।' | 'That was a big help.' ('Badi Didi, aapke aane se bahut help ho gayi.'); to her husband, when he turns out right, the everyday 'Maan gayi.' | 'मान गई।' | 'I'll give you that.'; at most once a chapter, the pen comes down on a spoken 'Tick.'; to vendors and strangers, 'Thank you, Bhaiya ji.', English in every mode; to you, besides the words, from Friday she stops reading your plan back, and her typed lists to you lose their 'Correct?' line. THANKS, RECEIVED: from family, the real brush-off of an Indian house, where a thank-you between relatives sounds too formal: 'Ghar mein thank you nahin chalta.' | 'घर में थैंक यू नहीं चलता।' | 'No thank-yous at home.'; from a vendor, 'Thank you, Bhaiya ji.' back. CONGRATULATIONS: 'Congratulations.' in Hinglish and English, 'बधाई हो।' in Hindi mode, with a full stop, then the one practical question she cannot help ('Joining kab se?'). LOVE: plain and short at a parting, once the desk has finished its line: 'Ticket, tiffin, done. Agli baar kab?' | 'टिकट, टिफ़िन, सब रख दिया। अगली बार कब?' | 'Ticket, tiffin, done. When will you come next?', the one question she cannot help, and she waits for a day. Otherwise never in feeling words, and left open: the one line she never ticks, 'Beti ka bag', at the top of every wedding list, and the pen held over it on the wedding evening; Mama ji's item, which she always ticks first, and his hand, the only one allowed to write on her list.

habits: DEVICE: a large-screen smartphone in a plain navy-blue case, text at the normal size, kept in her bag and out only for a call (at her right ear, the pen slid into the clipboard's clip) or for the night's list. Two quick thumbs. A plain power bank for everyone else's phones. In chapter 5 her phone stays off screen, like Mama ji's.

SCRIPT: Roman letters only, in the city's Hinglish: English items and statuses, Hindi people and verbs, and the office verbs with kar ('Rooms done. Chaabiyan kiske paas?', 'Envelopes Tinku ko handover karo'). Never Devanagari, which is too slow for her. Devanagari versions are given in case the owner applies rule 65 to typed messages; they drop the comma between a thing and its status, as her spoken Hindi does. Her lines to you mark no gender ('You take over Thu evening').

FORMAT: one item per line, a capitalised noun and its status symbol, with a comma before any detail ('Keys, yours ✅'). No line numbers and no digits in any message on screen: that is the typing half of the number cap. No full stops at line ends, no whole words in capitals (capitals read as shouting, realism), no exclamation mark. The first line names the list and the day ('Wedding list, Thu'). On every wedding list the second line is 'Beti ka bag', with no symbol, the only line she never gives a status; then 'Papa, trains ✅', the one item she never has to chase. Family lists end on 'Correct?'; vendor lists end on 'Thank you'.

APART FROM THE OTHERS: Papa types single facts with full stops and times, Mummy lowercase one-liners that end on a figure, Tinku lowercase stretched letters and scores, and you the lowercase colon form ('keys: sorted'), which is why her detail takes a comma, not a colon.
STATUS SYMBOLS, her only emoji: ✅ done, ⏳ pending, ❓ not known. No faces and no hands (👍 is Mummy's; the folded hands wait on the owner), no stickers.
VERSIONS: she never sends a correction; she resends the whole list with 'revised' after the day ('Wedding list, Thu, revised'), so the header carries no figure. On screen, one message card at a time.

THE THANK-YOU IN TYPE: from Friday her lists to you drop the closing 'Correct?' line. Nobody else's list ever does. To family she types no thank-you, as she says none; every vendor list ends on 'Thank you'.
TIMING: lists go out at eleven at night, after her shift and dinner; in the day she replies within the minute; if 'Correct?' has no answer, she rings.
VOICE NOTES: never sends one ('you cannot tick a voice note'); when one comes, such as Mausi's long ones, she replies with a summary list of it ending on 'Correct?'.
FORWARDS: none, ever. Her one reply to a forward: a single ✅ under Papa's good-morning flower, every morning, the only reply he gets.
CALLS: Nani is rung, never texted, every evening since May for the BP; vendors are rung first and then sent a list of what was agreed, ending 'Thank you'.
FIGURES: the monthly BP log she sends Nani's doctor is the one thing she types with figures in it, and it stays off screen.
TYPOS: none; she rereads every list before sending; autocorrect on.

ON SCREEN: single messages only, as live text on a painted blank phone or a message card (rules 30 and 40); no app look, no 'forwarded' or 'edited' label, no group chat on screen (owner, 23 Oct). The Sunday list to you is the one worth showing, early in chapter 5 if the writers have room, because it is where the player first sees the line with no status.

test_lines.moment: 1. The lights go out in the middle of dinner. (To you, at the table, while Mama ji goes on eating in the dark; the joke is the picture's, so she says only the plain line. Tests her exclamation at its right size, dismay, and her crisis pace, the same as at tea: the quietest line at the table, and no torch, which five others reach for. In Hindi no comma sits between a subject and its verb. Hindi fallback, ready: 'अजीब। बत्ती चली गई।')
test_lines.en: Ish. The power's gone.
test_lines.hinglish: Ish. Light chali gayi.
test_lines.hi: इश्श। बत्ती चली गई।

test_lines.moment: 2. Someone everyone was waiting for arrives two hours late. (To the cook, the clipboard turned round to face him. Her anger: slower, read from the list, polite to a vendor to the end and closed with her icy counter thanks. No figure: the lateness is told by the meal, not the hours.)
test_lines.en: It's written here, Bhaiya ji: lunch. It's teatime. Thank you.
test_lines.hinglish: Bhaiya ji, yahan likha hai: lunch. Ab chai. Thank you.
test_lines.hi: भैया जी, यहाँ लिखा है: लंच। अब चाय। थैंक यू।

test_lines.moment: 3. A cousin phones to say they have got their first job. (To the cousin, on the line. The home voice: a plain congratulation, the one practical question she cannot help, the answer said back, and a warm word. The cousin's gender stays open: the joining carries the grammar.)
test_lines.en: Congratulations. When's the joining? Monday? Very good.
test_lines.hinglish: Congratulations. Joining kab se? Somvaar? Bahut achha.
test_lines.hi: बधाई हो। जॉइनिंग कब से? सोमवार? बहुत अच्छा।

test_lines.moment: 4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it. (To Mama ji, who made it, as she hands the cup back. A polite no in her own words, and his favourite word, extra, handed back to him.)
test_lines.en: Sugar, extra. Like your guest list. Not on mine.
test_lines.hinglish: Cheeni, extra. Tumhari guest list jaisi. Meri list mein nahin.
test_lines.hi: चीनी एक्स्ट्रा, तुम्हारे मेहमानों जैसी। मेरी लिस्ट में नहीं।

test_lines.moment: 5. In front of the family, someone shows that they had a fact wrong. (She is the one who had it wrong: the cook moved to Saturday, she missed it and told everyone Friday. To Mummy, in front of the family. Her sorry in plain everyday Hindi, then the right entry at once.)
test_lines.en: I missed that, Didi. Please write Saturday.
test_lines.hinglish: Mujhse chhoot gaya, Didi. Shanivaar likhiye.
test_lines.hi: मुझसे छूट गया, दीदी। शनिवार लिखिए।

test_lines.moment: 6. Someone they love is leaving, and they say goodbye on a railway platform. (To the one leaving, at the coach door. The desk finishes its line, then the home voice asks the one question she cannot help, and she waits for a day as the train moves. No status in the goodbye. Tinku's line at the same door opens 'Jaldi aana, yaar.', so hers shares none of its words. The question has no verb, so it holds if the one leaving is you.)
test_lines.en: Ticket, tiffin, done. When will you come next?
test_lines.hinglish: Ticket, tiffin, done. Agli baar kab?
test_lines.hi: टिकट, टिफ़िन, सब रख दिया। अगली बार कब?

test_lines.moment: 7. Someone thanks them for something they did. (To anyone in the family who thanks her, you included. Thanks received: the everyday brush-off of an Indian house, where a thank-you between relatives sounds too formal, and the pen goes back to the list.)
test_lines.en: No thank-yous at home.
test_lines.hinglish: Ghar mein thank you nahin chalta.
test_lines.hi: घर में थैंक यू नहीं चलता।

test_lines.moment: 8. A neighbour passes on a rumour that the corner sweet shop is closing. (To the neighbour who brought it. She judges the talk, never the shop or the person, and checks at the source the way the desk does, a notice on the shop, never proof from the teller. Rule 22 guard: never used in a chapter that holds a report twin. She does not open on Closing?, which three others do.)
test_lines.en: Is it? Status not known. Any notice on the shop?
test_lines.hinglish: Achha? Status not known. Dukaan pe koi notice hai?
test_lines.hi: अच्छा? अभी पता नहीं। दुकान पर कोई नोटिस लगा है?

test_lines.moment: 9. Heavy rain floods the lane outside the house. (To Mummy. Her worry comes out as the insurance claim, her own desk's work and the July list Mummy used line by line, with an office verb on kar.)
test_lines.en: Didi, bills in plastic. Photos, definitely. I'll file the claim.
test_lines.hinglish: Didi, bill plastic mein, photo zaroor. Claim main file karti hoon.
test_lines.hi: दीदी, बिल प्लास्टिक में, फ़ोटो ज़रूर। क्लेम मैं भरती हूँ।

test_lines.moment: 10. Someone asks them how they are. (Asked by the tent man. She files herself as a joke, with no figure, and turns at once to his child, which is quietly about her own.)
test_lines.en: Me? All clear. Did your daughter's result come out, Bhaiya ji?
test_lines.hinglish: Main? Sab clear hai. Aapki beti ka result aaya, Bhaiya ji?
test_lines.hi: मैं? सब ठीक है। आपकी बेटी का रिज़ल्ट आया, भैया जी?

test_lines.moment: 11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table. (To the child, at the same pace as tea. A home moment, so no status pair: the child first, her dismay at its gentlest and the sleeve asked about, then the papers, which she picks up herself, said with its hoon. Hindi fallback, ready: 'आस्तीन गीली हुई? कागज़ मैं उठा लेती हूँ।', with no sound, since 'अजीब' to a child would sound like a scolding.)
test_lines.en: Ish. Did your sleeve get wet? I'll get the papers.
test_lines.hinglish: Ish. Aasteen geeli hui? Papers main utha leti hoon.
test_lines.hi: इश्श। आस्तीन गीली हुई? कागज़ मैं उठा लेती हूँ।

test_lines.moment: 12. A phone call brings good news. (To the room, after the call. Joy in the home voice, with no exclamation, since hers is kept for dismay, and her list turned to joy: the good news goes in at the very top.)
test_lines.en: That's wonderful news. It goes right at the top.
test_lines.hinglish: Bahut achhi baat hai. Isko sabse upar likhti hoon.
test_lines.hi: बहुत अच्छी बात है। इसे सबसे ऊपर लिखती हूँ।

Shanivaar likhiye.' | 'मुझसे छूट गया, दीदी। शनिवार लिखिए।' | 'I missed that, Didi. Please write Saturday.', and the moment now says why it fits (the cook moved to Saturday and she missed it). 'ISH' (real-India note and cast note 7): kept for dismay and sympathy only (test 1, the cook's child's fever, test 11's spilt glass). The first slice is now 'That wasn't on my list.' with no exclamation, as she laughs; test 12's good news drops it too.

COMMON FILLERS ARE FREE (cast note 1): the never list no longer bans achha, arre, chalo, dekho, bas, theek or 'Koi baat nahin'; it bars only other people's owned phrases ('Arre waah.', a one-word 'Theek.' or 'Lo.', 'Bas.' as a closer, 'Suno, suno, suno!'). SHARED BITS (cast note 6), checked against the revised Mummy, Mama ji, Mausi, Nani, Tinku and Mausa ji files: test 12 avoids Mausi's 'Achhi khabar', test 11 avoids 'Koi baat nahin' and 'only water', test 8 avoids 'Band?' and Mummy's shutter, test 2 reaches for no cold food, and test 1 reaches for no torch (Mummy, Nani, Mama ji, Mausa ji and you all have one). URDU-ROOTED WORDS (cast note 8): she now says fikr ('Fikr mat karo.'), zaroor ('photo zaroor', test 9) and yakeen as the town's everyday words.

Always.' are gone, replaced by what an Indian English speaker says: 'No thank-yous at home.', 'I missed that, Didi.', 'Have you had your tea?', 'The power's gone.', 'Me?
