voices.name: You (the player, a voice only)

voice.register: Short, calm and level: the steadiest voice in a loud house, and the one that puts the listener's name on every line, which is how a young person in an Indian home talks to elders (the readers marked it as ringing true). THE SHAPE: one or two short beats (a polite request, an offer, a short closed question, or 'Pehle ___'), with the listener's name on them. In Hinglish and Hindi the name opens the bubble, after it a comma ('Papa, zara dikhaiye.' | 'पापा, ज़रा दिखाइए।'); in English it closes the bubble ('Let me see, Papa.'). Only a small word comes before the name: your exclamation ('Badhiya. Papa, jaldi aaiye.'), a common filler ('Achha, Mummy.', 'Theek hai, Papa.'), or a set English phrase that keeps its own order in every mode ('Thank you, Mausa ji.', 'Good morning, Papa.'). Two to six words a bubble as a rule, eight at most, always inside rule 62's ten; a bigger job never makes a longer bubble, it waits for the next exchange. Your lines carry their verbs: requests end on -iye, offers ask in the subjunctive ('Torch main laaun?'), and comfort lines keep their 'hai' or 'hain' ('Nani, sab yahin hain.'); only questions of fact and the closing 'Sab set.' stay bare. Full stops, not exclamation marks: 'Badhiya.' is said level, and you raise your voice once in the year, at the noise in December ('Ek-ek karke!'). Questions are short and closed and ask for facts, never feelings ('Nani, dard?'). You speak last in an exchange, never open a scene, never speak between a decision's question and its pick, and sit in an outcome beat only as its fixed reply (rules 38 and 42). HOW THIS SHORT VOICE DIFFERS FROM THE OTHER SHORT ONES: Nani's closed fragments carry no name and send 'koi' to do the job; Mausa ji drops the subject and does the job himself; Captain sahab gives the call, then one reason; Tinku ends on a score and 'haan?'; Mami reads your words back and asks 'Correct?'. You name the listener, ask to see, offer rather than announce, and put someone else first. WHEN CROSS: you stay polite (your politeness never rises or falls, unlike Mummy's), but the name stands alone at the front, closed with a full stop, and 'Pehle' names whoever was left waiting or left off ('Mama ji. Pehle Nani se miliye.' | 'Mama ji. Go and see Nani first.'). Your anger is on someone else's behalf, never at a person. BUDGET (proposal, kept from the cast file): three to six `you` bubbles a chapter, at most one a scene, the same whatever the player will pick (rule 38).
voice.mix: You mirror the listener, because being understood by each of them is your job, and that mirror is where most of your words come from. With Nani: plain everyday Hindi with Hindi verbs ('phone kijiye', not 'call kijiye'), and no English beyond her own nouns (doctor, BP, ward, ticket, cake, torch). With Mummy: her shop nouns (shutter, stock, bill, slip) on a Hindi frame, but never her counter verbs for home things ('cup return karo', 'MCB check karo' are hers). With Papa: careful Hindi with his railway English (PNR, coach, berth, confirm) and his 'Reached', which stays in English letters in every mode. With Mama ji: the most English you speak to an elder, and his own words handed back ('sorted', 'Don't worry'). With Tinku: young Hinglish, तुम and -ओ commands, a 'yaar' now and then, her name 'Tinku' (and 'scorer' at most once a chapter, at the moment the scorebook matters), and her scorebook noun 'score'. With Mausi, Mausa ji, Masterji, Captain sahab and Mami: polite Hinglish with -इए, using their own nouns only when you hand one back. YOUR OWN ENGLISH, when nobody sets it: the verbs of the phone and the booking, said with kar or ho the way nearly everyone under fifty says them ('call kijiye', 'video call kar lijiye', 'ticket book kar doon?', 'confirm kar diya', 'score update karo', 'shutter down kar doon?'), always in a shape that marks no gender (a polite command, an offer in the subjunctive, a ने past that agrees with the thing). Mummy turns home things into counter English; you turn family business into phone English, because you are the family's switchboard. YOUR OWN HINDI: everyday Hindustani, with the town's common words ('fikr mat kijiye', 'zaroor', 'waqt') and the fillers everybody says ('achha', 'theek hai', 'arre', 'haan', 'zara', 'bas' inside a line), bent back towards Hindi by a small-town home: the shape of the younger speakers in the Dehradun study (realism notes [1]). In Devanagari 'sorted' and 'set' are both 'सेट', never तय, which means 'decided'. HINDI MODE: lines are rebuilt from shapes that mark no gender (rule 66), never translated word for word, and carry only the English a Hindi-first home already says in Hindi (सॉरी, थैंक यू, सेट, स्टॉक, शटर, टिकट, बर्थ, बुक); a phone verb becomes फ़ोन करो and a congratulation becomes बहुत बढ़िया. Numbers: none in speech in any mode. In a message, digits, and only when the fact is a number (ward 3, bed 12, berth 36, 2 days off).
tics: The name on every line. Hinglish and Hindi: the name first, then a comma ('Nani, sorry.' | 'नानी, सॉरी।'). English: the name last ('Sorry, Nani.'). A set English phrase keeps its own order in every mode ('Thank you, Mausa ji.', 'Good morning, Papa.'). Name first in Hindi also keeps rule 66's third check quiet, since नानी, मौसी, मामी and मौसा जी end in -ी. The only lines without a name are to someone the scene leaves unnamed (a child at the table, a cousin on the phone) and to a group, which you call 'sab' | 'सब' | 'everyone'.

You ask to see before anything, with the 'zara' everyone puts on a polite ask: 'Zara dikhaiye.' In every chapter your first line at the hand-over is 'Let me see' with the giver's name. To Tinku and to children it is 'Zara dikhao', the one place your respect form drops, and readers hear the sibling. Only ever about work handed to you: a list, the slips, a scorebook, a clipboard.

Someone else first: 'Pehle ___'. One thing first, then at most 'phir' and one more ('Tinku, pehle score update karo. Phir chai.'); you never count on to a second or third, so no ordinal ever enters. It is how your fear shows: nobody left waiting, nobody left off.

One phrase for a whole job: 'Sab set.' | 'सब सेट।' | 'All set.', said to the person the job was for ('Nani, sab set.'). Never item by item: Mami itemises ('Keys, pending. Envelopes, done.') and you total.

Asked about yourself, you answer with the same words you close a job with, 'Sab set.', and the asker moves on. The switchboard files itself as a job. It is not a dodge: never turned back on the asker, never a figure, never somebody else's news.

Offers, not announcements: where another voice says what it will do, you ask whether you should, in the subjunctive, which marks no gender in Hindi ('Torch main laaun?', 'Ticket main book kar doon?', 'Shutter down kar doon?'). Nothing about yourself: no line says how you feel or what you want, except the album's one line.

You hand people their own words back, and only to their owner, with the owner's name in the same bubble, at most one line in three: Papa's 'Reached' and his timetable, Mama ji's 'sorted', 'pakka' and 'Don't worry', Tinku's 'score', Masterji's 'naap', Mummy's 'stock' and 'shutter', Captain sahab's 'toss', Nani's 'sach-sach'. Never a figure, never a judging note's words (rules 36 and 38), and never Mami's or Mausi's words, so the two chapters where you work beside them never blur. Typed, you copy each person's way of writing back to them.
Short closed questions for facts, never for feelings: 'Nani, dard?', 'Mausa ji, dawai ka time yaad hai?'. Never two question marks (Mausi's typed '??').
catchphrases: 'Zara dikhaiye.' | 'ज़रा दिखाइए।' | 'Let me see.' (to Tinku and children: 'Zara dikhao.' | 'ज़रा दिखाओ।'). The year's refrain, said to each person who hands you the work: 'Papa, zara dikhaiye.' | 'पापा, ज़रा दिखाइए।' | 'Let me see, Papa.' 'Let me see' is the ordinary English phrase; 'Let's see' sounded like a quiz host (readers). If rulebook Q8 puts it on a button, where 'me' is barred, the English button reads 'Let's have a look, Papa.'. Rule 66: the polite command the rule itself names (लिस्ट दिखाइए). Rule 22: only for work handed over, never in answer to anyone telling of harassment or a dowry demand, where it would sound like asking for proof.
'Pehle ___.' | 'पहले ___।' | '___ first.' Someone else always goes first: 'Chaliye, pehle sab paani pee lein.' | 'चलिए, पहले सब पानी पी लें।' | 'Come on, everyone. Water first.'

'Sab set.' | 'सब सेट।' | 'All set.' The one phrase for a whole job, and your answer when anyone asks how you are. To Mama ji, in his own English: 'Mama ji, sorted.' | 'मामा जी, सब सेट है।' | 'Sorted, Mama ji.', the sentence he most wants to hear (his file). Rule 66: सेट never changes with gender. None of the three carries a number.
voice.exclamation: 'Badhiya.' | 'बढ़िया।' | 'Great.' Said level, with a full stop, never '!'. Straight for good news ('Badhiya. Scorer, khud likho.' | 'Great. Write it yourself, scorer.'), and deadpan when something goes wrong, which is your humour ('Badhiya. Captain sahab, toss andar?' | 'Great. Toss indoors, Captain sahab?'); the readers found both uses real. English mode says 'Great.', which Indian English uses both straight and dry; 'Lovely.' sounded British. For big news it grows by one word ('Bahut badhiya.' | 'बहुत बढ़िया।'). It means 'excellent', an everyday word in every community, and calls on no one; 'Great' carries no hidden god's name either, unlike the mild English exclamations under never. Gender: बढ़िया never changes with gender; rule 66's third check flags it when it ends a sentence (-ा), and a native reader clears it. Nobody else in the cast has 'Badhiya.' or 'Great.' as their exclamation; anyone may still say 'badhiya' inside a line.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: the plain English word, as a young person says it at home, with the name, and then the other person put in the right rather than yourself put in the wrong: 'Nani, sorry. Aap hi sahi thin.' | 'नानी, सॉरी। आप ही सही थीं।' | 'Sorry, Nani. You were right.' (थीं agrees with Nani, not you). One sorry, never tripled and never with food (Mausi's "Sorry, sorry, sorry!"); no blame made bigger (Mama ji's "poora kasoor mera"); no count put right (Tinku's "Sorry, meri galti. 14 nahin, 15."). 'Maaf kijiye.' | 'माफ़ कीजिए।' | 'Sorry to bother you.' is for strangers only (the night nurse, someone at a counter), as it is in life. THANKS: 'Thank you' with the name: 'Thank you, Mausa ji.' | 'थैंक यू, मौसा जी।' | 'Thanks, Mausa ji.' (and he leaves the room). English mode says 'Thanks', so it stays apart from Mami's "Thank you, Bhaiya ji." to vendors. 'Shukriya' | 'शुक्रिया' only to a stranger who has helped; to your own uncle it would sound formal or filmy. THANKED YOURSELF: you turn it away from yourself, plainly, the way the young do with an elder, then send it on to whoever would be left out: 'Mami, mujhe nahin. Pehle Mausa ji ko boliye.' | 'मामी, मुझे नहीं। पहले मौसा जी को बोलिए।' | 'Not me, Mami. Thank Mausa ji first.' (मुझे marks no gender). Never 'Kis baat ka?', which Captain sahab and Tinku say in this moment. The fear of the one left off the list; never Tinku's handing the credit back to the thanker, never the elders' "Isme kya" (Mummy, Mama ji, Mausa ji). CONGRATULATING: the short form your own generation uses, then Nani first: 'Badhiya, congrats. Pehle Nani ko khud call karo.' | 'बहुत बढ़िया। पहले नानी को ख़ुद फ़ोन करो।' | 'Great, congrats. Call Nani yourself, first thing.' ("Badhai ho" is Mummy's and "Congratulations." Mami's, if the owner allows them; "Mubarak ho" stays unused, so the congratulation leans to no one community.) LOVE: never said all year, until the album: Nani counts heads and ends "Aur tum.", and you say the only line of the year about yourself, 'Nani, main bhi.' | 'नानी, मैं भी।' | 'Me too, Nani.' (proposal; cast map owner question 6). All year it shows only as their own love handed back in their own words: Papa's "Reached" asked of Papa ('Papa, pahunchkar "Reached" bhejiye.'), the credit Tinku always gives away given back to her in plain words ('Tinku, ye tumne kiya.'), Nani's plain truth asked of Nani ('Nani, dard? Sach-sach bataiye.'), and Mama ji's own "Don't worry" said back to him at eight in the morning.
uses: Polite requests to every elder, many with 'zara': dikhaiye, dijiye, chaliye, kijiye, baithiye, bataiye, miliye, bhejiye, sunaiye, aaiye, boliye, soiye, so jaiye | दिखाइए, दीजिए, चलिए, कीजिए, बैठिए, बताइए, मिलिए, भेजिए, सुनाइए, आइए, बोलिए, सोइए, सो जाइए
Commands to Tinku, to a cousin your own age and to children: dikhao, batao, likho, rakho, le aao, call karo, update karo | दिखाओ, बताओ, लिखो, रखो, ले आओ, फ़ोन करो

Offers in the subjunctive, the main place 'main' appears: 'Torch main laaun?', 'Ticket main book kar doon?', 'Shutter down kar doon?', 'Kal jama kar doon?', 'Shaam ko call karoon?' | टॉर्च मैं लाऊँ?, टिकट मैं बुक कर दूँ?, शटर मैं गिरा दूँ?, कल जमा कर दूँ?, शाम को फ़ोन करूँ?
English phone and booking verbs with kar or ho, in shapes that mark no gender: call, video call, book, confirm, update, down (a shutter) | Hindi mode keeps बुक and कन्फ़र्म and turns call into फ़ोन

Everyday fillers and Hindustani, free for everyone: achha, theek hai, arre, haan, haan ji, zara, bas (inside a line), fikr mat kijiye, zaroor, waqt, kya pata | अच्छा, ठीक है, अरे, हाँ, ज़रा, बस, फ़िक्र मत कीजिए, ज़रूर, वक़्त, क्या पता

Handed back, to their owners only: 'Reached' and the timetable (Papa), 'sorted', 'pakka' and 'Don't worry' (Mama ji), 'score' (Tinku), 'naap' (Masterji), 'stock' and 'shutter' (Mummy), 'toss' (Captain sahab), 'sach-sach' (Nani)
never: Any Hindi form that marks your gender (rule 66): futures in -ूँगा/-ूँगी, -ोगे/-ोगी, -ेगा/-ेगी, -ेंगे/-ेंगी; मैं आ गया/गई, पहुँच गया/गई, थक गया/गई; कर रहा/रही हूँ; थका/थकी हूँ; अकेला/अकेली; a participle before रहो or रहना (cast note on rule 66's fourth flag); 'Main ready hoon'; 'Call karti hoon' and every English verb with a gendered Hindi tail.
A word that fixes your gender, said by you or accepted from others: beta, beti, bhaiya, didi, bhai, bro (rule 8); no 'bro', 'dude' or 'champ' to anyone, and no 'yaar' to an elder.
How you feel or what you want ('I'm tired', 'I'm fine', 'I'm worried', 'I want'), except the album's one line. Each also invites a gendered Hindi ending.
Turning a question about yourself back on the asker ('You first, Mausi.'), a figure, or somebody else's news in its place.
Any figure in speech: no counts, clock times, prices, scores or ordinals (the cast's two number leaners are Papa and Tinku). 'Ek-ek karke' is an idiom, not a count.
An exclamation mark, except the year's one 'Ek-ek karke!'.

Someone else's set phrase (the common words inside them stay free for you): Nani's 'Bas.' as the closer of an argument, 'Baap re', 'Chai piyo', 'Ab ye bhi', 'Khush raho', jobs sent to 'koi'; Mummy's 'Haan ji, boliye', a bare typed 'haan ji' as a whole reply, 'Had hai', 'Aur kuch?', 'mere khaate mein', 'Badhai ho' and her counter verbs for home things; Papa's 'Kamaal hai', 'Darj hai', 'Noted', and 'Reached?' as your own question; Mama ji's 'Oho', 'Pakka?' closing a worry, 'Ek kaam karo', 'Full'; Tinku's 'Gazab', 'haan?' as a tag, 'Kitaab mein', 'Faisla tumhara', 'Seriously? Phir se?', 'Mera wicket'; Mausi's 'Haaye', 'Suno, suno, suno!', 'Sorry, sorry, sorry!', 'hai na?', '??'; Mausa ji's one-word 'Theek.' and 'Lo.', 'Hain?', 'Isme kya', 'Galti ho gayi'; Masterji's 'Uff', 'Chalo, phir se', 'Jeete raho'; Captain sahab's 'Arre waah' and his calls ('Not out', 'Next ball', 'Well played', 'Front foot'), except one call handed back to him, once, never mocking; Mami's 'Ish', 'Correct?' or 'Sahi?' as a tag, 'Tick', 'done', 'pending', 'Congratulations.', ordinals, numbered or ticked items and the 'thing, status' line.
A blessing to anyone ('Khush raho', 'Jeete raho'): the old bless the young, never the other way round.
तुम to any elder, Mummy and Papa included; तू to anyone.
A card person's name, relation, job, looks, pronoun or note word before or during their decision (rule 36); after a pick, only the fixed template line (rule 38).
Agreement or disagreement with any judging note ('Sahi.', 'Haan, moody hai.', 'Not true.'), a rule for choosing ('Pick the fastest.'), or any line that changes with the pick (rule 38).

Any doubt of a report of harassment or of a dowry demand; the words 'misunderstanding' or 'adjust kar lo' (rule 22). Near a report, none of your fact-checking shapes: not 'Zara dikhaiye' or 'Let me see', not 'Sach-sach bataiye', not 'Kya pata', and no proof word (saboot, likhit, proof, in writing; cast note 5).
'well done', 'oops', 'sorry', 'please' or a joke in a chapter outcome beat (rules 46 and 64).

A god's name or religious exclamation (Hai Ram, Bhagwan, Inshallah, Allah, Rab, Wahe Guru, Oh God, Jesus, Ishwar, Mata ji as a goddess), a mild English word that hides one (Gosh, Goodness, Heavens, Thank God), a caste word or a brand (rule 3); a greeting that leans to one community (Ram Ram, Salaam, Sat Sri Akal): you greet by name or with 'Good morning'.
Mataji, Ammi, Abba, Khala, Mamu (realism notes: these lean towards one community).

MUMMY: 'Mummy' | 'मम्मी', आप and -इए, exactly as to Papa (realism notes [6]).
PAPA: 'Papa' | 'पापा', आप; your yes is 'Ji Papa', and 'Theek hai, Papa' when you take a job on.
MAMA JI: 'Mama ji' | 'मामा जी', आप; your most English, with his own 'sorted', 'pakka' and 'Don't worry' handed back.

TINKU: 'Tinku' | 'टिंकू' by default, the name a sibling uses; 'scorer' | 'स्कोरर' at most once a chapter, only at the moment the scorebook matters (the tease in chapter 4, its payoff in December), so it never turns into a label or into Captain sahab's habit of naming people by their job; तुम and -ओ commands, a 'yaar' now and then; never तू, never 'oye' (hers to you), never bhai, bro, didi or bhaiya. No thumbs-up in your messages to her: to her age it reads cold (her file).
MAUSI | मौसी, MAUSA JI | मौसा जी, MASTERJI | मास्टरजी, CAPTAIN SAHAB | कप्तान साहब, MAMI | मामी: their family name or title and आप with -इए; 'haan ji' or 'zaroor' as your yes to them.
A COUSIN your own age (the phone call in moment 3): तुम and -ओ commands, 'congrats', a 'yaar' now and then; no name unless the scene gives one and no word that gives them a gender.
A CHILD: no name unless the scene gives one, तुम and -ओ commands only ('Pehle haath dikhao.').

MINOR VOICES (the night nurse, the cook, the tent man, neighbours): आप and their name or job word, 'ji' in Hinglish, 'Maaf kijiye' and 'Shukriya' as to any stranger, and no word that gives them a gender the story has not shown.
CARD PEOPLE of any age: first name and आप, only after a pick, in the fixed template ('Mumtaz, station ka kaam aapke naam.').
A GROUP with any elder in it: 'sab', 'Chaliye,' and the polite plural subjunctive ('Chaliye, pehle sab paani pee lein.').
GREETINGS: by name or 'Good morning', in words only; touching feet, a palm on the head or a hand on the shoulder stay between painted people, never towards you (rule 7).

HOW THEY ADDRESS YOU (rule 66): the household says तुम only in commands ('Pehle khao', 'So jao'), 'who should' asks ('Chhat par kaun jaaye?') and lines where you are not the doer ('Faisla tumhara', 'Pen tumhara'); never a future or a past about you (करोगे, आ गए). No family word for you while rulebook Q7 is open, never बेटा, भैया or दीदी. Mama ji calls you 'In-charge' (his file); Tinku uses no word, or 'oye'; Masterji teases once with आप ('Ab toh aap in-charge hain.'); Nani counts you in once, 'Aur tum.'. The game's own voice says आप.

habits: Your phone: a plain smartphone in a plain charcoal-grey case, no sticker or charm, painted only in the present day lying face up on the bedside table, its screen a pale blank glow, every word live text (1.01; rule 30). Never in a hand, never an app's look, an app name, a maker's shape or a 'forwarded' label (rule 3). In a world chapter your messages appear as a plain message card under the panel (rule 40).

You always pick up and never leave a message unanswered; that is why everyone calls you. The story never says when, from where or how fast you answer, so a player on night shifts or an early bus fits (India review). You never write first about yourself.

You mirror each recipient's script and punctuation, which the readers marked as ringing true: a voice note to Nani; Mummy's own lowercase with commas and no full stops; Papa's full stops and one fact a line, so he never reads you as cross; English to Mama ji, one message where he sends five; Tinku's lowercase; sentence case to the chapter voices.

What stays yours whatever the recipient: one message, never a burst; the recipient's name opens it, then a comma (a message is addressed like a letter, unlike your speech, where English puts the name last), except when the first word is their own word handed back or a set phrase ('Reached, Papa.', 'Good morning, Papa.', 'Thank you, Mausa ji.'), and the family group gets no name; no line about yourself; never all capitals (realism notes [9]); never '??' (Mausi's); never a numbered list, a tick or a 'thing, status' item line (Mami's); your closer is 'sab set', so 'done' (Mami's) and a bare 'haan ji' (Mummy's) never need to appear.

Your closer to elders: 'sab set' with a thumbs-up, the one emoji you send (default yellow, no skin tone). To Tinku the same words with no emoji, because to her age a thumbs-up reads cold (her file). No other emoji: the plain smiles are Mausi's and Tinku's; no person, skin-tone hand, coloured heart or folded hands (realism notes 3.2; rule 3). No stickers. In these samples the emoji is written as 👍.

English verbs do your messages' work, as they do in your speech: bare participles that mark no gender ('Reached' to Papa only, his word, in English letters in every mode; 'Booked'; 'Sorted' to Mama ji only), and phone verbs with kar in a ने past or an offer ('confirm kar diya', 'call karoon?'). In Hindi mode the rest is rebuilt from ने pasts that agree with the thing (बिल भेज दिया, छुट्टी ले ली) or no verb, never पहुँच गया/गई.
Sorry and thanks type the way you say them, plain and with the name, in the recipient's own case ('sorry mummy', 'Thank you, Mausa ji.').
Digits only when the fact is a number (ward, bed, berth, days off, the head-count of 14); no prices, no scores, no clock times except when Papa asks for one.
Voice notes: you send them only to Nani, who speaks to her phone rather than typing. Mausi's long voice notes get one typed line back.
Forwards: never. Papa's good-morning picture gets 'Good morning, Papa.' back every morning, with no clock time attached.
No typos. The family group can be mentioned, never shown (owner, 23 Oct; rule 47); if the story needs your post there, it is a single message card.

changed: SORRY (real-India note on the stiff sorry and thanks; cast note 3): 'Maaf kijiye' to your own Nani was what you say to a stranger you bump into. Now the plain English word a young person uses at home, in every mode: 'Nani, sorry. Aap hi sahi thin.' | 'नानी, सॉरी। आप ही सही थीं।' | 'Sorry, Nani. You were right.' (test moment 5; थीं agrees with Nani, not you). It sorts apart from the cast's other plain sorries by what follows it: you put the other person in the right, Tinku puts the count right, Mama ji makes the blame bigger, Mausi triples it over food. 'Maaf kijiye' stays, for strangers only (a new sample to the ward's night nurse).

THANKS (same notes): 'Mausa ji, shukriya.' sounded formal or filmy; now 'Thank you, Mausa ji.' | 'थैंक यू, मौसा जी।' | 'Thanks, Mausa ji.', the set phrase in its own order. 'Shukriya' stays for a stranger who has helped. Being thanked (moment 7) no longer answers thanks with thanks: 'Mami, mujhe nahin. Pehle Mausa ji ko boliye.' | 'मामी, मुझे नहीं। पहले मौसा जी को बोलिए।' | 'Not me, Mami. Thank Mausa ji first.', the thanks turned away from yourself, then sent to the one who would be left out. It avoids the elders' 'Isme kya' (Mummy, Mama ji, Mausa ji).

THE REFRAIN (real-India note): 'Papa, dikhaiye.' becomes 'Papa, zara dikhaiye.' | 'पापा, ज़रा दिखाइए।' | 'Let me see, Papa.' at every hand-over: the everyday 'zara' on a polite ask, and the ordinary English phrase instead of the quiz host's version. Rulebook Q8 bars 'me' on a button, so the English button form is 'Let's have a look, Papa.'. The Tinku hand-over is now its own sample ('Tinku, zara dikhao.').

EXCLAMATION (real-India note): the English-mode exclamation that sounded British becomes 'Great.', which Indian English says both straight and dry ('Great. Toss indoors, Captain sahab?', 'Great. Write it yourself, scorer.'). 'Badhiya.' is unchanged in Hinglish and Hindi, straight and deadpan, both of which the readers found real; 'Bahut badhiya' is added for big news.

FILLERS ARE FREE (cast note 1; real-India note on the most sterile speech): you now say achha, theek hai, arre, haan, haan ji, bas and zara inside a line or before the name ('Achha, Mummy. Pen dijiye.', 'Theek hai, Papa.', 'Arre, theek hai.', 'Bas, Mausi, abhi nahin.', 'Haan, Mama ji. Sab set, pakka.'). The never list no longer bans a single common word: it names only other people's set phrases ('Arre waah', a one-word 'Theek.', 'Bas.' as a closer, 'Suno, suno, suno!', 'Haan ji, boliye', 'Isme kya') and says the common words inside them stay free. You are told apart by the name on every line, the ask to see, the offer in the subjunctive and 'Pehle', not by owning a word.

ENGLISH VERB WITH kar OR ho (cast note 2): your own English is now the phone and booking verbs a 25-year-old uses, always in shapes that mark no gender: 'Nani ko video call kijiye', 'Ticket main book kar doon?', 'Shutter down kar doon?' (moment 9), 'Pehle Nani ko khud call karo' (moment 3), 'score update karo', 'confirm kar diya', 'Shaam ko call karoon?'. Mummy turns home things into counter English; you turn family business into phone English, because you are the switchboard. 'Call karti hoon' and every other gendered tail stay out (rule 66). set.line: Four spoons, Mausi? We'll all get diabetes, haan?

set.moment: 4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it (to Tinku, who made it).
set.line: Tinku, this one's going back. Less sugar, new cup.

set.moment: 7. Someone thanks him for something he did (Nani, for the edge he finished on her shawl). He makes the favour small, plainly; no turn.
set.line: Only an edge, Nani ji. Think nothing of it.

set.moment: 5. In front of the family, someone shows that they had a fact wrong (you were wrong; to Nani, who was right; a plain sorry, and she is put in the right).
set.line: Sorry, Nani. You were right.

set.moment: 10. Someone asks him how he is (you ask; a plain answer, then his knee in depot words; no figure, no dodge).
set.line: I'm fine. Just the knee, in for servicing.

set.moment: 11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table (to the child, his handkerchief already out: the child before the table)
set.line: No problem! Not hurt? Here, take my hanky.

set.moment: 11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table. (To the child, at the same pace as tea. The things first, each with its status, and the child last, as the item that matters, asked with its hai.)
set.line: Papers, safe. Glass, safe. Is your sleeve wet?

set.moment: 1. The lights go out in the middle of dinner (to the table, Nani among them, so 'Rukiye', then to Mausa ji; no exclamation, since 'Arre waah' is only for good cricket; dry humour).
set.line: Hold on. Lineman sahab, you're in.

set.moment: 2. Someone everyone was waiting for arrives two hours late (to the tent man at the gate: people first even when cross, then the run-on breaks into single words with a chop of the hand; no figure; kept as the readers marked it true)
set.line: You're here, bhai? All well at home? Right. Tent. Now.

set.moment: 2. Someone everyone was waiting for arrives two hours late. (To the cook, the clipboard turned round to face him. Her anger: slower, read from the list, polite to a vendor to the end and closed with her icy counter thanks. No figure: the lateness is told by the meal, not the hours.)
set.line: It's written here, Bhaiya ji: lunch. It's teatime. Thank you.

set.moment: 10. Someone asks her how she is (to you; 'Bas' instead of 'I'm fine', then the question goes straight back)
set.line: Enough about me. Tell me your news.

set.moment: 9. Heavy rain floods the lane outside the house. (to the room)
set.line: River in the lane? Notebooks up! Come on, come on!

set.moment: 4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it. (To Tinku, who made it. The plain verdict, then his kind word, then he drinks every drop.)
set.line: Too much sugar, Tinku. It'll do.

set.moment: 6. Someone they love is leaving, and they say goodbye on a railway platform. (to you, as the train starts)
set.line: The 7:25 is moving. I'm here till the last coach goes.

set.moment: 1. The lights go out in the middle of dinner (to the whole table, you among them, so no -ते रहो; no exclamation, since a power cut does not surprise her)
set.line: Someone fetch a torch. The rest of you, eat.

set.moment: 5. In front of the family, someone shows that they had a fact wrong (she is the one corrected; said to the family, you included; check 3 flags अच्छा, a filler, and ग़लती, a noun, so a native reader clears both).
set.line: Oh? My mistake. / Fine, that one's on me.

set.moment: 5. In front of the family, someone shows that they had a fact wrong (Tinku's count was the wrong one; to the family; the readers' line).
set.line: Sorry, my mistake. Fifteen, not fourteen.

set.moment: 8. A neighbour passes on a rumour that the corner sweet shop is closing (to Captain sahab). The turn is to his own fear, on a real collocation (afwaah udna); sweet-shop talk only, never near a report beat.
set.line: Just talk, Captain. Why is it never the ready-made shop?

set.moment: 6. Someone they love is leaving, and they say goodbye on a railway platform (to Papa at the coach door; his own love-word asked of him; kept).
set.line: Send 'Reached' when you get in, Papa.

set.moment: 11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table (to the child, a grandchild at the table; plain comfort; 'khiladi' fits any child).
set.line: Never mind, player. It happens.

set.moment: 12. A phone call brings good news (he rings Mummy first, before anyone, and makes it bigger: the whole lane, sweets on him)
set.line: Oho! Didi! Tell everyone in the lane, sweets are on me!

set.moment: 12. A phone call brings good news. (To the room, after the call. Joy in the home voice, with no exclamation, since hers is kept for dismay, and her list turned to joy: the good news goes in at the very top.)
set.line: That's wonderful news. It goes right at the top.

set.moment: 2. Someone everyone was waiting for arrives two hours late (to Mama ji at the gate; a whisper bubble, the verdict finger up and kept up, no figure; plain Hindi, the old catch as the reason).
set.line: Now? That's how the catch went too.

set.moment: 3. A cousin phones to say they have got their first job (to the cousin: praise made bigger in words, the chain growing to the top; the cousin's gender stays open, since लगी agrees with नौकरी)
set.line: A job? Next a promotion, then higher, then the top!

set.moment: 3. A cousin phones to say they have got their first job. (To the cousin, on the line. The home voice: a plain congratulation, the one practical question she cannot help, the answer said back, and a warm word. The cousin's gender stays open: the joining carries the grammar.)
set.line: Congratulations. When's the joining? Monday? Very good.

set.moment: 10. Someone asks her how she is. (no dodge: she answers plainly; कैसी हूँ and बताती हूँ mark her own gender, which check 2 flags and a native reader clears)
set.line: How am I? I'll tell you! Knee aches, heart doesn't!

set.moment: 11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table (to the child, gently; water is cheap, ghee was dear)
set.line: It's only water. Not ghee. Someone fetch a cloth.

set.moment: 5. In front of the family, someone shows that they had a fact wrong. (He had said the new socket was wired right. To everyone; then he kneels and rewires it while they watch.)
set.line: My mistake. Wired it backwards.

set.moment: 7. Someone thanks them for something they did. (the everyday brush-off, then the next job)
set.line: It's nothing, I do it every day. / Now for the return tickets.

set.moment: 1. The lights go out in the middle of dinner. (to the room)
set.line: Haay! Dark? Never mind! You've still got my voice!

set.moment: 2. Someone everyone was waiting for arrives two hours late (to Mama ji; her cross tell, palm pressed down, no figure)
set.line: Enough. Your plate's gone cold. Sit.

set.moment: 6. Someone they love is leaving, and they say goodbye on a railway platform (to you, at the coach door; check 3 flags करना, an infinitive used as a gentle command, and the Hinglish hai, both of which mark no gender, so a native reader clears them).
set.line: Torch, charger, extension lead, it's all in the bag. / Ring when you get there. Anything else?

set.moment: 6. Someone they love is leaving, and they say goodbye on a railway platform (to you; आना is a command and गिनूँगी is Tinku's own verb; flagged, cleared).
set.line: Come back soon, yaar. I'll be counting the days.

set.moment: 9. Heavy rain floods the lane outside the house. Cross, so the turn stops: the drain, then the cloth to save.
set.line: Uff. Drain's overflowing again. The cloth has to go up.

set.moment: 7. Someone thanks them for something they did (Mami thanks you; you wave it off, as the young do with an elder, and send it on to the one who would be left out).
set.line: What for, Mami? Thank Mausa ji first.

set.moment: 12. A phone call brings good news (to the caller; his exclamation, quiet).
set.line: Arre waah. Right off the middle of the bat.

set.moment: 3. A cousin phones to say they have got their first job (to the cousin on the phone; his once-a-year praise, then an infinitive command, so the cousin keeps no gender).
set.line: Well played. Now stay at the crease.

set.moment: 4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it (to Papa, who made it: he cannot say no, so he asks for more, and the joke is on himself)
set.line: Jija ji, it's practically dessert! A drop more. Don't tell Boss.

set.moment: 4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it. (To Mama ji, who made it, as she hands the cup back. A polite no in her own words, and his favourite word, extra, handed back to him.)
set.line: Sugar, extra. Like your guest list. Not on mine.

set.moment: 11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table. (to the child; लगी agrees with चोट)
set.line: Come, come. Never mind! Did you get hurt?

set.moment: 12. A phone call brings good news (to the caller; the one moment that earns 'Baap re', said low)
set.line: Baap re. Say it again. Slowly.

set.moment: 6. Someone they love is leaving, and they say goodbye on a railway platform. (To one of his grown children at the junction. He thumbs the peel off a sweet lime, sets half on the seat by the window, and walks off down the platform before the train moves, the way he leaves a room when thanked.)
set.line: Here. Half. For the journey.

set.moment: 8. A neighbour passes on a rumour that the corner sweet shop is closing. (to Captain sahab, who brought it; he asks when, then makes a plan for their walk; no proof demanded)
set.line: Really? When does it close, Captain sahab? / We'll go that way on tomorrow's walk.

set.moment: 2. Someone everyone was waiting for arrives two hours late. (to Munna at the gate; louder and faster)
set.line: Munna, Munna! Now you come? Late mark! Hold your ears!

set.moment: 3. A cousin phones to say they have got their first job (to the cousin; a good wish with no religious word in it, and no verb about them, so no gender)
set.line: Well done. The sweets are on you.

set.moment: 10. Someone asks him how he is. Kept as the readers heard it.
set.line: Like my waistcoat. New lining, same old cloth.

set.moment: 7. Someone thanks them for something they did (Captain sahab thanks her for ten years of the book; their cricket, kept).
set.line: That run's yours, Captain sahab. You gave me the book.

set.moment: 7. Someone thanks them for something they did (Mausa ji, at the counter, for the fuses she keeps aside).
set.line: Oh, it's nothing, Jija ji. / Tinku, next customer's bill.

set.moment: 8. A neighbour passes on a rumour that the corner sweet shop is closing (to Tinku; deadpan and practical, with no word on the neighbour or the shop).
set.line: Get the jalebis today, scorer. Just in case.

set.moment: 1. The lights go out in the middle of dinner (to the table). His one mood picture in the set, on a real idiom (munh phulaana).
set.line: Uff. Power's gone. Then again, the clouds sulked all day.

set.moment: 4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it (to Masterji, who made it; a polite no, the reason from the depot).
set.line: Too sweet, Master. Like the depot canteen's.

set.moment: 5. In front of the family, someone shows that they had a fact wrong (it was his; to Mummy: a plain sorry, then the whole blame, no anger at family)
set.line: Sorry, Didi, I had it wrong. All my fault!

set.moment: 5. In front of the family, someone shows that they had a fact wrong. (She is the one who had it wrong: the cook moved to Saturday, she missed it and told everyone Friday. To Mummy, in front of the family. Her sorry in plain everyday Hindi, then the right entry at once.)
set.line: I missed that, Didi. Please write Saturday.

set.moment: 12. A phone call brings good news. (to the room)
set.line: Haay! Good news? Whose? Ours! Tell Amma right now!

set.moment: 7. Someone thanks them for something they did. (Then he stands up and leaves the room.)
set.line: Hmm. It's nothing.

set.moment: 9. Heavy rain floods the lane outside the house.
set.line: The tracks will be under water too. I'll check the 8:15.

set.moment: 3. A cousin phones to say they have got their first job. (to the room, the phone held out; the cousin's gender stays open: लग गई agrees with नौकरी)
set.line: Listen, listen, listen! A job! Didn't I tell you?

set.moment: 4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it (to Mausi, who made it; she pushes the glass back)
set.line: Sugar in the tea? Or tea in the sugar?

set.moment: 11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table (to the child). Comfort first, then a tailor's stain fact; no turn.
set.line: Leave it. Don't be scared. Water doesn't stain.

set.moment: 8. A neighbour passes on a rumour that the corner sweet shop is closing (to Masterji, over the wall).
set.line: Closing? Their shutter went up today, delivery and all.

set.moment: 8. A neighbour passes on a rumour that the corner sweet shop is closing (to Mummy).
set.line: Mummy, that shop's "closed" three times this year.

set.moment: 9. Heavy rain floods the lane outside the house (to Mummy; her shutter, and your offer with an English verb and kar).
set.line: The key, Mummy. Shall I pull the shutter down?

set.moment: 2. Someone everyone was waiting for arrives two hours late (to Captain sahab, who wants to scold). The India reviewer's line, with his 'Dekhiye'; no turn.
set.line: Look, Captain, train must be late. Everything's late in the rains.
